articles.title: From ban to boundaries: how 100 high-impact journals regulate AI-generated images after the 2026 policy shift
articles.authors: Shirley Yang
articles.abstract: Generative AI can draw explanatory figures and can also fabricate research images. We asked how the 100 highest-impact journals regulate AI-generated images and how those rules changed in a year. On 30 September 2026 we captured each journal’s author instructions and the publisher policies they cite. We retrieved archived versions from September–October 2025 and coded rules for five image types. At baseline, 79 journals belonged to publishers that prohibited AI-generated images. Between May and August 2026, Taylor & Francis, Elsevier and Springer Nature replaced these bans with rules that depend on image type. By September 2026, 55 journals explicitly permitted AI-generated explanatory illustrations and 58 permitted AI-assisted data visualisations, usually with disclosure or reproducibility conditions. For 89 journals, AI-created or AI-altered primary research images were prohibited; no journal permitted them. Rules for graphical abstracts and covers varied most. The Science journals, The Lancet family and JAMA Psychiatry still restricted illustrative uses. Twenty-seven journals gave instructions that contradicted or lagged behind their publisher’s current policy, including 20 of 31 Springer Nature journals. Authors need to check journal-level instructions, and publishers need to align them.

articles.title: Whose responsibility is research culture change? Insights from research communities in UK universities
articles.authors: Catherine Davies
articles.abstract: Research culture reform has received fluctuating attention within UK higher education and research funding over the past decade. Given the need to sustain positive research cultures while the sector faces significant financial pressures, it is important to understand which parts of the research system are best placed to set, maintain, and improve research culture. This study reports findings from semi-structured interviews with UK researchers and university professional services staff (n = 30), analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants described a hierarchical model of responsibility spanning individual researchers, principal investigators, research groups, universities, and funders. Although many favoured a shared responsibility model, meaningful systemic change was seen to depend disproportionately on funders and research organisations, whose levers operate at scale and whose interface represents a critical locus for change. We argue that responsibility should be distributed according to power, recognising that research culture cannot be improved through individual goodwill or local initiatives alone. We further argue that institutions require the organisational capability to operationalise this responsibility, with greater attention to the translation layers linking funder incentives, institutional resources, and everyday research practice. These findings have direct implications for how research funding and research-performing organisations design, resource, and evaluate research.

articles.title: Repurposing, redefining, and reimagining: A paradigm shift towards person-driven neuroscience in the digital age
articles.authors: Becky Inkster; Mark Sheppard
articles.abstract: The focus of neuroscience has traditionally hinged on collecting quantifiable physiological data that are often distanced from the lived experiences of people. In contrast, qualitative, subjective, and situational information provides rich context, but lacks the empirical precision needed to map to neural processes. To reconcile this gap, we established ‘The Lαβ’ as an interdisciplinary initiative that fuses person-driven experiences, personal reflection, and empirical neuroscience. People engage with their chosen experiences in their chosen settings while wearing a portable EEG headset. Timestamped information is then collected from a variety of sources. We introduce our novel neurotriangulation approach: A person‑driven synthesis of quantitative electrophysiological signals, qualitative observations, and subjective and situational information into a single analytic stream. Our aim is to provide people with opportunities for neuro-self-reflection. We use an ethics-first approach to preserve data sovereignty, privacy, autonomy, and agency for the individual. In this paper, we present real-world case studies to demonstrate our data collection, real-time field analysis, and co-interpretation methodologies. These case studies also underscore the neurotriangulation model as an approach to move beyond reductive, data-centric models toward a person‑driven paradigm. This shift allows neurodata to be more accessible, inclusive, and personally meaningful, while prioritising safety and subjectivity. This has the potential to reshape how we think about neuroscientific applications in fields such as education and training, anthropology, creative arts, wellbeing, and mental health. By repurposing and redefining the use of extant neurotechnology, we are reimagining a future in which our understanding of ourselves is person-driven, reality-based, and ethically sound.

articles.title: Short-term Cultural Evolution in Response to COVID-19:  Integrating Quantitative Analysis with AI-Assisted Thematic Analysis
articles.authors: Aiya Wang; Patricia M. Greenfield
articles.abstract: Using Greenfield’s Theory of Social Change, Cultural Evolution, and Human Development as a framework, we examine psychological, cultural, and behavioral shifts in China during the first 70 days of COVID-19. We focus on three levels—mortality salience at the psychological level, collectivism at the cultural level, and subsistence activities at behavioral level. Our big-data sample consists of over 200,000 social media posts. Quantitatively, we found a significant increase in mentions of mortality salience, collectivism, and subsistence activities, consistent with prior results established in the U.S., Mexico, Indonesia, and Japan, suggesting a universal response to existential threat. Qualitatively, AI-assisted thematic analysis, an innovation of the present study, identified the most frequent recurring themes across three levels, which complemented the quantitative analysis by providing in-depth insight into the COVID experience. A methodological strength was to compare expert human coder to AI coding, establishing both the reliability and validity of AI coding.

articles.title: A Community-Based Implementation of The Family Check-up Is Associated with Lower Pediatric Emergency Room Utilization and Acute Care Services: A Health Service Utilization and Cost Analysis Study
articles.authors: Maria Schweer-Collins; Jonathan Woodward; Elizabeth Stormshak
articles.abstract: A large number of studies have shown that the brief three session Family Check-Up intervention is effective in promoting children’s social and behavioral development and in reducing problem behaviors. Research in this area has begun to examine the effectiveness of this program through real-world implementation studies. This brief report describes how a community-based implementation of the Family Check-Up is associated with reduced healthcare utilization, specifically acute care services including emergency department, inpatient, and urgent care utilization. Future implementation trials may benefit from including administrative data to examine the outcomes of the Family Check-Up in conjunction with cost and service utilization data.

articles.title: Embodied mirroring increases interpersonal synchrony of movement and positive experience in subsequent conversations
articles.authors: Yasemin Abra; Christine Falter-Wagner; Irene Sophia Plank
articles.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony, the alignment of behaviours between individuals, plays a key role in social interactions. The degree of synchrony depends on many factors, including interaction partners, context, and goals. Brief playful warm‑ups may prime synchrony and improve subsequent conversations between strangers. We used the Mirror Game, a fundamental exercise from theatre where two players nonverbally imitate each other’s movements, to examine whether instructed interpersonal synchrony of movement would carry over to spontaneous interpersonal synchrony. We used recordings of facial expressions, gaze patterns, movement, and speech to capture multi-modal conversational behaviour. In line with our preregistered hypothesis, dyads who played the Mirror Game before conversing exhibited greater interpersonal synchrony of movement than those who performed a non-social movement exercise. Furthermore, playing the Mirror Game prior to the conversation also increased positive social experience and rapport. Exploratory analyses also revealed that conversational behaviour capturing interpersonal adaptation of the individual predicted social experience in the conversation. While these effects may not be specific to the Mirror Game, we argue that the embodied, collaborative and improvising nature of the Mirror Game make it a promising tool for fostering positive social interactions. These findings may inform interventions for populations with reduced interpersonal synchrony, such as individuals with autism.

articles.title: From Exposure to Experience: Measuring Gaze-Based Visual Experience with Faces During Naturalistic Viewing
articles.authors: Nitzan Guy; Guy Malka; Galit Yovel
articles.abstract: Research across face recognition, social cognition, and clinical psychology treats visual experience as a primary mechanism for learning and successful categorization. As the field has shifted toward naturalistic, dynamic stimuli, there is a need to dissociate between exposure, which is the amount of time a target is presented, and experience, which is the amount of time an observer is looking at a certain target. Here, we present a pipeline that dissociates exposure from experience with faces during naturalistic viewing of a movie with multiple characters. This is achieved by combining screen-based eye tracking with deep neural network-based face detection and recognition to measure each participant's gaze-based visual experience with faces during naturalistic viewing, on a frame-by-frame basis. With a sample stimulus, we benchmarked our pipeline as an identity exposure extractor and achieved high face detection (~98%) and face recognition (85-88%) accuracies. In a proof-of-concept experiment, participants watched two episodes of a television series while their gaze was recorded. Our pipeline revealed participants looked at individual characters for less than 27% of their appearance time on average indicating that character appearance time overestimated participants' actual visual experience. Moreover, participants showed reliable individual differences in face-directed gaze, both in overall face-viewing tendencies and in character-specific preferences, with stable idiosyncratic preferences emerging when two characters competed for visual attention. Together, these findings demonstrate a meaningful gap between exposure and idiosyncratic gaze-based visual experience, highlighting the importance of dissociating experience from exposure when studying the role of visual experience in naturalistic viewing.

articles.title: Delegating Knowledge: Belief in AI Sufficiency and its Consequences for How People Process Information
articles.authors: Sangwon Lee; Sebastián Valenzuela
articles.abstract: Generative AI produces information on demand, raising the question of why one would ever learn something that a chatbot can always retrieve. In this paper, we introduce Belief in AI Sufficiency (BAS): the belief that acquiring and retaining knowledge is less valuable because AI can provide it when needed. BAS represents a qualitatively distinct conceptual domain from the Google effect, cognitive offloading, and the “News Finds Me” perception. Using four preregistered studies in the United States (development, N = 307; validation, N = 903; experiment, N = 767; test-retest, N = 298), we present evidence for a 12-item BAS measure with a strong general factor structure. In the validation survey, higher BAS was associated with greater reliance on heuristic and less systematic processing, and with reduced factual knowledge. In the experiment, BAS strongly predicted the likelihood to delegate a learning task to AI. The relationship between BAS and the gap between self-reported and measured knowledge was smaller, reflecting reduced accuracy rather than an illusion of knowledge. Finally, BAS scores were approximately equal in mean level and showed moderate rank-order stability across a 3-month period. BAS is one way to measure how far AI is becoming central to the study of how people learn.

articles.title: Fact-Checking Using AI
articles.authors: Thomas Renault; Mohsen Mosleh; Hause Lin; Gordon Pennycook; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can both correct inaccurate beliefs (1, 2, 3) and manipulate attitudes (4, 5, 6). As LLMs are increasingly deployed as fact-checkers on social media, their impact depends not only on the models’ technical capability, but also on the choices of their designers and the attitudes and behaviors of platform users. Here, we shed light on all three dimensions of this sociotechnical system. We analyze an exhaustive sample of 1,555,281 English-language fact-check requests sent to Grok and Perplexity bots on X from February through September 2025 and a random sample of 184,124 fact-checks from Grok from September 2025 to August 2026. We also benchmark 19 frontier LLMs against professional fact-checkers’ evaluations of hundreds of news headlines, and conduct a preregistered survey experiment (N=1,592) to evaluate correction efficacy. On the user side, Grok requesters skew heavily Republican; familiarity with and trust in specific LLMs vary substantially, such that trust in AI is no longer a unitary construct; and revealing that a fact-check comes from Grok reduces belief updating among Democrats while increasing belief updating among Republicans. Examining LLM outputs, we find that from a technical perspective, LLM fact-checks can match or exceed agreement among professional fact-checkers. Yet we also show that this capacity is readily undermined by designers’ choices: for example, restricting sources (e.g. Truth Social AI) or disabling search can degrade accuracy. Designers and users, more so than technical capability, are now the primary binding constraints.

articles.title: Gender bias across LLMs is common and highly heterogeneous
articles.authors: Edoardo Bolzoni; Valerio Capraro
articles.abstract: Understanding gender biases in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important as these systems become embedded in decision-support tools with real consequences. Prior research has focused only on a small set of models, leaving open the extent to which gender biases are common and heterogeneous across LLMs. We address this gap across ten models released between April 2025 and June 2026, spanning nine vendors, using two paradigms: gender attribution to stereotyped phrases (Study 1) and moral judgment of abuse or torture against a woman or a man to prevent a catastrophic outcome (Study 2). In Study 1, two of ten models attributed masculine-stereotyped phrases to female writers more often than the reverse, while three models showed the opposite pattern. In Study 2, several models converged on a male-disadvantaging asymmetry that was directionally consistent with a documented human tendency to protect female targets from harm, though the specific conditions under which this asymmetry emerged varied by model; three other models, by contrast, showed no variation across conditions. These results indicate that gender-related biases are common in LLMs. Their direction and magnitude, however, are highly heterogeneous, to the point that some models behave in diametrically opposite ways to others. Bias auditing should therefore be treated as an ongoing, multi-vendor process, rather than a one-time assessment.

articles.title: The Moral Mechanism of Norms and Political Polarization
articles.authors: Julie Maria Ejby Pedersen; Adam Moore
articles.abstract: Political polarization continues to divide people across the world, threatening the safety of individuals and of democracy. We propose a theoretical account of the emergence and maintenance of political polarization as a social identity phenomenon, driven by moral values as an ingroup norm representation. Norms play a crucial role in intergroup processes as a representation, both supporting signaling and inference of ingroup membership, and approximating a shared concept of the group that needs to be inferred and updated itself. Yet, little work on political polarization has addressed the role of norms, despite a large literature on its social identity mechanisms. Here, we argue that moral values are highly suitable as an ingroup norm representation and implement this as a formalized computational account of echo chamber formation. In this model, we also account for the cyclical interaction between these social identity pressures on moral values and moral cognitive processes such as moral disengagement and moral drift. When simulating this model under different conditions (Study 1 and 2), we find systematic differences in how liberals and conservatives form groups, corresponding to empirical investigations of interactions with people and news online. We discuss how the resulting polarization emerges as an interaction between the structure of liberal and conservative moral values, observed in empirical data, and their role as an ingroup norm representation. Finally, we consider how this moral mechanism of political polarization influences how we study political polarization, and we posit that liberals and conservatives may have different pathways to political polarization.

articles.title: Grounding-Specific Effects of Valence in Word Recognition: Evidence from Pain-Related Language.
articles.authors: Eleonora Borelli; Riccardo Costantini; Elena Bandieri; Mario Luppi; Leonardo Potenza; Francesca Pesciarelli
articles.abstract: Affective valence is widely regarded as a core organizing dimension in word recognition, yet findings on its role remain inconsistent. We argue that this inconsistency reflects a longstanding operationalization of valence as a domain-general signal. Using pain-related language as a test case, where physical and social pain words share conceptual and affective features but diverge in their dominant experiential grounding, we examined whether valence differentially modulates lexical access as a function of grounding type. Reaction times from a lexical decision task were modeled using multiple regression, testing interactions between pain type and valence alongside other semantic and lexical predictors. Greater negative valence predicted faster lexical access for social pain words, whereas no valence effect emerged for physical pain words, and this dissociation was statistically significant. No other predictor showed a significant interaction with pain type. These findings indicate that valence operates as a grounding-specific facilitator rather than a domain-general signal, and align with multiple representation frameworks in which affective, sensorimotor, and social dimensions interactively ground conceptual knowledge.

articles.title: “It’s not that I don’t have a life, it’s that I choose to have many”: A Qualitative Exploration of Video Gamers’ Perceived Motivations for Gaming and their Impact on Psychological Health.
articles.authors: George Farmer; Tom Buchanan; Nina Smyth; Tina Cartwright
articles.abstract: While several factors have been highlighted as either facilitators or inhibitors of basic psychological needs in video gaming, there is little evidence to identify the specific mechanisms by which these effects operate. Using qualitative semi-structured online interviews with 15 video game players (MAge = 38.28, SD = 12.65) and analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis, this study explored experiences in video games and gaming culture that provided either a source of need satisfaction or need frustration. Participants discussed experiences that provided a sense of competence, mood management, social connection, and positive disengagement, as well as experiences that could be unfair, unpleasant, toxic, or generally stress-inducing. This study highlights specific factors that promote positive well-being and contribute to negative well-being in players and illustrates less-explored experiential factors that are vital to video gaming as a psychologically restorative activity.

articles.title: Acoustic correlates of allophonic versus phonemic dimensions in monolingual and bilingual infants' input
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Amanda Seidl; k onishi; Golnoush Alamian; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract:
Allophones are diverse phonetic instantiations of a single underlying sound category. As such, they pose a peculiar problem for infant language learners: These variants occur in the ambient language, but they are not used to encode lexical contrasts. Infants' sensitivity to sounds varying along allophonic dimensions declines by 11 months of age, suggesting that there must be information to phonological status available to pre-lexical infants. The present work tests one specific type of information: acoustic implementation. It was hypothesized that the acoustic
distance between two vowel categories is smaller when the dimension along which the two vowels differ is allophonic (e.g., vowel nasality in American English, vowel tenseness in Quebec French) compared to when it is phonemic (e.g., vowel tenseness in American English, vowel nasality in Quebec French). Monolingual mothers speaking either English or French and bilingual mothers speaking both languages were recorded while they described objects to their 11-month-olds. Results provided weak support for the main hypothesis.

articles.title: The Association Between Family-Related Variables and Cross-Cultural Adaptation: A Meta-Analytical Review and Migrant Family Adaptation Framework
articles.authors: Kinga Bierwiaczonek; Aisha Vogel; Dinh-Hung Vu; Colleen Ward; Rongtian Tong; Mike W.-L. Cheung; Nora C. G. Benningstad; Evita Willemiek van Duin; Karine Lindholm; Jonas R. Kunst
articles.abstract: With global migration at an all-time high, understanding the role of family-related factors in cross-cultural adaptation is crucial yet underexplored. This paper proposes a new Migrant Family Adaptation Framework and reports a meta-analysis of the association between a large set of family-related variables and cross-cultural adaptation with data from 449 studies (Nparticipants = 308,335; neffects = 1,174) conducted between 1988 and 2022. Specifically, we tested nine broad categories of family-related variables underpinning key processes of family resilience (family cross-cultural adjustment, family functioning, lack of family-work conflict, family support, contact with family, presence of family, relationship status, family characteristics, and family attitudes towards living abroad) and three adaptation outcomes (overall, psychological, socio-cultural). Three-level models showed that family cross-cultural adjustment was the strongest and most consistent predictor of migrants’ overall, psychological, and socio-cultural adaptation. In terms of more nuanced sub-indicators, family satisfaction, spousal support, low family conflict, and positive family attitudes towards living abroad showed robust effects. Effects were comparable across migrant, refugee, student, and expatriate samples, except that the effect of family support was stronger for expatriates than migrants, whereas family presence mattered more for migrants than expatriates. Comprehensive sensitivity checks (excluding studies at risk of bias, unpublished reports, and statistical outliers) left the pattern and magnitude of effects virtually unchanged. No evidence of small-study or publication bias was observed. Theoretical implications in light of the new theoretical framework, directions for future research, and policy implications are discussed.

articles.title: Fifteen Years of Child-Centered Long-Form Recordings: Promises, Resources, and Remaining Challenges to Validity
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Loann Peurey; Marvin Lavechin; Tarek Kunze; Manel Khentout; Lucas Gautheron; Emmanuel Dupoux; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Audio-recordings collected with a child-worn device are a fundamental tool in child language research. Long-form recordings collected over whole days promise to capture children’s input and production with minimal observer bias, and therefore high validity. The sheer volume of resulting data necessitates automated analysis to extract relevant metrics for researchers and clinicians. This paper summarizes collective knowledge on this technique, providing entry points to existing resources. We also highlight various sources of error that threaten the accuracy of automated annotations and the interpretation of resulting metrics. To address this, we propose potential troubleshooting metrics to help users assess data quality. While a fully automated quality control system is not feasible, we outline practical strategies for researchers to improve data collection and contextualize their analyses.

articles.title: Do we hear and read the same? Attention to detail in narrative storytelling while reading and listening with reduced distraction
articles.authors: David Berga; Benan Demir; Anita Dieckhoff; Monica Moreno-Dionis
articles.abstract: Most research agrees that reading and listening are equally efficient. But research on multimedia learning searched for modality specific processes that could improve learning efficiency, this is relevant considering the current panorama and worldwide usage of intelligent text-based agents. Our brief study compares the audio-verbal channel with the visual-verbal channel, facilitating exact wording identification after a reading or a listening task. We focus on comparing reading and listening overall performance, but also category specific performance by modality. Twenty-six native Spanish speakers read one text and listened to another one. Each text had five instances of each word category (color, feeling, object and person) and there were 3 questions per category. Each question framed 3 possible answers and the participants had to recognize which one was correct. We tested if the correct answers were recognized and whether abstract or concrete concepts or specific word categories affected encoding. We minimized distraction for both modalities and standardized the word rate, to avoid text backtracking. Results have shown that for non-demanding material, there isn't a significant difference in regard to input modality. Both reading and listening modalities are not effectively different, and processing of category-specific wording is not either.

articles.title: TAIL: A Test of AI Literacy for Adolescents and Teachers
articles.authors: Tomas Lintner; Ivan Ropovik; Lukas Plch; Adam Klocek; Libor Juhaňák
articles.abstract: Most instruments that claim to measure AI literacy inquire how competent people feel rather than test what they know, and almost none has been validated for both students and teachers. We developed the Test of AI Literacy (TAIL), a multiple-choice test of AI literacy built on an established four-aspect framework and piloted with cognitive interviews and item analysis. We evaluated it among Czech secondary-school students tested in fall 2025 (n = 2,441) and six months later (n = 1,669; 897 linked across the two measurement waves), and among teachers (n = 564). In every sample the items fitted a one-factor model, whereas the four content aspects could not be distinguished as separate factors. Three weakly discriminating items were removed after the first wave, leaving a 17-item form with internal consistency of .79 to .87 and item response theory reliability of .80 to .84. Item parameters were almost identical across waves. Six-month test-retest reliability was .63, with a standard error of measurement of 2.4 points. Teachers scored .41 standard deviations above students, and teachers of information and communication technologies, grammar-school teachers, and students with a university-educated parent scored higher, as predicted. Teachers' self-rated AI self-efficacy was practically unrelated to their tested knowledge, and students who used and relied on AI more knew less about it. TAIL is a short, knowledge-based measure that places adolescents and their teachers on one scale.

articles.title: Trilingual language control – interference patterns in mixed ability speakers reveal a complex interaction between age of acquisition and proficiency
articles.authors: Maya Thille; Sophie Slaats; Alexis Hervais-Adelman
articles.abstract: A widely accepted framework in multilingual control is the inhibitory control model (ICM, Green, 1998). According to this framework, the level of inhibition required to suppress a language is dependent upon the dominance of that language, such that a more dominant language requires more inhibition. A study by de Bruin and colleagues (2023) evaluated L1 and L3 intrusions in L2 target trials in a speeded trilingual picture naming task, reporting more intrusions from L3 than L1, consistent with lower inhibition of L3. Here, we expand on this and investigate whether patterns of cross-linguistic interference and reaction times (RT) in all three languages can be accounted for by the ICM. Furthermore, we explore how proficiency and age of acquisition (AoA) influence these patterns. Sixty-nine participants with some proficiency in English (NL1=22), French (NL1=21), and German (NL1=26) completed a trilingual speeded picture naming task. Patterns of intrusions did not fully align with a dominance-based inhibitory account: L2 produced more intrusions than (expected) L3 in L1 target trials. Analysis of the role of proficiency and AoA showed that intrusions are more likely between languages with similar proficiencies and AoAs, with an interaction such that languages with mismatched profiles (early AoA/low proficiency or late AoA/high proficiency) are most likely to intrude. RT patterns revealed asymmetric switch costs and a large influence of AoA. The pattern of results points to the need for a more nuanced understanding of the factors influencing how languages are accessed and controlled, beyond the construct of an ordinal dominance hierarchy.

articles.title: Her Canvas, Her City: Gender, Gaze, and Empowerment in Art Engagement Among Women Artists and Viewers in Pune, India
articles.authors: Sakina Bharmal; Samrddhee Pathare; Tanvi Raghuram; Esha Phadke; Prafull Botre; Nishkala Reddy; Tithi Roy; Madhura Deshmukh; Sanjana Edwankar; Raju Sutar
articles.abstract: Feminist visual theory holds that the devaluation of women’s art is reproduced not only by institutions but by how people look. We report a preregistered, mixed-methods study in Pune, India, connecting women artists’ lived experience with viewers’ perceptual responses. In an online experiment, 49 viewers (30 women, 18 men, 1 non-binary person) rated 12 artworks (7 by women, 5 by men) without knowing the artist’s gender, on liking, objectification, empowerment, immersion, and emotion. Neither artist gender nor viewer gender significantly predicted objectification, empowerment, or liking, although descriptive trends favoured works by women. Art experience was the most consistent predictor of engagement. Viewers who reported immersed rather than detached enjoyment perceived depicted subjects as more empowered (p < .001), consistent with feminist critiques of disinterested spectatorship. Exploratory analyses showed that closer alignment between artists’ stated intentions and viewers’ interpretations predicted transcendence-related responses, resonating with the rasa concept of the attuned viewer (sahṛdaya). Thematic analysis of interviews with 37 women artists showed that becoming, remaining, and being recognised as an artist depends on unequally distributed access, the continual negotiation of gendered expectations, and audiences and markets that confer legitimacy unevenly. Implications for feminist psychology, empirical aesthetics, and arts practice are discussed.

articles.title: Embodied Copresence Confers No Advantage Over Screen-Based Delivery in Robot-Facilitated Language Learning
articles.authors: Nathan Caruana; Aitor Miguel Blanco; Emily S. Cross
articles.abstract: The past decade has seen growing interest in deploying social robots as assistive technologies in educational settings. Key unresolved questions concern the extent to which, and possibly when, the embodied copresence of a robot confers benefits over screen-based alternatives. This is an issue with applied significance given the logistical and cost constraints of deploying physical robots at scale. In a preregistered between-subjects experiment, 40 adults completed a Spanish language learning task alongside a Pepper humanoid robot that was either physically co-located next to participants (Embodied, n = 20) or presented via live video feed on a large screen next to participants (Screen, n = 20). Contrary to our predictions, conditions did not differ on any objective measure of task engagement (accuracy, completion time, voluntary continuation), self-report indices (enjoyment, difficulty), attention allocation to the robot or task (subjectively coded gaze orientation), or validated measures of robot perception and affiliation (Godspeed questionnaire; Self-in-Other scale), with the exception of greater perceived task difficulty and robot awareness in the Embodied than Screen condition. Reflexive thematic analysis of post-task interviews identified three cross-condition themes: robot learning companions (1) create experiences of invigilation; (2) are expected to fulfil multiple social roles (motivational coach, tutor, and companion); and (3) are expected to interact in a human-like, intelligent, and adaptive manner. These findings suggest that, for adult learners engaged in short-duration tasks, such as the simple language-learning task explored here, screen-based delivery may be functionally equivalent to physical co-presence, with implications for the scalable deployment of social robots in educational contexts.

articles.title: Liberal paternalism: Weak-victim narratives facilitate the disempowering treatment of refugees and low-income individuals
articles.authors: Christina Bauer; Steve Rathje; Gregory M Walton
articles.abstract: Refugees, low-income individuals, and other groups that are systemically disadvantaged often show substantial strength and agency, including in contending with the adversity they face. Yet, media, politicians, and other stakeholders sometimes portray these individuals as weak and passive victims. In eight studies (Ntotal=226 newspaper articles & 1,895 participants in the UK, US, & Australia) focused primarily on refugees (Studies 1-4), and secondarily on low-income individuals (Studies 5a-b), we show that i) weak-victim narratives are common in both media portrayals and mental representations, especially in liberal (vs. conservative) media and minds (Studies 1-2c & 5a), and ii) that weak-victim narratives facilitate functionally disempowering behaviors among liberals (Studies 3, 4, & 5b).

articles.title: Adolescent anxiety and gaming: a case study of stability loops
articles.authors: Tiina Auranen; Roope Holopainen; Veli-Matti Karhulahti
articles.abstract:
This research presents two longitudinal case studies of intensively gaming adolescents who 
express clinically significant anxiety symptoms in the Finnish cultural context. By means of 
Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, two shared themes were constructed based on in-depth 
qualitative data from both participants: self-reinforcing loop between interpersonal problems and 
gaming, and self-reinforcing loop between lacking affordances and gaming. Collectively, the themes 
point at a developmental mechanism that we call stability loops: anxiety-gaming interactions that 
minimise changes over time in socioecological systems. These exploratory findings highlight how 
individual experiences of circumstances create potentially different loop trajectories, which can both 
complicate and support age-relevant development depending on the social context. As such, the study 
offers an alternative to diagnostic gaming frameworks by modelling the activity as a part of 
psychological development in a world where technology is rapidly evolving and ubiquitous.

articles.title: From what they hear to what they say: The distribution of word classes in the output of young English-speaking children and their caregivers
articles.authors: Antje Endesfelder Quick; Karsten Schmidtke-Bode
articles.abstract: Usage-based approaches propose that children assimilate the statistical regularities of their input. While prior studies have documented such input–output correlations for specific constructions, more systemic properties like word-class distributions have received less attention. The present study examines twelve English-speaking children aged two to three from the Manchester Corpus, comparing their part-of-speech (POS) distributions with their mothers' at three time points. Maternal distributions remain highly stable; children's speech is initially noun-heavy but approaches maternal patterns by age 2;9. These findings suggest that, even at more abstract levels of grammatical organization, children's developing grammars reflect the distributional properties of their input.

articles.title: Metacognitive Ownership in Human–AI Regulation: Construct Definition, Boundaries, and a Research Agenda
articles.authors: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin; Daniel H. Chang
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can suggest criteria, evaluate learners’ work, and recommend or carry out revisions, yet it is often unclear how learners direct these decisions when they study with AI. In this conceptual paper, we introduce metacognitive ownership: learners’ governance of standards, evaluative judgments, and actions within a learning episode in which AI or another external source contributes to at least one of these functions. Here, governance refers to how learners direct the use of that contribution. Drawing on self-regulated learning, human–AI regulation, agency, and evaluative judgment, we define three components: standards appropriation, monitoring-judgment governance, and control authorization. These components address the criterion a learner uses, how the learner reaches an evaluation, and what guides the next action. Control authorization also requires a realistic opportunity to act differently. A hypothetical example illustrates how a learner can evaluate AI advice and reach an incorrect conclusion, or accept correct advice without examining it. After distinguishing metacognitive ownership from related constructs, we set out four principles for interpreting evidence about each component. We then offer two tentative propositions about later advice decisions and continued learner regulation when support is reduced. The research agenda asks whether these interpretations are reproducible, add to existing explanations, and withstand evidence that challenges them. The framework provides a basis for examining learner-governed assistance; its relationships with learning require empirical evaluation.

articles.title: Motivational and Consummatory Anhedonia Represent Distinct Affective and Behavioral Responses to Effortful and Rewarding Activities in Daily Life
articles.authors: Tatiana Pillsbury; Samantha A. Betters; Marta Migo; Shiyin Liu; Aje Oluwagbohunmi; Sarah Etuk; Wenwu Sun; Caroline Conway; Michael Tilghman Treadway; Jessica Cooper
articles.abstract: Anhedonia is a common psychiatric symptom defined as a loss of interest in or ability to enjoy previously rewarding activities. Although early definitions of anhedonia conceptualized it as a unitary construct, more recent formulations have emphasized the potential importance of distinguishing changes in motivation (motivational anhedonia; “MA”) from changes in hedonic capacity (consummatory anhedonia; “CA”). Evidence for these two domains has been derived from animal models highlighting distinct neurobiological pathways supporting motivational and hedonic responses, as well as human behavioral and pharmacological work highlighting distinct effects of these pathways on motivated and consummatory behavior. While this foundational work has been broadly supportive of the distinction between MA and CA, it remains unknown whether these two domains produce clinically meaningful differences in lived experience of daily activities. In the current work, we used an experience sampling approach in 162 adults (48.7% with current anhedonia as determined by clinical interview) to determine whether self-reported differences in MA and CA severity would be differentially associated with effort and reward levels of activities planned and completed in daily life. Consistent with the hypothesis that MA and CA are meaningful constructs, we observed markedly different associations with behavior in daily life. While elevated MA was associated with effort aversion, higher CA was associated with selective deficits in selecting rewarding activities. Moreover, symptoms of MA and CA were associated with distinct patterns of affective responses to levels of effort and reward in experienced activities. These data provide evidence for distinct manifestations of MA and CA in daily life and further support the hypothesis that they reflect distinct etiopathophysiologies that may benefit from different treatment strategies.

articles.title: Rethinking empathy in the age of AI
articles.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Daryl Cameron; Madeline G. Reinecke
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for empathic support, often reporting feelings of being cared for and supported. Longstanding models of empathy, however, center the empathizer’s embodied emotional experience, which AI fundamentally lacks. This tension between human experience and traditional researcher-imposed empathy definitions raises important scientific questions as to what it truly means for AI to “empathize.” In the present paper, we propose an alternative definition and approach to studying empathy which eases this tension, emphasizing the multiple dissociable functions that empathy serves within various relational schemas. Taking a functional-relational approach redefines the study of empathy by centering practical meta-scientific concerns (e.g., surrounding the exploration of empathy within study contexts, foregrounding lived experience). In doing so, we seek to future-proof empathy as a construct, ensuring that our science remains relevant, generalizable across time, and responsive to lived human experience as technology advances and new forms of relationships emerge.

articles.title: When and Why are Social Categories Overused Relative to Individuating Information? A Bayesian Approach to Identifying Biases in Impression Formation Processes
articles.authors: Thalia Vrantsidis; Wil Cunningham
articles.abstract: When making inferences about others, people often need to integrate multiple types of information, including the person’s social categories (e.g., occupation) as well as other “individuating” information (e.g., their behaviors). The current work re-examines this integration process, to understand when and why it produces biases involving over-reliance on category information. We identify two key challenges in identifying such biases, and develop a novel Bayesian modelling approach to overcome them. As a first step in applying this approach, the current work examined a set of novel predictions based on viewing the Continuum Model of impression formation in light of this Bayesian approach. Specifically, a series of six studies tested whether occupation categories might be overused in general, or especially in conditions thought to reduce effortful processing (i.e., greater cognitive load or information consistency). Results showed no evidence of category overuse, nor of shifts in this direction, in any of these conditions (though some ambiguity remained about the load manipulation’s effectiveness). This provides initial evidence against the idea that intrinsic differences in how these categories are processed or represented will lead to their overuse. A seventh study provided the first direct evidence of a case where categories were overused: when contextual factors (i.e., background goals) made them the category especially relevant, while processing resources were limited. More broadly, the current work developed the theoretical and methodological foundations for identifying category overuse that stems from biased inference processes, and demonstrated the power of this approach for understanding when and why such biases occur.

articles.title: Baselines Matter: Cardiovascular Baseline Procedures in Affective Psychophysiology
articles.authors: Maciej Behnke; Wadim Leszek Krzyżaniak; Szymon Jęśko-Białek; Patryk Andrzej Maciejewski; Audrey-Ann Journault; Sylvia D Kreibig; Jeremy Jamieson; James Gross
articles.abstract: A baseline is necessary to define biological reactivity in psychophysiological research. However, the conceptualization and implementation of baseline measurements are often underdescribed and weakly justified. This poses a problem because poor baseline decisions have the potential to introduce noise, reduce comparability across studies, and bias interpretations of data. In this article, we focus on laboratory studies using cardiovascular measures to examine how baselines are described and used in affective psychophysiology. To describe heterogeneity in baseline procedures, Study 1 reviewed 310 psychophysiological studies and coded baseline activities, durations, analyzed intervals, and theoretical justifications. To examine within-baseline stabilization, Study 2 analyzed the POPANE dataset to assess minute-by-minute changes in cardiovascular activity in 1,010 participants during a standard 5-minute baseline. To test whether these patterns replicated and whether baseline estimates differed across sessions, Study 3 analyzed the CEPAV dataset in 300 participants across two separate laboratory visits. Finally, to assess generalizability across a larger and more heterogeneous sample, Study 4 replicated these analyses using compiled laboratory data from 2,395 participants. Across studies, results indicate that baseline procedures vary considerably, are often insufficiently reported, and may meaningfully impact the interpretation of cardiovascular data. Although different cardiovascular indices may stabilize differently during a 5-minute baseline, findings suggest that this procedure is a reasonable, pragmatic choice and that separate-session baselines should not be assumed to be superior. More broadly, findings highlight the need for stronger justification, standardization, and reporting of baseline procedures in psychophysiological research.

articles.title: Selflessness, Self-Centeredness, and Mental Health in Dyads: Indirect Associations Through Affective and Functional Pathways
articles.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: Mental health is embedded in interpersonal contexts, yet little is known about whether psychological modes of functioning can affect the mental health of close others through dyadic processes. Drawing on the Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM), this article examined whether selflessness and self-centeredness were indirectly associated with another person’s mental health through two interpersonal pathways: emotional contagion and functional convergence. Two dyadic studies were conducted among French pairs who knew each other and interacted regularly: a student-close other sample in Study 1 and a general population sample in Study 2. Across both studies, no direct partner effects were found. However, indirect effects emerged via the proposed affective and functional mediators: selflessness was associated with higher partner positive mental health, whereas self-centeredness was associated with lower partner positive mental health and higher partner negative mental health. Additional invariance analyses supported the robustness of these structural paths across samples and relationship types. These findings suggest that selflessness and self-centeredness may have interpersonal implications for mental health through affective and functional mediating pathways.

articles.title: Executive Function and Perceived School Well-Being Across Child- and Adult-Centered Educational Contexts: An Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Laura González; Marina Oliva Lozano; María Jesús Pardo-Guijarro; Silvia Guerrero
articles.abstract: Children’s socioemotional and cognitive development is shaped by the contexts in which they grow, with school playing a key role in well-being and executive function (EF). This study examined whether the association between EF and perceived school well-being differed across school contexts aligned with Child–Environment Interplay (CEI) and Teacher–Text–Centered (TTC) models. 105 preschool and primary school children participated (NCEI = 70; NTTC = 35). EF was assessed through inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility tasks. Perceived school well-being was explored through a structured interview addressing engagement, environment and support, and aggression-related experiences. No overall differences emerged in EF or interview-based well-being. However, higher well-being was associated with lower EF in TTC, but not CEI, schools, while higher perceived aggression was associated with lower EF across both approaches. A qualitative subsample provided insight into how young children interpreted school experiences. These findings suggest that the association between cognitive skills and perceived school well-being may vary across educational contexts and highlight the value of young children’s perspectives into research on school life.

articles.title: Near-random behavior in strategic games
articles.authors: Tal Boger; Dorsa Amir; Sami Ryan Yousif
articles.abstract: Humans struggle to produce random behavior when asked to do so, leading some to suggest that our ability to randomize is attenuated (or even absent). Here, we demonstrate that the capacity for random behavior is much greater than previously acknowledged: Humans can behave in (near) optimally random ways when the context demands it. We created a custom, online version of the game Battleship in which participants competed against one another. On each turn, one player chose a tile on a 3x3 grid to place a ship, while the other player tried to guess the ship’s location. Across six preregistered studies, this strategic context led to dramatic increases in random behavior relative to closely matched non-strategic tasks. Such random behavior was also remarkably flexible and optimal depending on context; both players readily incorporated varying information about the game (e.g., that tiles can differ in value) while simultaneously accounting for their opponents’ knowledge of that information. A computational model validated these findings and revealed nuanced differences across contexts. Contrary to decades of work finding that humans fail to randomize, we find that strategic games promote highly flexible, near-random behavior.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-reported Emotional Sharing in Social Interaction: A Meta Analysis
articles.authors: X. Jia; Karen Holtmaat; Y. Mo; ZIHAO Zeng; M. Kaneva; Annet Kleiboer; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: Through emotional sharing, individuals can make their emotional experiences available to others, creating opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation. Although gender differences in these behaviours have been documented across various domains, findings regarding their magnitude and consistency remain inconclusive. This meta-analysis examined gender differences in emotional sharing among adults. A systematic search identified 32 articles comprising 37 independent samples, 155 effect sizes, and 13,147 participants, including 8,504 women and 4,643 men. Overall, women reported higher levels of emotional sharing than men, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]. This effect was not significantly moderated by (1) functions (emotional expression, emotional disclosure, emotional expression as coping), (2) temporal level (dispositional, situational), (3) emotional valence (negative, positive or unspecified), (4) specific negative emotion (anger, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame/guilt, and unspecified negative emotions), and (5) the interpersonal target (romantic partner, friend, other, or no partner specified). Despite the absence of significant moderation effects, pooled estimates within most subgroups remained significantly positive, indicating higher levels of expression and disclosure among women than men across a wide range of emotional contexts and interpersonal relations.

articles.title: Manipulating Temporal Expectations to Accelerate Recovery After Cataract Surgery:  A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.authors: Peter J Aungle; Juliette Bross; Viknesh Nagarathinam; Daniel L. Chen; Peter Rapoza; Ethan Brass; Sophie Cate; Ellen Langer
articles.abstract: Perceived time can objectively influence physiological outcomes, but such effects have been produced using false temporal feedback in laboratory settings, which is difficult to extend clinically. Drawing on the Embodied Models of Health (EMH) framework, in which beliefs shape health by orienting attention and expectation, the present study tested whether shifting patients' temporal expectations could influence post-surgical recovery. Patients undergoing bilateral cataract surgery (N = 147) were randomly assigned to a fast healing condition, comprising a preoperative video emphasizing faster recovery timelines and daily surveys directing attention toward healing variability, or a standard healing condition, comprising conventional information and surveys unrelated to healing. Visual acuity was assessed at baseline and at 1-day, 1-to-2-week, and 3-month follow-ups. Group-level differences across conditions were directionally consistent but modest. The theoretically motivated analyses, however, revealed an Attention × Sensitivity interaction consistent with the framework's core prediction: among patients who absorbed the faster expected healing times, greater daily attention to healing variability predicted faster recovery; among those who did not, attention had little effect. By the morning after surgery, and at every follow-up through three months, high-attention patients with strong healing expectations or high sensitivity to the faster-healing message held an acuity advantage over belief-matched controls equivalent to reading print roughly 10% smaller at the same distance, and reported at least 50% greater improvement in self-reported visual function. These findings provide the first clinical evidence that attention functions as a belief-weighted mediator between psychological and physiological processes, extending laboratory demonstrations of mind-body unity to clinical practice.

articles.title: Low-certainty modals not future tenses cause increased psychological discounting
articles.authors: Cole Robertson; Sean Roberts; Asifa Majid; Tammy Lu; Phillip Wolff; R. I. M. Dunbar
articles.abstract: Speaking a language that obliges the future tense for linguistic Future Time Reference (FTR) has been hypothesised to cause speakers to perceive delayed outcomes as temporally distal and therefore less valuable (“temporal discounting”). Conversely, we hypothesise that the obligation to use low-certainty modal verbs, e.g. may, causes speakers to construe risky and delayed outcomes as riskier and therefore less valuable (“combined discounting”). We experimentally elicited free-text FTR responses and measured construals of future temporal distance and discounting of (risky) delayed rewards in speakers of Dutch (which does not oblige FTR marking) and English (which does). We used statistical mediation models, which parse out an indirect effect of a predictor on an outcome via a mediating variable, a direct effect of a predictor on an outcome, and a total effect—the other two combined. English speakers construed future events as temporally proximal, which in turn caused less (rather than more) temporal discounting (indirect effect). The direct effect went in the opposite direction, meaning there was no population-level difference in temporal discounting (no total effect, Study 1). When we measured combined discounting, English speakers discounted more (a total effect, Study 2). Further, English speakers used more low-certainty language and this caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). Future tense use did not impact construals of temporal distance, meaning future tense use did not mediate an effect on combined discounting (Study 2). We addressed possible cultural confounds by testing Dutch-English bilinguals (Study 3). When bilinguals were tested in English, they used more low-certainty modal verbs, which in turn caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). This was moderated by self-reported English proficiency, indicating language, not culture, is responsible for effects. Results suggest effects of FTR grammar are not driven by obligatory future tenses affecting temporal discounting, but by obligatory low-certainty modals affecting combined discounting.

articles.title: The When, Who, Why, and How of Crocodile Tears: Manipulative Crying is Associated with Specific Situations, Traits, Motivations, and Expressive Behaviors
articles.authors: Janis Zickfeld; Monika Wróbel; Paweł Ciesielski
articles.abstract: The notion of crocodile tears suggests that crying can be used strategically to manipulate others. However, systematic evidence on manipulative crying remains limited. Here, we addressed this gap by examining the prevalence of crocodile tears, along with the contexts, motivations, individual traits, and expressive behaviors associated with this phenomenon across seven studies. In the first three studies (N = 2,036), participants from seven regions reported real-life experiences of being manipulated with crying or using crying to manipulate others. Results indicated that crocodile tears are a widespread yet relatively infrequent manipulative strategy, primarily occurring in close relationships and typically intended to evoke compassion or induce guilt. Women, younger participants, individuals scoring higher on Machiavellianism and psychopathy, and participants from lower-trust countries reported more frequent use of crocodile tears. Manipulative crying was also associated with intense expressive behaviors, including exaggerated facial expressions, face-touching, and loud vocalizations. Another set of four studies (N = 4,514), conducted across five regions, experimentally manipulated crying-related behaviors to examine how expressive cues shape perceptions of crying. Machine learning analyses revealed that crying was perceived as most “crocodile” when it involved high-intensity behaviors but no tears. Moreover, intense expressive behaviors combined with the absence of tears improved participants’ accuracy in detecting fake crying. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive empirical account of crocodile tears, highlighting how multimodal expressive cues, as well as social, individual, and cultural factors, shape the strategic use and perception of crying.

articles.title: Psychopathology-AI-interaction (PAII) framework: Disorder-specific dynamics in conversational AI
articles.authors: Alexander Diel; Niels Weber; Martin Teufel; Alexander Bäuerle
articles.abstract: Chatbots based on large language models (LLM-CBs) are increasingly used for mental health support by both individuals with and without mental health conditions. Simultaneously, potential risks and harms of LLM-CB use for mental health are widely discussed, typically in disorder-unspecific terms, evaluated through single-turn benchmark and vignette designs, and rarely linked to established models of psychopathology. The current work presents the Psychopathology-AI-interaction (PAII) framework, which conceptualizes harmful human-chatbot interaction as arising from three interacting components: human factors (disorder-specific pathology, individual vulnerabilities, and personality dispositions), chatbot factors (model-specific safety failures and design principles), and interaction factors. Drawing on established models of technology-associated psychopathology, LLM-CBs are presented as a new domain in which disorder-specific maladaptive patterns emerge. A roadmap for future research is presented, focusing on psychopathology-based multi-turn benchmarks, experimental induction of vulnerabilities and manipulation of chatbot risk factors, and analysis of naturalistic conversation logs.

articles.title: Five More Items Matter: Comparing Structural Validity, Response Bias, and Nomological Networks in 10- and 15-Item Big Five Measures Across Nations
articles.authors: Zhangchu Xu; Yuke Yang; Zhihao Ma
articles.abstract: Ultra-short Big Five measures are widely used to reduce respondent burden while retaining acceptable measurement quality. Yet when personality domains are represented by only two or three items, it remains unclear whether modestly greater item coverage translates into better measurement performance across cultural contexts. The present study compared the Ten-Item Personality Inventory (TIPI), the 10-item Big Five Inventory (BFI-10), and the 15-item Big Five Inventory-SOEP (BFI-S) across four sources of validity evidence: factor structure, measurement invariance, response bias, and nomological networks, using three large-scale cross-national datasets. Conventional confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) models showed inadequate fit across all three measures and were frequently affected by Heywood cases. Exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM) analyses indicated that BFI-S showed better recovery of the expected five-factor structure than TIPI and BFI-10, although cross-cultural variability remained. TIPI and BFI-10 were not subjected to measurement invariance testing because their baseline structures did not support meaningful comparisons, while BFI-S demonstrated relatively robust demographic invariance but weaker cross-national invariance. All measures showed directional response bias, with the largest contribution observed in BFI-10 and the smallest in BFI-S. Moreover, greater response bias was associated with larger deviations in personality–criterion associations across countries. Despite limited item coverage, all three measures reproduced theoretically expected nomological associations, with BFI-S showing greater cross-national consistency. Overall, expanding from two to three indicators per Big Five domain was associated with improved structural recovery, reduced response bias, and more consistent external associations. However, this modest increase in item coverage did not eliminate the inherent limitations of ultra-short personality assessment, highlighting the continued importance of considering measurement purpose, context, and cultural applicability.

articles.title: A puzzling situation: How cooperation and social observation influence visuospatial problem-solving
articles.authors: Federico Cassioli; Nellia Bellaert; Mandy Rossignol; Clay B. Holroyd; Rudi De Raedt
articles.abstract: Human problem-solving rarely occurs in social isolation. Yet how cognitive performance and subjective experiences vary across social situations, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in social anxiety (SA), remains underexplored. In this preregistered, within-subject experiment, 101 healthy young adults completed a visuospatial problem-solving task, involving tangram puzzles of different difficulty levels (1,818 trials total) across three social conditions: alone or joined by an experimental confederate acting as either a scrutinizing observer or an active cooperator. Using hierarchical Bayesian modeling, we modeled task performance and post-trial self-reported experiences, and tested whether SA, measured with the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, moderated the effects of social condition. Both performance and self-report ratings were modulated by task difficulty and social condition. Relative to performing alone, being observed was associated with a decrease in the probability of success and higher post-trial anxiety. Cooperation facilitated performance and reduced perceived difficulty. Crucially, SA moderated the effect of cooperation on post-trial anxiety: cooperation produced the largest reduction in post-trial anxiety among participants with greater fear of being observed. This buffering effect was specific to social-evaluative fear rather than general trait anxiety or task performance. Our findings reinforce the view that cognitive performance and participants’ experiences are jointly shaped by the social context in which they occur.

articles.title: On the importance of effort perception in stroke care: From evidence to an ideal care pathway – An opinion paper
articles.authors: Maëlle Charonitis; Fabienne Collette; Benjamin Pageaux
articles.abstract:
Post-stroke rehabilitation has traditionally relied on objective assessments of motor and cognitive abilities. However, one crucial factor remains underestimated in current practice: the perception of effort, that is, the conscious experience of task intensity and difficulty. Effort perception is strongly influenced by internal states such as fatigue and pain, two symptoms frequently reported after stroke, even without major neurological deficits. While these symptoms are often treated separately, they converge into a shared experience: heightened perceived effort.
Recent literature suggests that both physical and mental fatigue, along with pain, increase perceived effort by impacting available resources and motivation to engage and persist in cognitive and physical tasks. This modulation can directly affect patient engagement and adherence to rehabilitation. When effort is perceived as disproportionate—even for a simple task—it may lead to reduced participation or withdrawal from the care plan. Conversely, a better understanding of effort perception could pave the way for personalized interventions that consider not only patients’ actual capacities but also their subjective experiences.
It is therefore urgent to consider the perception of effort as a clinical indicator in its own right—one that sits at the intersection of body, brain and lived experience. By integrating this dimension, research could better explain why some patients disengage from post-stroke care, despite good recovery potential and clinical practice could refine motivational strategies and therapeutic adherence models. The stakes are twofold: improving the understanding of the mechanisms underlying effort perception and harnessing it as a lever for optimizing post-stroke care trajectories.

articles.title: An Integrative Theory of the Noradrenaline System: Meta-Control through Expected Information Gain
articles.authors: Riccardo; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles.abstract:
Living organisms constantly balance exploration and exploitation to adapt to changing environments.
While the neuromodulator noradrenaline (NA) is known to regulate arousal, attention, and information
seeking, its precise computational function remains elusive. Here, we propose an integrative theory of
the noradrenergic system, suggesting that it encodes expected information gain (EIG), a measure of how
informative the environment is over time, and that it uses this quantity for the meta-control of adaptive
behavior. We illustrate this theory using a hierarchical active inference model in which the NA system
acts as a higher-level meta-controller that dynamically adjusts a set of parameters (η) of a lower-level
behavioral controller, modulating exploration rate, the balance between deliberative and habitual control,
perceptual precision, learning rate, and cognitive flexibility. Simulations demonstrate that NA-based
EIG estimation and meta-control enhance performance in volatile environments by promoting directed
exploration, facilitating rapid shifts away from maladaptive habits, sharpening sensory evidence, and
accelerating learning following context changes. These results unify multiple facets of noradrenergic
function under a single computational objective, providing a novel perspective to explain tonic and
phasic NA activity in estimating EIG and meta-controlling behavior. Summing up, this framework
provides a principled link between neuromodulation, exploration, and adaptive behavior, suggesting
that the noradrenergic system implements a fundamental mechanism for inferring and exploiting the
informational richness of the environment.

articles.title: Affordance-Based Control in Driving Behavior: Integration of Perception and Action by Extending rho Coupling and Satisficing
articles.authors: Takayuki Kondoh; Hiroyuki Mishima; Nobuhiro Furuyama
articles.abstract: Action-control models in ecological psychology have evolved from pursuing a single optimal solution toward affordance-based control within safety regions. However, mathematically integrating these approaches with rho coupling theory remains insufficient. This study theoretically re-examines the "risk feeling formula (RFF)"—a linear sum of two optical variables derived from real-world driving data. Our analysis demonstrates that the RFF is structurally equivalent to rho coupling, yet its "intercept" distinctly functions as a "satisficing" threshold. Rather than representing an internal computational compromise, this threshold signifies direct perceptual attunement for initiating avoidance behavior while maintaining a safety margin. Furthermore, we propose an integrated mathematical representation of affordances as the linear sum of two action-scaled pi values, reflecting the extended body effectivities, corresponding to overt risk (rho_LF) and potential risk (rho_GF). By extending rho coupling to encompass satisficing, this framework elegantly models how actors dynamically balance contextual pressures without error-nulling. This integrated theoretical approach explains diverse human adaptive strategies and provides fundamental insights for future ecological human-centered design, including advanced driver assistance systems.

articles.title: Sex and gender differences in functional and participation experiences of students with developmental coordination disorder in higher education
articles.authors: Clare Copley; Kimberly Petersen; Madeleine Pownall; Lucy H Eddy
articles.abstract:
Background: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent motor coordination difficulties that negatively impacts daily functioning and participation across the lifespan. Despite a high prevalence (5-6%), DCD remains under recognised in adulthood, creating particular challenges in contexts requiring high levels of independent participation, such as higher education. Sex and gender are also important to examine, given their potential to influence the recognition, presentation and lived experience of DCD. However, there is a notable lack of research exploring how sex and gender identity may impact these experiences. 
Aims: This exploratory study aimed to investigate whether functional challenges and participation experiences differed according to sex and gender identity among higher education students with DCD.
Methods: Data were collected via an online self-report questionnaire completed by 77 higher education students with DCD/dyspraxia across the UK and Ireland.
Results: Findings indicate high levels of functional difficulty and participation restriction across the sample, with fatigue often reported as a consequence. Females with DCD were significantly more likely than males to report challenges related to gross motor skills (p<.05, d=.60) and executive function skills (p<.05, d =.60). Participants who identified as a gender minority reported a higher incidence of difficulty with fine motor skills (p<.05, d=–.63) and executive function (p<.05, d =–.60) compared to cisgender participants. 
Conclusions: Findings indicate that students with DCD experience persistent functional challenges that restrict participation in higher education.  Experiences and support needs may also differ based on sex and gender identity.

articles.title: Perceived and evidenced benefits of videogame play amongst neurodivergent populations: A scoping review
articles.authors: Emily J Smith; Jonathan Farnell; Lacey-ann Carter; Roshan Rai; Benjamin Gibson
articles.abstract: There are meaningful concerns that videogame play is harmful for neurodivergent populations, including people with autism spectrum disorders. However, there is a disproportionate focus in the literature on dangers, and there are fewer efforts to consider why such populations may be more likely to play videogames in the first place. In considering benefits to play, this scoping review attempts to map out a more balanced view of videogame engagement amongst a range of neurodivergent populations. A search of academic databases identified 9 articles comprising a mix of qualitative and quantitative studies. Using a narrative synthesis, we found that benefits to play included (1) friendship and belonging, (2) immersion, escapism, and emotional regulation, and (3) development, growth, and autonomy. In the future, we recommend a pivot away from a deficit-focused approach to investigations, and a larger investment in research that considers motivations, attitudes, and consequences of play from a lived-experience perspective.

articles.title: Psychological inoculation against deepfakes
articles.authors: Cambridge Social Decision-Making Lab; Liana Cheetham; Kelly Wong Kar Yee; Sander van der Linden
articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in countering the threat of deepfake misinformation, most interventions aimed at enhancing human detection have thus far proven unsuccessful. In the current study we explore the potential of a popular psychological intervention: cognitive inoculation—which to our knowledge—has not been tested in the context of deepfakes. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 297), we evaluate whether an inoculation-based video intervention improves people’s deepfake detection skills compared to a control intervention. The inoculation intervention forewarned participants they may be manipulated by deepfake content and prebunked it by deconstructing deepfake misinformation in weakened form. Following the intervention, participants were asked to classify a series of 10 videos as either real or deepfaked. We find that mean detection accuracy of deepfakes was significantly higher in the inoculation compared to the control group (d = 0.625, 95% CI [0.39, 0.86]) without shifting response bias, indicating that the inoculation intervention substantially improved deepfake discernment. Further investigation of the mechanisms behind the inoculation process finds that both motivation to resist deepfakes and self-reported ability to recognize them increased following the intervention. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of inoculation interventions to build resistance to deepfake misinformation.

articles.title: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D): A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing the Therapeutic Alliance
articles.authors: KHAIRUL KORAI
articles.abstract:
Individual with dyslexia frequently experience persistent reading difficulties that extend far beyond academic environments, contributing to heightened anxiety, low self-esteem, and chronic psychological distress. In traditional mental health counseling, literacy-heavy tools such as written intake questionnaires, thought journals, and dense psychoeducational handouts impose a heavy extraneous cognitive load. This load exhausts working memory and triggers reading anxiety, effectively diverting mental bandwidth away from core therapeutic processing. To address this barrier, this paper introduces a conceptual framework: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D). Grounded in a narrative synthesis of existing literature, this model positions artificial intelligence not as a replacement for human clinicians, but as an accessible cognitive scaffold managed under ethical oversight. The framework synthesizes Cognitive Load Theory, the Triadic Therapeutic Alliance model (Client, Therapist, and AI), and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles. By leveraging Generative AI summaries, speech-to-text journaling, and multimodal text-to-speech presentation, AAIC-D offloads reading and writing effort, restoring the client's emotional capacity for therapeutic engagement. Finally, we address critical counseling practice governance concerns including algorithmic bias, data privacy under HIPAA/GDPR, and client over-reliance offering actionable guidelines to humanize and democratize psychological care. 

Keywords: Dyslexia, Assistive AI, Therapeutic Alliance, Cognitive Load Theory, Universal Design for Learning, Counseling Psychology, Cyberpsychology

articles.title: The Hidden Friction of Action: A Framework for Autistic Inertia
articles.authors: Hari Srinivasan
articles.abstract:
Autistic inertia describes difficulty initiating, sustaining, stopping, or shifting action and cognitive state despite conscious intention. Existing accounts, including executive dysfunction, monotropism, predictive processing, autistic burnout, and disability-oriented perspectives, capture important aspects of the phenomenon but remain fragmented. We propose the Hidden Friction Framework (HFF), which addresses how intention can remain intact while its translation into flexible action becomes disrupted. The HFF proposes that autistic inertia may emerge from interacting predictive, transition, sensory–motor, executive–cognitive, emotional, and environmental forms of friction. Rather than treating inertia solely as a problem of action initiation, the framework considers difficulty flexibly entering, sustaining, exiting, or shifting cognitive, sensory, emotional, and behavioral states. It also helps explain why inertia may vary across contexts and why similar behavioral outcomes may arise from different configurations of friction. The HFF integrates cognitive, embodied, environmental, and lived-experience perspectives and generates testable predictions about how different sources of friction may independently and cumulatively shape action and state transition in autism.

Keywords: autistic inertia, autism, embodiment, epistemic injustice, neurodiversity, disability theory.

articles.title: From Self to Others? Testing Whether Brief Mindfulness Reduces Intergroup Bias through Decentering or Self-Compassion
articles.authors: Gabriela Gorska; Pawel Holas
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Brief mindfulness reliably changes how individuals relate to their own internal experiences, but whether these intrapersonal changes generalize to intergroup responding remains unclear.
