This preregistered experiment (N = 91) examined whether mindfulness-related processes—decentering and compassionate self-responding—were associated with socio-affective responses toward in-group and out-group members. Participants completed an adapted Socio-affective Video Task using AI-generated images to assess compassion, personal distress, and prosocial giving. Brief mindfulness was significantly linked to increased decentering and compassionate self-responding. Contrary to preregistered hypotheses, the intervention did not reduce intergroup bias in compassion, personal distress, or the empathic Dictator Game. Findings suggest that brief mindfulness primarily influences proximal intrapersonal processes, whereas changes in intergroup socio-affective responding may be limited.

articles.title: “It's my destiny.”: A Qualitative Exploration of Motivating Factors for submissives who Hold BDSM and Kink Identities
articles.authors: Briana Louise Kunstman; Jaime Derringer
articles.abstract: Although Dominant-submissive dynamics are among the most widely recognized forms of BDSM and kink, popular media often portray these relationships as inherently abusive or exploitative. Such representations contrast with growing evidence that BDSM identities and practices emerge through diverse developmental, social, and personal pathways. Building on prior research calling for greater attention to role-specific experiences within BDSM communities,the current study evaluated the themes present among 52 participants reporting submissive identities. We found that participants’ descriptions of their motivations for being a submissive consistently referred to the following themes: upbringing and past experience; submission as an identity; control and power exchange; positive mental health outcomes; and feelings of shame associated with stigma. Apart from stigma concerns, participants overwhelmingly discussed positive aspects of their experiences. This shows that there are complex motivating factors for participants to engage with or identify as submissive, opening up potential directions of exploration to understand the development of kink and BDSM identities and experiences. These findings specific to submissive motivations and BDSM identities will help work towards the destigmatization and depathologizing of kink and BDSM through increased understanding. In turn, this will allow for better mental health outcomes for community members, informed safe practice, and improved general understanding of BDSM and kink identities in our society.

articles.title: Can Accurate Information Change Identity-Linked Political Beliefs? Evidence From Republicans’ Attitudes Towards Election Integrity
articles.authors: Michael Nicholas Stagnaro; Eran Amsalem; Andrea B Mullin; Hause Lin; Adam J. Berinsky; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Psychological research suggests that identity shapes beliefs and impedes updating in response to contrary evidence. A prominent example is many Republicans’ persistence in believing that the 2020 election was stolen. We test whether credible factual information can shift Republicans' beliefs about election integrity. Immediately before the 2024 presidential election, we randomly assigned 861 conservative Republicans to an intensive informational intervention or a control matched with civic content. The intervention presented extensive, accurate, politically balanced evidence and encouraged sustained engagement. Treated participants reported stronger beliefs in US election integrity overall, greater confidence in the 2020 election, and more positive expectations for the 2024 election (.5 < ds < .8), including those who started lower in electoral confidence (.5 < ds < .97). Effects were still detectable two weeks later, after Trump’s victory. Though learning was incentivized, belief reporting was not – showing that when attended to, credible balanced evidence can change minds.

articles.title: Toward a Multidimensional Operationalization of Feminist Identity: Associations with Sexism and Weight Bias
articles.authors: Daemon St-James; Annie Raymond; Annie Duchesne; Benoit Brisson
articles.abstract: Feminist identity is typically operationalized through self-identification and endorsement of select beliefs, leaving movement affiliation and competing ideologies, such as meritocracy and social dominance orientation, unaccounted for. This study explored whether a multidimensional operationalization of feminist identity reveals distinct profiles and whether these profiles relate differently to discriminatory attitudes associated with feminism: ambivalent sexism and weight bias. Adults in Quebec (N = 917; 90% women) completed the Anti-Fat Attitudes Scale, the Ambivalent Sexism Inventory, the Perceptions of Meritocracy Inventory, the Short Social Dominance Orientation Scale, a bespoke feminist movement affiliation questionnaire, and the Feminist Belief and Behavior measure. Cluster analysis yielded six profiles: four feminist-identifying profiles distinguished by movement affiliation (liberal, radical, intersectional, postmodern) and two non-identifying profiles, including Affiliated Non-Labelers, who endorsed feminist beliefs and affiliated with a feminist movement while rejecting the feminist label. They reported meritocratic and dominance-oriented scores comparable to Non-Feminists. Profiles differed on hostile sexism, benevolent sexism, and weight controllability. Compared with Zucker's (2004) two-dimensional typology, the profiles offered no clear incremental predictive value but described configurations not represented by conventional typology. Findings suggest that the combination of feminist identities a person holds alongside their beliefs shapes how feminist identity relates to discriminatory attitudes.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Advancing Global Social Science through Cross-Societal Online Behavioral Economic Games (CoBEx): Lessons Learned and A Practical Guide
articles.authors: Shuxian Jin; Vanessa Christina Clemens; Laura Carlotta Hoenig; Carsten De Dreu; Angela Rachael Dorrough; Catherine Molho; Marina Orifici; Angelo Romano; Shaul Shalvi; Ayse K. Uskul
articles.abstract: Understanding human behavior across diverse cultural settings is essential for advancing theories that address pressing global social challenges. Recent advances, which use an innovative methodology—cross-societal online behavioral economic games (CoBEx)—have revealed key insights into cross-cultural differences and similarities in the mechanisms and functions of human behavior. To foster this emerging field, we discuss the key successes and lessons learned from ten years of experience in designing and conducting CoBEx studies. We illustrate the theoretical and methodological benefits of CoBEx, and offer practical recommendations on key design considerations, study materials preparation, ethics and funding, as well as analysis, interpretation, and dissemination processes. This paper aims to equip researchers around the globe with the necessary tools to conduct methodologically rigorous and culturally informed CoBEx studies, ultimately advancing the field of psychological science and beyond.

articles.title: Who can re-enter the loop? A scoping review on cognitive abilities and task re-engagement in human-AI interaction
articles.authors: Han Zhang; Bianca Done; Stefanie Schneider; Nithya Rajan; Manhua Wang
articles.abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) promise a near future in which humans and AI systems work together to solve complex problems. Although offloading tasks to AI reduces immediate cognitive demands, the system may later require human input or decision-making, at which point the human must “re-enter the loop” by redirecting attention, reconstructing the task state, and responding appropriately. Whether individual differences in cognitive ability predict the capacity to re-enter the loop remains unclear. Here, we conducted a scoping review of studies relating cognitive ability to loop re-entry performance. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Among them, most studies examined conditionally automated driving, and none examined interactions with generative AI systems. Working memory capacity was the most frequently studied ability and was generally associated with better loop re-entry performance, whereas results for attentional control were mixed. The evidence was further limited by small samples, single-task measures of cognitive abilities, and inconsistent outcome measures. As human oversight becomes increasingly central to AI safety, understanding who can re-enter the loop effectively remains an important open question. We offer concrete recommendations to guide future research.

articles.title: From Psychological States to Self-Reports: A New Perspective on Response Bias
articles.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles.abstract:
Self-report measures are a cornerstone of psychological science, yet little attention has been
devoted to the processes through which internal experiences become observable responses. We
propose a theoretical account of self-report in which responses reflect two concurrent sources of
information: the latent states individuals seek to communicate and the response processes
governing how those states are expressed. We formalise this framework for Likert-type data using
the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, an ordinal-threshold approach that
separates latent state expression from response style processes. Across applications to novel and
previously published data, we show that response styles are stable across time and survey
instruments, while individuals retain the capacity to modify their response style without changing
the latent states they wish to express. We further demonstrate a novel prediction of the
framework: that response style information obtained in one context can be used to reduce
response style confounding in another. Together, these findings support a view of self-report as a
communicative decision process rather than a direct reflection of latent states. More broadly, they
suggest that understanding psychological measurement requires explaining not only what people
experience, but also how they choose to express those experiences

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, in nearly all cases, one must register in order to vote—yet, a substantial portion of the eligible electorate remains unregistered. Despite this, relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that a voter registers. Here, we tested the impact of 10 expert-crowdsourced, theoretically-based psychological interventions on a sample of eligible, yet unregistered, U.S. voters ahead of the 2024 presidential election (N = 12,896). Eight of the interventions increased intentions to vote, and five led individuals to click on the voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, which sequentially employed several social pressure strategies, was the strongest intervention across these outcomes. However, none of the interventions had a significant effect on actual voter registration or voter turnout. The results highlight a substantial disconnect between voters’ intentions and their ultimate behaviors. We discuss potential structural and psychological barriers that undermine the translation of intent into action.

articles.title: Beyond Lineups: An ROC-Expected Utility Framework for Eyewitness Identification
articles.authors: Yueran Yang; Justice Healy; Janice Burke; Max Guyll
articles.abstract: How should the legal system and scholars evaluate lineup performance? To answer this important question, this paper introduces a receiver operating characteristic-expected utility (ROC-EU) framework, which bridges two prominent evaluation methods in eyewitness research. The framework emphasizes investigators as the primary decision-makers who use eyewitness evidence for classifying suspects’ guilt. This perspective shift not only helps clarify confusions in interpreting lineup ROC analysis but also expands the scope of lineup evaluation. Specifically,  the expected utility component of the framework enables a holistic assessment across distinct investigative stages: the prior probability of guilt captures independent incriminating evidence collected before a lineup; likelihoods of investigator classification outcomes capture factors that shape witness responses during a lineup; and utilities of investigator classification outcomes capture the real-world legal and societal consequences that follow investigator classification decisions after a lineup. By positioning lineup evaluation within the broader investigative context, the ROC-EU framework provides a more comprehensive approach to understanding and

articles.title: From Population–Case Mismatch to Cumulative Homogenisation in AI-Assisted Cognition
articles.authors: Fangxing Bai
articles.abstract: A growing literature reports homogenisation under generative AI assistance and offers diverse explanations, yet a unified account grounded in AI’s statistical foundations remains underdeveloped. Through a parallel thought experiment, this Perspective derives how population–case mismatch creates differences between model-based and independent human trajectories, and how AI intervention can turn these differences into cumulative homogenisation. The degree and rate of homogenisation vary with the stage of intervention. The same mechanism also explains why AI can support scientific research under conditions that limit mismatch and support independent judgement.

articles.title: Mapping Behavioural and Psychological Factors Associated with Engagement in Online Activism: A Critical Scoping Review
articles.authors: Benjamin Gibson; Jekaterina Schneider; Mark J. Forshaw
articles.abstract: Online activism can be a powerful means of supporting social and political engagement. However, there are genuine concerns that online behaviours do not translate into social and political action, while nascent research suggests that online activism may affect well-being and feelings of identity more negatively compared to traditional (i.e., in-person) forms of activism. This scoping review attempted to map out the evidence so that the reader may better understand the psychological and behavioural factors associated with engagement in online activism. A search of academic databases and registers identified 24 articles comprising 28 studies and examined various forms of online activism including hashtag campaigns, online petitions, and social media engagement. Online engagement was shown to support a range of (further) online and offline activist behaviours, to foster collective identities, and to provide psychological benefits such as increased self-efficacy and feelings of empowerment (which in turn encouraged further political action). However, contextual and individual factors likely influence both behaviours and opportunities for psychological benefits. This review highlights the blurred boundaries between online and offline activism, while evidencing that even “passive” digital engagement may serve as a gateway to broader civic participation.

articles.title: Causal Inference in Mediation Studies When Using Psychological States as Mediators
articles.authors: Guangyu Zhu; Yiyun Shou; Michael Smithson
articles.abstract:
The growing interest in the underlying causal mechanisms of phenomena has led to the widespread application of mediation models in social science research. Researchers usually employ regression-based approaches (such as Baron and Kenny’s criteria, Sobel test and SEM) to explore causal relationships. However, the effectiveness of regression-based approaches in establishing causal relationships relies on two key assumptions: temporal order between variables and the elimination of confounders.
Previous literature has cautioned researchers about these restrictions, but misuses of regression-based approaches persist when the assumptions are not satisfied or not testable. In addition, researchers may encounter various challenges in assessing the causal relationship between variables, especially when using psychological states as mediators. These challenges include but are not limited to: (1) Psychological states are latent variables; (2) Discrepancy between measurement lag and causal lag; (3) Potential unknown or uncontrolled confounders; and (4) Bad control problem.
This article discusses the limitations of regression-based approaches and the challenges in assessing causal mediation relationships when using psychological states as mediators. It then elaborates several advanced approaches to address these challenges.

articles.title: “Who Will Marry a Mad Doctor?”: A Qualitative Study of Associative Stigma Among Mental Health Professionals in India
articles.authors: Deepti Dilip Moar; Rajat Kanti Mitra; Sunil Mittal
articles.abstract: Mental health professionals (MHPs) can experience stigma through their professional association with mental illness and mental healthcare. Existing studies have often focused on particular professions, service populations, or specific aspects of associative stigma, making it difficult to identify recurring patterns across professions and beyond the workplace. This study explored associative stigma among MHPs in India across professional, family, and wider social contexts. Semi-structured interviews with 22 MHPs, including psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counsellors, psychiatric social workers, and psychiatric nurses, were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist framework. Eight themes were developed, spanning misconceptions about MHP roles and abilities, mistrust of expertise and motives, concerns about how mental health work might affect them, devaluation of mental health work, exclusion involving social distancing and concealment, role expectations extending beyond work, ambivalent responses in which admiration or reliance coexisted with misunderstanding, avoidance, or devaluation, and differences in professional standing. Across the analysis, experiences that might otherwise appear separate were connected by recurring meanings attached to mental illness and mental healthcare. The study broadens understanding of the social and professional reach of stigma surrounding mental illness. Through professional association, these meanings can shape how MHPs, their expertise, and mental health work are understood and valued.

articles.title: Can Large Language Models Code Reality Criteria in Autobiographical Statements? Reliability and Validity of an Artificial Intelligence–Based Tool for Criteria-Based Content Analysis
articles.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Laureen Gräflich; Johannes Zimmermann; Renate Volbert
articles.abstract: Objective: Coding for Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA) to differentiate fabricated from experience-based autobiographical statements is slow and depends on trained coders whose agreement is imperfect. We developed the large language model (LLM) based system CBC-AID and evaluate its reliability and validity in coding CBCA. Hypotheses: As preregistered, AI–human consistency is non-inferior to the interrater reliability of trained coders (H1: total score; H2: each criterion), and AI-based scores discriminate between experience-based and fabricated statements at least as well as human scores (H3: total score; H4: each criterion). Method: Two versions of an LLM-based coding tool (CBC-AID), a single-prompt and a multi-agent system, coded 957 transcripts from 399 persons in nine laboratory studies with human CBCA codings and known truth status. Bivariate Bayesian multilevel models estimated within-study correlations and standardized truth effects under global rating and weighted frequency. Results: AI–human correlations of the total scores (ρ = .53–.67) fell short of the benchmark of .66 in all four combinations of version and scoring scheme; Version 1 under global rating came closest (ρ = .67, 95% CrI [.62, .72]). The AI assigned higher scores than human coders (0.7–2.7 SD). Truth effects were similar for AI-based (δ = 0.17–0.32) and human coding (0.16–0.24; Δδ = −0.06 to 0.12); non-inferiority was supported for one of four combinations, and human coding itself discriminated weakly. Conclusions: LLM-based coding approximated but did not reach the consistency of trained coders and preserved their modest discriminative validity. It may serve as a traceable supplement to human coding in research; forensic use requires field validation and human oversight.

articles.title: When the Same Leader Helps and Harms: Inconsistent Leadership Behavior in Team Meetings
articles.authors: Amelie Verena Güntner; Kai N. Klasmeier; Catrin Millhoff; Nora Gosch; Simone Kauffeld
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The same leader often displays constructive and destructive behaviors at once, a
phenomenon known as inconsistent leadership. Inconsistency has been linked to negative
follower outcomes, yet it has almost exclusively been studied as a follower perception. This
study examines inconsistent leadership as enacted behavior, asking how and under what
conditions the co-occurrence of instrumental and destructive leadership shapes team behavior in
meetings.
Design/methodology/approach: Using a multilevel moderated mediation model, we tested our
model on 30 videotaped team meetings (5,430 coded behaviors), rating leaders' instrumental and
destructive behavior and coding leaders' action planning and team members' conflict-related
communication.
Findings: Instrumental leadership was associated with more action planning, which in turn
reduced conflict-related communication, but only when destructive leadership was low. When
leaders behaved destructively alongside instrumental leadership, this indirect effect disappeared.
Practical implications: Occasional destructive behavior can undo the benefits of otherwise
constructive leadership, so what matters for teams is not only what leaders do well but whether
they do it consistently. Organizations can address this through leadership development that helps
leaders recognize and reduce inconsistent behavior in meetings.
Originality/value: Inconsistency has almost always been studied as a follower perception. This
study extends its consequences beyond follower attitudes to observable team communication and
to the leader's own planning, showing that inconsistency also shapes the enacting leader. It offers
a behavioral, micro-level operationalization that complements existing perception-based
measures.

articles.title: Relationships Between Auditory Statistical Learning and Reading Skills in Children with Reading Difficulties
articles.authors: Anqi Hu; Brynn Siles; Monique Montoute; Kelly Hay Yee Chan; Sarah Young-Hong; Amanda Van Horne; Morten H. Christiansen; Zhenghan Qi
articles.abstract:
Purpose. This study evaluated the psychometric implications of a novel gamified SL task for school-aged children with reading difficulties and examined the relationships between auditory syllable-based statistical learning (SL) and literacy skills.

Methods. Two groups of children aged 7–11 with reading difficulty were recruited. In Experiment 1, 13 children piloted a child-friendly, non-gamified auditory SL task at two timepoints, with learning assessed via a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) test at both timepoints and a statistically induced chunking recall (SICR) test at Timepoint 2. In Experiment 2, 22 children completed a gamified version of the SL task, with learning assessed via 2AFC and SICR at both timepoints and reading skills (nonword and sight-word fluency) assessed at Timepoint 1.

Results. Children showed learning at the group level across timepoints, as measured by SICR in both gamified and non-gamified tasks, and as measured by 2AFC in the gamified task only. SICR showed higher internal consistency than 2AFC across tasks. Test-retest reliability for 2AFC was higher for the gamified (r = .64) than non-gamified (r = .14) task.  Children’s performance on 2AFC and SICR in the gamified task were significantly associated with their nonword and sight-word reading fluency.

Conclusions. Gamification and the use of a statistically induced chunking recall task in an auditory SL task improved the task’s psychometric properties in school-aged children with reading difficulties. Auditory SL was also associated with concurrent reading skills in these children, suggesting that the implicit learning of regularities in spoken language input may additionally support reading development.

articles.title: When does cortical coherence carry shared content? Compatibility and self-reconstruction as testable conditions
articles.authors: Sebastian Bobadilla-Suarez
articles.abstract: Synchrony accounts treat collective phase order as the mechanism that integrates distributed cortical activity. We show formally that shared content and a self-model each need a condition beyond phase order, and state it. Three conditions are separated: coherence (collective phase order), compatibility (agreement of independently decoded local descriptions where regions overlap) and self-reconstruction (accurate recovery of the global state from an internal encoding). Compatible local descriptions determine a unique global state. Coherence bounds disagreement between overlapping descriptions only through shared encoders of bounded sensitivity, and the bound grows as the square root of the population read: on one simulated cortical sheet it constrains at most 10 sites, chaining through overlapping patches extends it to 0.312 mm, and across distant regions the link from coherence to content is an assumption. A contracting self-map fixes one state but reconstructs accurately only states within a diameter set by its error and contraction factor. Lean 4 verifies these implications; one model satisfies all connecting hypotheses at once, showing consistency, not cortical realization. The conditions yield a disconfirmable comparison: at matched phase coherence and single-region decoding accuracy, decoders fitted independently on two regions should agree more, beyond their separate accuracies, on perceived than on unperceived stimuli classified by a no-report marker. Choosing the overlapping regions by what each decodes makes the unity correlate operational relative to a pre-registered decoder and criterion. An exploratory EEG analysis is a measurement check only. Unity and a minimal self remain interpretations that need an independent experiential endpoint.

articles.title: Varying Dimensions of Language Input Predict Language and Executive Function Development Across Socioeconomically Diverse Families
articles.authors: Rachel R Romeo; Alexus Guadalupe Ramirez; Klaudia I. Kulawska; Amy E. Carolus; Katie A McLaughlin; Meredith Rowe; Liliana Lengua
articles.abstract: Children’s early language experiences are linked to their language and executive functioning (EF) development, and vary by socioeconomic status (SES). However, unique features may support different cognitive domains because input is multifaceted. The present study characterizes the dimensional structure of maternal language input and examines how these dimensions vary by SES and predict language and EF development across the preschool years. Thirteen metrics of maternal speech were extracted and/or manually coded from semi-structured play with 275 mother-child dyads when children were 3 years (137 male, 138 female; 65% White, 4% Black, 2% Latino, 2% Asian, 28% multiracial). Children’s language and EF were assessed four times between ages 3 and 5 years (data collected 2008–2012). Exploratory factor analysis revealed four input dimensions: linguistic quantity, linguistic complexity, interactiveness, and conceptual input. These differentially predicted children’s baseline language and EF performance, but not growth. Specifically, interactive and conceptual input predicted language skills, while complexity predicted EF skills. The four dimensions jointly mediated the relationship between SES and baseline language (β=0.053), and a serial pathway linked SES through input and language to EF (β=0.052). These findings reveal distinct pathways through which specific features of early input support children’s language and EF.

articles.title: Approach-avoidance contingencies shape expression memory and valence evaluation
articles.authors: Arijit De; Kinkini; Jeeviga Yasokaran; Ashvit Varaganti; William A. Cunningham; Adrian Nestor
articles.abstract: Facial expressions guide approach and avoidance, but actions toward a person may also change how that person is later represented. We tested whether learned action-category relations shape the accuracy of later expression-memory reports and affective evaluation. Across three online experiments, participants (N = 629 in primary analyses) learned either a congruent mapping (approach Happy, avoid Disgust) or the reversed mapping. Experiment 1 implemented approach and avoidance as looming and receding faces; Experiments 2-3 used stationary faces and response-contingent monetary progress, and Experiment 3 changed both identities and target-expression intensity. After training, participants reported previously encountered expressions using an identity-cued continuous-report wheel built from neural-network-generated expression continua and rated faces for valence and arousal. Reversing the mapping produced a crossover interaction: each expression category was reported more accurately when assigned to approach than to avoidance. This crossover persisted after exact chance adjustment and controls for face-recognition ability and final rule sensitivity. Further, each category was rated more positively when approached; this evaluative effect extended to once-exposed identities in Experiments 1–2 and never-trained identities in Experiment 3. No corresponding arousal interaction was detected. These findings identify learned action-category relations as a source of structure in subsequent expression-memory accuracy and evaluation, linking action learning to the reporting of remembered emotional content and the evaluation of new category members.

articles.title: Faculty Evaluations of DEI Statements for Academic Hiring
articles.authors: Nathan Honeycutt
articles.abstract: Diversity, equity, and inclusion (“DEI”) statements have become a popular additional evaluative criterion for academic hiring and promotion, but little to no empirical research has been conducted to assess how university faculty evaluate these statements. The present set of experiments sought to fill this void. Across seven studies (ntotal=4,953), tenured/tenure-track university faculty rated DEI statements that did not discuss race/ethnicity and gender diversity actions or efforts (i.e., statements that lacked equalitarian content) significantly lower than those that did. Specifically, faculty perceived these “alternative” statements to be weaker DEI statements, and perceived the applicants who submitted these statements to be less competent, less hireable, and less likable. Furthermore, faculty were less likely to recommend–often by a large margin–that the applicants behind these “alternative” statements pass an initial screening and be advanced for further review. Evaluative penalties were most severe toward DEI statements focusing only on viewpoint diversity actions and efforts (Studies 1-4), but also manifested for statements focusing only on rural diversity (Study 6), or only on socioeconomic diversity (Study 7). Findings for disability diversity (Study 5) were mixed. These studies provide novel insight on how DEI statements are perceived and evaluated by university faculty.

articles.title: Computational and neuropsychiatric dimensions of motivation differentially predict everyday physical activity
articles.authors: Sara Z. Mehrhof; Camilla Nord
articles.abstract: Physical activity benefits physical and mental health, yet population-level engagement in physical activity is low and variable, particularly among individuals with mental health problems. We investigated how neuropsychiatric and computational variables of motivation relate to physical activity in a large, general-population sample (N = 1,105). Both neuropsychiatric (apathy and anhedonia) and computational (effort sensitivity during effort-based decision-making) measures predicted total physical activity. Decomposing physical activity into activity stage and intensity revealed clear dissociable and independent effects: Apathy and anhedonia, but not effort sensitivity, primarily predicted whether individuals participated in activity at all, as well as amount of sedentary time. Computational effort sensitivity, on the other hand, predicted the amount of activity individuals engage in, with effects scaling with intensity. Our findings suggest neuropsychiatric and computational dimensions of motivation govern distinct components of real-world physical activity, with implications for the development of targeted physical activity interventions.

articles.title: Flexibility in Abstract Thought: Context-Dependent Representations of Integer Magnitude
articles.authors: Nicholas Allan Vest; Martha W. Alibali
articles.abstract: Negative numbers are challenging because they lack direct perceptual referents and require reasoning about magnitude in a relational, bidirectional space. This review examines how people represent and use integer magnitude on the mental number line, a cognitive tool that learners initially use for positive numbers, focusing on the flexibility with which this tool is deployed across contexts. Synthesizing evidence from cognitive psychology, developmental science, and mathematics education, we evaluate three broad representational accounts: componential accounts, which treat sign and magnitude as separable symbolic elements; extension accounts, which posit a continuous magnitude representation extending across zero; and reflection accounts, which propose a symmetry-based organization of magnitude around zero. Across experimental paradigms, task formats, and age groups, findings reveal substantial variability in behavioral signatures of integer processing. We argue that this variability reflects context-dependent recruitment of multiple coexisting representations rather than a single, fixed structure or a stage-like developmental progression. On this view, the mental number line functions as a dynamic cognitive tool that can be reparametrized in the moment to support rule-based, analog, or relational reasoning. Understanding how integer magnitude is flexibly represented and used provides insight into the mechanisms of abstract thought, coordination of representations, and conceptual change.

articles.title: Eye Tracking and NLP: A Survey and an Outlook
articles.authors: Yevgeni Berzak; David Robert Reich; Omer Shubi; Lena A. Jäger
articles.abstract: With the rise of LLMs, NLP has been redefining itself as a field of study, with an increasing interest shift towards areas such as NLP for science, model analysis, human-centered AI and user-facing applications. As part of this transformation, in recent years, a new area of NLP which combines text processing with eye movements in reading has been emerging. Recent work has demonstrated that this area has a strong potential for driving innovation in NLP and enhancing its scientific and societal impact. In this survey, we characterize the main streams of work on the intersection of eye tracking for reading and NLP, provide critical commentary on promises and challenges, and identify key open directions that can guide future work in this area.

articles.title: Exploring the Renin–Angiotensin System as a Potential Approach for Managing Perimenopausal Depression
articles.authors: Helena Jelenska; Andrea Reinecke
articles.abstract:
Perimenopause is characterised by debilitating psychological symptoms, including
a two- to four-fold increased risk of depressive symptoms during this sensitive time. Current first-line treatment strategies, such as antidepressants and hormonal therapy, are proven to be only moderately effective and linked to severe adverse effects. With the population of perimenopausal women rapidly growing due to rising life expectancy, novel strategies to prevent or mitigate perimenopausal symptoms of depression are of increasing importance.
Perimenopause is marked by pronounced sex-hormone changes, primarily declining oestrogen. Both have been linked to increased depression risk. On the other hand, the renin–angiotensin system (RAS), an endocrine system involved in blood pressure regulation, has been linked to depression, with RAS-based pharmacological manipulations having antidepressant effects. Perimenopausal hormonal changes closely interact with the RAS by upregulating the depressogenic Ang II–ACE–AT₁R pathway and downregulating the protective Ang-(1–7)–ACE2–MasR/AT₂R pathway. This narrative review summarises research highlighting the RAS as a potential novel treatment target for depression in perimenopausal women and proposes a hypothesis-generating framework to guide future research.

articles.title: The ‘stickiness’ of disgust: Testing the hypothesis of disgust intractability in the context of instrumental reversal learning.
articles.authors: Emily Bagley; Camilla Nord
articles.abstract: Discrete emotion theories conceptualise fear and disgust as distinct emotions. This notion is supported by the finding that Pavlovian disgust conditioning is more resistant to extinction than fear conditioning—disgust may be ‘stickier’ than fear. Dimensional emotion theories challenge this, suggesting that categorical differences between emotions reflect variations along shared dimensions of valence and arousal. Reinforcement learning assumes a dimensional framework: assuming that learning from negative events depends on an outcome’s valence and arousal. Here, using a novel online reversal learning task and modelling framework (n = 340), we show that instrumental punishment learning is not ‘outcome agnostic’. Emotion-learning differs from points-based learning, and disgust-learning is uniquely ‘sticky’, altering perseverative error-rate, lose-shift probability, and a model-based ‘stickiness’ parameter, relative to other types of learning. This suggests that whilst some features of learning are shared between emotions, disgust has a distinct behavioural profile, with implications for emotion science and computational psychiatry.

articles.title: When Vision Disagrees with Language: Private and Population-Level Color Knowledge  in Red–Green Dichromacy
articles.authors: Jiahui Lu; Ziyi Xiong; Peijun Yuan; Xiaoying Wang; Yanchao Bi
articles.abstract: Human concepts are shaped by two distinct information sources: private sensorimotor experience and socially transmitted knowledge mainly conveyed through language in an abstract symbolic form. Because information geometry in these sources is largely aligned, their relative contributions to conceptual representation are difficult to disentangle. We exploit a group-level dissociation, in which the alignment between sensory color geometry and population-level language structure diverges systematically (red–green dichromacy vs. trichromacy), and a model-level dissociation (object-color geometry derived from large language models vs. from image-based sensory models), to disentangle vision and language contributions to object knowledge. Sensory color geometry differed behaviorally and neurally between dichromats and trichromats, yet behavioral object-color representations converged across groups and corresponded robustly with language-derived geometry. LadATL consistently expressed language-derived geometry across tasks and groups, whereas LpFG showed a group-dependent representational profile in the chromatic-object task: trichromats showed relatively greater correspondence with sensory-derived geometry, whereas dichromats retained correspondence with both geometries. Dichromats also showed stronger intrinsic connectivity of LadATL with LpFG and EVC. These findings reveal how the brain flexibly draws on sensory evidence and socially transmitted knowledge to maintain population-aligned conceptual representations across heterogeneous sensory experiences.

articles.title: The broken brain? Prevalence and consequences of brain framing of mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Sanil Shashank Pandhare; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Public discourse often frames mental disorders as brain disorders, yet little is known about how this framing shapes lay beliefs. We combined large-scale text analysis of 55,068 New York Times articles with one correlational study (N = 204) and four preregistered vignette experiments (total N = 2,445) to examine both the prevalence and consequences of “brain talk” about mental disorders. We find that brain framing has become much more prevalent since 1980, and especially since 2004. We find evidence that brain framing increases belief in other biological and genetic causes; reduces belief in psychological and environmental causes, and strengthens beliefs in the efficacy of medication as a treatment. Effects on pessimism about recovery varied across studies and disorders. Brain framing had no robust effects on perceived age of onset, duration, severity, or beliefs about efficacy of psychotherapy treatment. Public beliefs about mental disorders are malleable and can be shaped by framing, highlighting the cognitive and societal consequences of brain framing in communication about mental health.

articles.title: Longitudinal and Latent-variable Extensions of the Triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence
articles.authors: Shiyao Wang; Jennifer Dang Guay; Karla Van Leeuwen; Evelien Schat; Eva Ceulemans
articles.abstract: When modeling interpersonal processes within triadic systems, researchers commonly encounter two types of analytical complexity: observations collected repeatedly over time, and constructs measured via multiple items. The current study introduces longitudinal and latent-variable extensions of the standard triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (tAPIM) to accommodate these data structures. The longitudinal extensions, the concurrent tAPIM and the temporal tAPIM, account for temporal dependence and temporal precedence in repeated observations, while the latent-variable extension models each member’s construct as a latent variable measured from multiple observed items. In addition, we identify measurement invariance across triad members as a challenge specific to triadic data analysis and conduct a simulation study to investigate the consequences of its violation for the estimation of actor and partner effects. The results indicate that: 1) imposing invariance constraints that are not empirically supported may bias the estimation of nonzero actor and partner effects associated with the noninvariant member, while effects of invariant members and zero effects are accurately recovered; 2) relaxing invariance constraints avoids bias in point estimates, but standard errors of effects associated with the noninvariant member were still inflated, reducing power to detect true effects. The current paper offers practical guidance for researchers modeling interdependence in triadic systems using multi-item or longitudinal data.

articles.title: It's a small world of signs: Semantic network structure in American Sign Language based on free associations
articles.authors: Zed Sehyr; Karen Emmorey; Elana Pontecorvo; Naomi Kenney Caselli; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles.abstract: Semantic network analyses have shown that words in spoken languages are organized into efficient "small-world" structures that support rapid lexical access and retrieval. However, little is known about whether similar organizational principles generalize to sign languages. We present the first large-scale analysis of semantic network structure in American Sign Language (ASL) using a free semantic association task. Deaf ASL signers (N = 45) produced three associations to 2,714 cue signs drawn from ASL-LEX, resulting in almost 100,000 cue–response pairs. We constructed (a) directed associative networks based on cue-response relationships and (b) undirected conceptual similarity networks based on cue–to-cue cosine similarity and compared ASL with English using matched subsets of the Small World of Words norms. We estimated network statistics and evaluated network topology using bootstrapping and degree-preserving random graphs. Both languages exhibited small-world organization indicating similar pressures on efficient semantic organization across language modalities. However, the languages differed in topology. Across network types, ASL exhibited longer average path lengths, and in conceptual similarity networks, lower clustering, suggesting reduced integration. In associative networks, ASL showed lower modularity, while in the conceptual similarity networks, ASL showed higher modularity than English, indicating a more compartmentalized semantic space. Further, more frequent signs occupied denser and more diverse semantic neighborhoods, whereas iconic signs exhibited fewer semantic connections and lower response diversity. These findings suggest that semantic memory is shaped by modality-independent organizational principles while also reflecting language-specific network topologies and structural pressures. The dataset and tools provide a basis for future cross-linguistic investigations.

articles.title: De-Pathologizing Student Distress: Policy Lessons from Finland for Global Higher Education Governance
articles.authors: Nicholas Rowe
articles.abstract:
Higher education student mental health remains misunderstood and inadequately prioritized by
university leadership and policy bodies. Extending a foundational Finnish study across ten
countries (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Netherlands, Norway, Finland, Germany, South Korea,
Australia), the baseline findings transpose with remarkable statistical consistency. Diagnosable
poor mental health averages 33.07% (21.97% severe) versus 33.0%/31% in Finland, while
postgraduate distress reaches 40.87% (40.0% predicted in Finland). Student distress doubles the
national average rate (16.02%), and suicide ideation averages 13.87% (mirroring Finland's
12.4–13.2%), with severe distress surpassing military veteran and professional benchmarks. As
arguably the largest and worst-affected cohort, student distress accounts for 388,100 lost lifeyears across these ten nations, driving multi-million treatment costs even at 30% utilization.
Despite being contended to fail to protect students, current policies continue to rely on reactive
individualizing counseling that frames structural distress as personal vulnerability attributed to
student failures in lifestyle and self-care. Furthermore, paternalistic "young person" narratives
misclassify mature cohorts, masking root causes inherent to the academic environment. The
study further shows that while poor mental health and suicide ideation seem virtually identical
and age-related for 18–25 year old students and non-students, the rates of older postgraduate
students are significantly different, showing almost double rates of incidence in both categories.
By empirically validating these cross-national realities, this review supports Finnish student
union demands for European Union health programmes to prioritize student mental health,
providing governance bodies across all jurisdictions with a robust foundation for systemic
structural reform and a non-judicial duty of care.

articles.title: Minimal Clinically Important Difference Score Estimates for the Aphasia Communication Outcome Measure
articles.authors: William D. Hula; Michael Walsh Dickey; Diane Kendall; Julie Wambaugh; Angela Grzybowski; William Irwin; Ann St. Jacque; Patrick Doyle
articles.abstract: The purpose of this study was to provide initial anchor-based minimally clinically importance difference score (MID) estimates for the Aphasia Communication Outcome Measure (ACOM), a patient-reported measure of communicative functioning. Persons with aphasia who participated in one of three clinical trials of speech-language treatment (n = 63) or an intensive comprehensive aphasia treatment program (n = 87) were administered the ACOM before and after treatment along with one or more anchor measures used to identify those demonstrating minimal positive change. MID estimates ranged from three T-score points for the full ACOM to four-to-five points for the 12-item adaptive version.

articles.title: Partisans are more likely to entrench their beliefs in misinformation when political outgroup members correct claims
articles.authors: Diego A. Reinero; Elizabeth Ann Harris; Steve Rathje; Annie Duke; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become a global issue with potentially dire consequences (e.g., election
results, COVID-19 vaccines, international conflicts). The most common strategy to reduce
beliefs in misinformation is to issue corrections or fact-checks. However, fact-checks are often
ineffective for polarized issues and there has been debate over whether misinformation
corrections sometimes "backfire," causing people to become more entrenched in misinformation.
Across three experiments (N = 1,217) we identify a key feature – the partisan identity of the
source – that explains when corrections will be effective and when they will be most likely to
backfire. We found that while corrections work on average, backfires still occurred 23% of the
time and were 52% more likely to occur when the correction came from a political outgroup vs.
ingroup member – leaving people with more entrenched beliefs in misinformation. Indeed, the
effect of partisan bias on initial belief in misinformation was 5x larger than the effect of
corrections. Partisan bias was most prominent and corrections were least effective when famous
politicians were involved. In sum, corrections have small effects compared to partisan identity
congruence, and sometimes backfire–especially if they come from a political outgroup member.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-reported Emotional Sharing in Social Interaction: A Meta Analysis
articles.authors: X. Jia; Karen Holtmaat; Y. Mo; ZIHAO Zeng; M. Kaneva; Annet Kleiboer; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: Through emotional sharing, individuals can make their emotional experiences available to others, creating opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation. Although gender differences in these behaviours have been documented across various domains, findings regarding their magnitude and consistency remain inconclusive. This meta-analysis examined gender differences in emotional sharing among adults. A systematic search identified 32 articles comprising 37 independent samples, 155 effect sizes, and 13,147 participants, including 8,504 women and 4,643 men. Overall, women reported higher levels of emotional sharing than men, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]. This effect was not significantly moderated by (1) functions (emotional expression, emotional disclosure, emotional expression as coping), (2) temporal level (dispositional, situational), (3) emotional valence (negative, positive or unspecified), (4) specific negative emotion (anger, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame/guilt, and unspecified negative emotions), and (5) the interpersonal target (romantic partner, friend, other, or no partner specified). Despite the absence of significant moderation effects, pooled estimates within most subgroups remained significantly positive, indicating higher levels of expression and disclosure among women than men across a wide range of emotional contexts and interpersonal relations.

articles.title: Measuring What Matters: Development of the TRACE Measure (Trauma, Resilience and Adversity in Cultural Experiences)
articles.authors: Jessica Pryce; Yaacov Petscher; Sarah O'Dell; Chelsey Bowman; Stephanie Curenton-Jolly
articles.abstract:
Purpose
The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) framework has been instrumental in understanding the long-term effects of childhood adversity but has been critiqued for its limited attention to cultural context and resilience. This study introduces and pilots the TRACE measure (Trauma, Resilience, and Adversity in Cultural Experiences), a culturally informed extension of ACE that integrates traditional adversity indicators, culturally specific adversities, and resilience factors within a single framework. The purpose of this study was to examine the preliminary psychometric properties and structural validity of the TRACE measure.

Methods
The TRACE measure was administered to parents (N = 122) of kindergarten students participating in a longitudinal literacy project across eight elementary schools. The instrument included three domains: traditional ACE items, culturally informed ACE (C-ACE) items, and culturally informed resilience (C-Resilience) items. Confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) using weighted least squares estimation (WLSMV) were conducted to evaluate dimensionality and model fit. Competing models, including correlated factors and bifactor structures, were compared. Reliability was assessed using coefficient omega (ω).

Results
Item-level CFAs demonstrated good model fit and strong reliability for both ACE (ω = .95) and C-ACE (ω = .93) domains, with acceptable reliability for C-Resilience (ω = .78). The correlated factors model showed poor fit, whereas bifactor models demonstrated improved fit, supporting a general adversity factor (G-ACE) alongside domain-specific factors. The general factor accounted for approximately 55%–59% of the common variance among adversity indicators. A moderate inverse relationship between adversity and resilience was observed (r ≈ −.50), indicating that these constructs remain distinct.

Conclusions
Findings provide support for the TRACE measure as a psychometrically viable and conceptually meaningful extension of the ACE framework. By integrating culturally informed adversity and resilience within a single instrument, TRACE offers a more comprehensive and contextual approach to assessing childhood experiences. This framework has implications for research, practice, and policy by supporting more culturally responsive and asset-based approaches to understanding and addressing childhood adversity.

Keywords: Adverse Childhood Experiences, Resilience, Cultural Contexts, Psychometrics, Trauma

articles.title: Political Emotions Shape Preferences for Leaders’ Facial Traits: Anger Favors Dominance, Fear Favors Trustworthiness
articles.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Manos Tsakiris
articles.abstract: Past work shows that conservatives prefer more dominant-looking political leaders, whereas liberals prefer more trustworthy-looking ones. We extend this by showing that, beyond partisanship, discrete political emotions independently shape preferences for leaders’ facial traits. A balanced sample of U.S. Republicans and Democrats identified the political issue that made them most angry or most afraid and then chose which leader would best address that issue using computer-generated faces varying in dominance and trustworthiness. Participants chose a more dominant and less trustworthy-looking leader more often when angry (49.5 percent) than when fearful (46.5 percent). Mechanistically, anger shifted choices toward more dominant-looking leaders by increasing reliance on dominance cues and reducing reliance on trustworthiness cues, whereas fear selectively increased reliance on trustworthiness cues. These findings show that political emotions exert distinct influences on leader evaluation with implications for democratic decision-making and electoral choices.

articles.title: No convincing evidence for a mediated effect of childhood trauma on alexithymia among patients with depression: A reevaluation of Zhou et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Zhou et al., we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model linking childhood trauma and alexithymia in individuals with depression. Our analyses show that the same covariance structure is equally compatible with a conceptually distinct latent-variable framework that does not require the directional pathway advanced in the original study. In this competing model, self-reported childhood trauma, sleep disturbances, anhedonia, and alexithymia are viewed as manifestations of a broader latent factor, core self-evaluation. The findings highlight a general challenge in the interpretation of observational data: the same pattern of associations may often be accounted for by multiple theoretically plausible models. Consequently, correlational evidence alone offers limited justification for privileging one explanatory account over others. Consideration of alternative models should therefore constitute a standard component of efforts to infer psychological mechanisms from observational findings.

articles.title: The Development of Compositionality in Language and Thought
articles.authors: Eulalie Péquay; Isabelle Dautriche
articles.abstract:
Compositionality is the property of a representational system whereby com-plex meanings
arise from the combination of simpler meaningful elements. Here we take a developmental
perspective to understand the origins of compositional representational systems and their
relation to language—an issue that bears on longstanding debates in cognitive science about
the structure of the human mind. Based on our review, we conclude that (a) well-controlled
evidence for compositional abilities during language acquisition remains scarce, although
some studies suggest infants begin to understand specific multiword combinations during the
second year of life, and (b) the key computation underlying compositionality—function
application—can be observed in infancy during the first year of life, well before, and even out-
side, compositional language. These findings suggest the mind may support compositional
operations prior to the emergence of compositional language, while leaving open questions
about how the development of compositional thought and compositional language interact.

articles.title: AI Mindset – An Empirically Tested Theoretical Framework on the Psychological Factors Shaping AI Competence and AI Use
articles.authors: Shuyan Feng; Martin J. Koch; Astrid Carolus
articles.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool in the educational sector. Research
examining the factors that facilitate its practical application by teachers has increased
substantially. Although empirical studies highlight the importance of psychological factors in
shaping engagement with AI technologies, the systematic integration of cognitive, emotional,
and motivational variables into AI use research remains fragmented. To advance the
psychological foundation, the present study proposed and empirically tested a model for AI
Mindset, conceptualised based on prior psychological and social-cognitive theories. The AI
Mindset framework posits a triadic structure, comprising dispositional factors, contextual and
situational characteristics, and technology-related appraisals, to explain teachers’ use of AI.
Structural equation modelling of 224 teachers revealed that AI Mindset variables significantly
predict pedagogical AI competence and AI use. Specifically, dispositional factors of openness
and need for relatedness associated with AI use indirectly through pedagogical AI
competence. Contextual and social facilitations of habit demonstrated the strongest direct
effect on AI use and indirect effect via competence. In terms of technology-related appraisals,
fear showed a complex pattern, with a positive direct effect on AI use but a negative indirect
effect through AI competence. The effect of effort expectancy was fully mediated by
competence, whereas hedonic motivation exerted a direct positive effect on AI use. In sum, by
introducing and empirically testing the AI Mindset framework, the present study integrates a
psychological perspective into the AI use research, provides a foundation for understanding
AI-related use patterns, and informs professional development and AI technology design.

articles.title: An optimal parameter range for tactile symbol recognition using a Haptic Mesh
articles.authors: Yu Cheng; Kenji Yamaguchi; Daniel Zymelka; Toshihiro Takeshita; Tatsuhiro Nakamura; Hiroki Togo; Kenji Yoshinaga; Takashi Hanakawa
articles.abstract: Tactile stimulation offers a potential means of conveying symbolic information when visual or auditory communication is unavailable or impractical. However, the temporal conditions required for reliable recognition of complex tactile symbols remain unclear. We systematically examined how stimulus duration (Duration) and interstimulus interval (ISI) jointly shape the recognition of digit-like tactile trajectories presented to the palm. Ten healthy adults received nine digit-like trajectories presented through a 3 × 3 vibrotactile actuator array under 30 Duration × ISI combinations and rated recognizability, perceived continuity, and stimulus intensity. We defined an Optimal Parameter Region (OPR) a priori as the largest 4-neighbor contiguous set of conditions with group-mean recognition accuracy of at least 0.60. We identified a cluster of 11 adjacent conditions, primarily at Durations of 200–300 ms and ISIs of 100–250 ms, corresponding to apparent motion speeds of approximately 28–58 mm s⁻¹. Within the OPR, recognition was more stable, and misclassification entropy was lower than outside it. Recognition also varied among conditions with the identical apparent motion speeds, prompting us to examine time allocation between Duration and ISI. Apparent motion speed accounted for 39% of the variance in recognition performance; relative time allocation explained an additional 13%. Subjective recognizability was higher within the OPR and closely tracked objective accuracy, whereas perceived continuity and stimulus intensity did not consistently explain recognition performance. These findings indicate that tactile-symbol recognition is optimal within a range of Duration–ISI combinations whose effects cannot be reduced to apparent motion speed alone, while trajectory geometry imposes an additional constraint on robust tactile-symbol design.

articles.title: Capturing the Hostile Attribution Bias through Conditional Reasoning Tasks: The Hostile Reasoning Test as an Indirect Measure of Aggressiveness
articles.authors: Paul Bacher; Manuel Becker; Fabian Hölzenbein; Hannes Krahl; Karl Christoph Klauer; Sarah Teige-Mocigemba
articles.abstract: The Hostile Attribution Bias is considered a central component of aggressiveness. It is thought to be a rather impulsive mechanism which justifies (reactive) aggressive behavior as logical and reasonable. Therefore, reasoning tasks may provide an unobtrusive means to make the hostile attribution bias accessible to measurement. In this manuscript, we developed such a task, the Hostile Reasoning Test (HRT), and assessed its psychometric properties. In three studies, we found that the HRT is reliable, shows convergent and discriminant validity for a male (Study 1, N=206) and female (Study 3, N=207) sample, and demonstrates incremental validity beyond self-reported aggressiveness in predicting reactive aggressive behavior (Study 2, N=78). The present results indicate that reasoning tasks such as the HRT are a promising complement to self-report measures, in particular if the more reactive and impulsive aspects of aggressiveness are of interest.

articles.title: Moral Concern for AI in an Economic Game
articles.authors: Carter Allen; Joshua Lewis; Lucius Caviola
articles.abstract: How will people morally regard increasingly human-like artificial intelligence systems? We introduce the AI Harm Game, a novel paradigm examining whether people will harm AI for personal gain. In our study, 498 U.S. participants interacted with GPT-4o in a three-round economic game. In each round, participants chose whether to harm the AI for a small monetary bonus (causing it to vividly simulate suffering) or refrain from harming it (eliciting gratitude). Although participants were overwhelmingly skeptical that current AIs can suffer, their decisions and reasoning about whether to harm the AI varied considerably. Participants harmed the AI in 1.4 out of 3 rounds on average. Women and older participants were more reluctant to harm the AI, while participants higher on measures of selfishness and psychopathy were more willing. These findings reveal that even without attributing consciousness to them, many people hesitate to harm responsive AIs, suggesting people’s moral impulses may generalize to future human–AI relationships.

articles_hidden.title: Lifetime Prevalence and Co-occurrence of Offensive Gun Use, Defensive Gun Use, and Nonfatal Firearm Victimization in a National Sample of US Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Brian M. Hicks; Dorothy Stearns; Amanda Price; Mark A. Ilgen
articles_hidden.abstract: Firearm-related encounters have the potential for high risk of injury, but few studies have estimated the prevalence and co-occurrence among offensive gun use (OGU), defensive gun use (DGU), and nonfatal firearm victimization (NFV) in a national sample. We did so with data from the National Firearms, Alcohol, Cannabis, and Suicide survey (N = 7034) of US adults that assessed broad definitions of gun use and victimization (e.g., gun displays to shootings). Lifetime prevalence was 5.2% (95% CI 4.5% to 6.0%) for OGU, 12.6% (95% CI 11.5% to 13.7%) for DGU, and 31.5% (95% CI 30.0% to 33.0%) for NFV. Using survey weights to extrapolate to the US adult population, we estimate nearly 13.9 million adults have used a gun offensively, 33.3 million have used a gun defensively, and 83.3 million have experienced NFV in their lifetime. Most respondents (~80%) only reported gun use and victimization that did not involve firing a gun. There was a high rate of co-occurrence between OGU and DGU (OR = 33.8, 95% CI 23.7 to 48.0), and between NFV and OGU (OR = 5.3, 95% CI 3.9 to 7.2) and DGU (OR = 4.5, 95% CI 3.7 to 5.6). Rates of OGU, DGU, and/or NFV were higher among respondents who were males, lower income, lived in more dangerous neighborhoods, current gun owners, and had a job that required carrying a firearm. Occupational firearm carriage was associated with especially high rates of OGU (20.5%, 95% CI 15.8% to 26.1%), DGU (49.6%, 95% CI 43.9% to 55.2%), and NFV (50.9%, 95% CI 45.2% to 56.5%). A large minority of Americans have had a firearm-related victimization experience, and a smaller but substantial proportion have used a gun for defense. OGU, DGU, and NFV frequently co-occur but event-level information is needed to delineate the mechanisms of overlap.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Average Changes: How the Distribution of Youth Mental Health Shifted Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic
articles_hidden.authors: Lianne P. de Vries; Elske Marra; Imme Rahmon; Tinca JC Polderman; Meike Bartels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Stress can affect not only average levels of mental health, but also how positive and negative aspects of mental health relate to one another. The COVID-19 pandemic provides a unique context to examine those population-level differences. We investigated youth mental health before, during, and after the pandemic by examining mean levels, association between wellbeing and depressive symptoms, and latent mental health profiles.
	Using large population-based samples from the Netherlands of youth aged 12–25 years, we compared mental health before (N = 14,146, 58% female), during (N = 14,308, 55% female), and after the pandemic (N = 37,797, 62% female) in a repeated cross-sectional design.
	Wellbeing and depressive symptoms were stronger correlated during (r = −.70) and after the pandemic (r = −.69) compared to pre-pandemic (r = −.49, ps < .001). Latent profile analyses further showed differences in the population distribution of mental health. Pre-pandemic, two profiles were identified, whereas during and after the pandemic three-profile solutions provided the best fit, including a large group with intermediate levels of wellbeing and depressive symptoms (38-40%). Across periods, most youth were classified in a high mental health profile (51-86%), whereas a smaller proportion were classified in a low mental health profile (8-14%). Loneliness, self-rated health, optimism, and stress exposure consistently differed between profiles. 
	Youth mental health differed across periods in average levels, the strength of the association, and distribution of wellbeing and depressive symptoms. These findings show the value of moving beyond average effects when studying population responses to large-scale stress.

articles_hidden.title: The Link between Warm Glow and Pro-Environmental Behaviors is Positive and Robust: A Scoping Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Linli Zhou; Cameron Brick; Disa Sauter
articles_hidden.abstract: When we engage in pro-environmental behaviors that align with our personal values, we can experience positive feelings, known as warm glow. Theories suggest a potential positive feedback loop such that people who anticipate feeling more warm glow are more likely to act pro-environmentally, and acting in line with their personal values may in turn elicit warm glow, thereby encouraging further pro-environmental behavior. There is considerable empirical work from psychology, marketing and economics investigating these relationships, but to date this work has not been systematically synthesized. A test of the strength and robustness of the theorized links is needed to answer the question of whether warm glow is in fact consistently related to pro-environmental behavior. We report a scoping review and meta-analysis probing the robustness of the associations between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Following the PRISMA guidance, we identified 94 papers with 251 effects based on 58,313 participants. A pre-registered three-level random-effects meta-analytic model was used to estimate overall effects and to examine moderation by behavioral domain and measurement approach. Sensitivity analyses were performed to test the robustness of the findings. Results indicate robust medium-to-large associations between both anticipated and experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors (rs: .43 – .53). Substantial heterogeneity persisted after accounting for moderators, suggesting meaningful variation in effect sizes across studies. Overall, these findings provide strong evidence of a clear link between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Future research using experimental and longitudinal designs will help clarify causal pathways in the positive feedback loop.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Inclusive Developmental Science: Translating Community Perspectives into Research Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Maheen Siddiqui; Rianne Haartsen; Anita Song; Roksana Seif Amirhosseini; Ana Maria Portugal; Chiara Bulgarelli; Anna Gui
articles_hidden.abstract: Developmental science continues to face challenges in engaging diverse families and ensuring diversity within the research workforce, limiting whose experiences and perspectives are represented in research. This study provides an empirically grounded, parent-informed account of the barriers and conditions that shape inclusive research practice. We conducted three participatory focus groups with parents from ethnic minority backgrounds in the UK (n = 17; two online, one hybrid). Transcripts were analysed using thematic analysis and integrated with insights accumulated across a year of Diversity in Developmental Science Network activities, including an online seminar series and conference panel. Findings were organised into four themes: barriers and enablers to research participation; building trust with communities; inclusive research design and transparency; and representation and cultural safety. Parents highlighted accessible and flexible practices, meaningful representation, culturally responsive materials, transparent communication, and stronger researcher-community relationships. Network activities further highlighted structural barriers and diversity within research teams.

articles_hidden.title: Parsing structured semantic knowledge from arbitrary text with GenAI
articles_hidden.authors: A.T. Lopes Rego; Joshua Snell; Martijn Meeter
articles_hidden.abstract: Frame Semantics offers a compelling framework for representing meaning as structured conceptual scenarios (frames). FrameNet operationalizes this theory as a lexical resource linking words to frames and their conceptual roles (frame elements, FEs). However, applying Frame Semantics to arbitrary text has historically required either laborious manual annotation or complex, task-specific classification pipelines that presuppose known targets and/or frames. Here we present an open-source method that leverages Generative AI (GenAI) to automatically parse semantic frames and their FEs from any input text, without requiring pre-specification of frames or target spans, or task-specific model training. The tool combines a retrieval step, in which candidate frames are identified via embedding-based semantic similarity, with a selection step, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) is prompted, using zero- or few-shot examples, to determine which frames are evoked, which spans trigger them, and which spans fill their FEs, returning a structured, machine-readable output. We detail installation, execution, and output interpretation, and provide a built-in evaluation module supporting exact, semantic, and graph-based matching against FrameNet's human-annotated data. This freely available tool lowers the barrier to frame-semantic analysis for researchers across linguistics, who wish to explore structured semantic content in naturalistic text, including in relation to behavioral and neural measures of language comprehension.

articles_hidden.title: Antenatal infant sleep information in Western Australia: A mixed-methods study of what parents received and what they wanted
articles_hidden.authors: Heather Liebregts; Alex Metse; Andrea R. Steele; Kelli Kathleen MacMillan; Rhonda Marriott; Renita Almeida
articles_hidden.abstract:
Problem. Pregnancy is a finite window wherein parents' expectations of infant care develop, yet parents’ experiences of and preferences for antenatal infant sleep preparation are uncharacterised. 

Background. Parents in Western settings commonly report infant sleep problems, and interventions are predominantly behavioural. Antenatal provision addresses sleep safety rather than developmental-relational preparation. 

Aim. To describe what antenatal infant sleep information Western Australian parents received, their satisfaction, preferences for its timing and provider, and what they wished they had received.

Methods. A mixed-methods online survey of 185 Western Australian parents and expectant parents (180 with a child aged 0–3 years; five pregnant). Closed items addressed information received, satisfaction, and preferences; an open-ended item was analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Findings. Just over half (53.5%; 99/185) received no antenatal information; where provided, midwives were the most frequent source (34.0%; 63/185) and satisfaction was modest. The antenatal period and first month were most endorsed (75.0%, 135/180; 66.1%, 119/180), with child health nurses (35.6%; 64/180) and midwives (30.6%; 55/180) preferred as providers. Four themes captured parents’ preferences: preparation for likely bedsharing; recalibrated expectations; validation of responsive caregiving; and non-prescriptive guidance.

Discussion. Provision was limited and only moderately satisfying. Parents sought guidance positioning them as decision-makers engaging with biologically typical infant behaviour. 

Conclusion. Relational, non-prescriptive preparation, including how to bedshare more safely, initiated antenatally by midwives and continued postnatally by child health nurses, would address an unmet need within existing perinatal care.

articles_hidden.title: Roles of conceptual development in the training and acquisition of compassion practices
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Condon; Lawrence Barsalou
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conceptual development is a fundamental feature of contemplative practice but has received little attention in contemplative science. In Buddhism, for example, the eightfold path begins with right view, which includes comprehension of interdependence, suffering, and so on. In Tibetan traditions, foundational practices introduce conceptual frames, including aphorisms and visualizations, that help access capacities for compassion and wisdom. In this article, we take a lifespan approach to examine how conceptual development supports compassion training. We focus on relational practices adapted from Tibetan Buddhism, which involve calling to mind sources of love, comfort, and safety to establish a secure base and an internal holding environment–an embodied stance of stillness, curiosity, and care for all physical and mental patterns.
