articles_hidden.authors: Ryan L. Farmer; Emily Nicole Srisarajivakul; Samuel Y. Kim; Imad Zaheer
articles_hidden.abstract: Public schools are charged with educating every child who enters them under a legal and ethical mandate that practice be grounded in evidence, yet the gap between that mandate and routine practice remains substantial across public education. Using school psychology as a case study, we argue that evidence-based practice's (EBP) persistent failure to close this gap reflects a mismatch between the inherited framework and the structural and institutional conditions of public education, rather than practitioner values alone. Six interrelated failures are documented: conflation of EBP as a decision-making model with specific intervention adoption; inconsistent evidentiary standards; demographic mismatch between research samples and served populations; commercial capture of the evidence infrastructure; failures of contextual fit and transportability; and the absence of mechanisms for discontinuing ineffective practices. These failures persist through professional ossification and school psychology's location within education bureaucracies. In response, we propose an epistemological architecture adapted from evidence-based public health, operationalized here as the evidence-based school psychology (EBSP) model, with a three-level evidentiary sequence that provides the de-implementation mechanism the current framework structurally lacks. We offer recommendations for practitioners, trainers, and researchers to operationalize this model in practice.

articles_hidden.title: From Detection to Behavioral Change: A Scoping Review of Natural Language Processing in Substance Use Research
articles_hidden.authors: Erin Prince; Sheridan Fine; Francesca Filbey
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Natural language processing (NLP) has emerged as a promising approach for extracting
clinically relevant information from unstructured text that would otherwise be difficult to capture
through manual review alone. Although NLP in medical settings began in the 1960s, applications have
expanded rapidly in the 2000s, with broader use of digital narrative data such as electronic health
records (EHRs), clinical notes, psychotherapy transcripts, and other language-based data sources. In
substance use research, however, the literature on NLP applications remains fragmented across data
sources, methods, and clinical domains, making it difficult to identify areas of convergence and
important gaps. Accordingly, this scoping review examined NLP applications in substance use research,
focusing on clinical screening and phenotyping, risk prediction, treatment outcomes, and psychotherapy
process.
Method: A systematic search of nine clinical and technical databases identified studies published
between 2016 and 2026 to examine NLP applications related to substance use behaviors, treatments,
and clinically meaningful outcomes. Following screening and eligibility review, 28 studies were included.
Extracted data included substance use focus, setting, data source, NLP methods, outcome domain, and
key findings.
Results: Most studies (78.6%) utilized EHR clinical notes from U.S. healthcare systems, focusing primarily
on opioid outcomes. NLP methods consistently improved substance use detection compared to
structured diagnostic coding, contributing to nuanced models of overdose risk, relapse, treatment
attrition, and opioid prescribing. Recent work focused on detection and prediction to improve
multidimensional characterization and computational phenotyping of substance use populations. Across
psychotherapy studies, semantic, syntactic, contextual, and affective language features captured
clinically meaningful behavior processes and, in recent work, predicted subsequent alcohol use
3
outcomes. However, external validation performance often declined across datasets. Few studies
examined non-opioid substances, spoken language, or community samples.
Discussion: NLP methods demonstrate potential for improving substance use detection,
characterization, and modeling of behaviors across clinical and behavioral domains. Current work
suggests a shift from simple classification towards richer representations of behavioral and psychosocial
processes with notable limitations in generalizability, data diversity, and external validation remaining
challenging for substance use research.

articles_hidden.title: Implementation Outcomes and Effectiveness of a Personalized Single Session Cognitive Behavioral Intervention for Depression and Anxiety
articles_hidden.authors: Yui Ting Chloe Au; Yousheng Lester LAI; Jolie LOH; Mary Eileen McNamara; Jasper A. J. Smits; Kean J. Hsu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Single-session interventions (SSIs) have become increasingly popular
psychotherapeutic interventions in recent years due to their potential in providing a therapeutic
and problem-focused experience in one encounter. However, less focus has been given to
dissemination and implementation outcomes for SSIs within existing healthcare settings. This
study evaluated the effectiveness and suitability for broad implementation of a personalized
Single Session Cognitive Behavioral Intervention (SSCBI) for depression and anxiety,
delivered in a university-based training clinic in Singapore. Using a mixed-methods design,
adult therapy clients (N = 24) completed pre-treatment and follow-up measures assessing
depression, anxiety, and cognitive and affective subjective well-being. Quantitative analyses
showed reductions in both symptoms of depression (d = 0.94, p < .001) and anxiety (d = 0.45,
p = .038). Semi-structured interviews were conducted with clients (n = 9) and clinicians (n =
9), and thematic analysis identified twelve key themes mapped to five implementation
outcomes: acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, fidelity, and adoption. Both clients and
clinicians reported high acceptability of the intervention, highlighting its structure, relevance,
and utility in supporting coping skill development. Clinicians felt the protocol was feasible and
appropriate for clients with relatively less complex presentations, with full protocol adherence
achieved across all therapeutic sessions. Recruitment (63.5%) and completion (78.1%) rates
exceeded the pre-registered feasibility benchmarks. These findings provide preliminary
evidence supporting our personalized SSCBI as an effective and scalable brief psychological
intervention, particularly suited for resource-limited settings. Future research should
investigate its longer-term impact, cost-effectiveness, and broader applicability in community
and primary care contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Parent and Youth Perceptions of Attachment:  Validation of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI)
articles_hidden.authors: Jason W. Payne; Sebastian Dys; Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Attachment is a robust protective factor for youth mental health. This study examined the factor structure and validity of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI), a 16-item measure of youth (8–18 years) attachment in parent and other caregiving relationships. Structural validity was assessed using parallel youth and parent report formats among over 2,000 respondents from both clinical and community samples.
Method: Participants were caregivers in three independent clinical samples and one community sample (N = 571, 407, 220, and 551) and youth self-reporting in the first clinical sample (N = 571). Youth were 7.5 to 18 years old (sample means 13.4 to 14.6), 51% to 61% female, and 61% to 78% White. Caregivers were predominantly mothers (80% to 96%). Confirmatory factor analyses were followed by multi- informant models and tests of associations with caregiver-reported internalizing and externalizing problems.
Results: A two-factor structure replicated across all samples under a single specification, whereas a one- factor model fit poorly. Differential associations with youth internalizing and externalizing problems supported the discriminant validity of each subscale. Multi-method analyses confirmed that anxiety and avoidance were distinguishable across informants, while moderate parent-youth convergence suggested complementary rather than interchangeable perspectives.
Conclusions: The findings support the AAAAI as a measure of attachment anxiety and avoidance in both parent and youth report. For research and clinical practice, the two subscales capture distinct attachment patterns, and parent and youth forms together show where caregivers and youth see the relationship similarly and where they differ.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in eye movements dynamics of free viewing conscious and unconscious naturalistic scenes
articles_hidden.authors: Shaked Lublinsky; Yoni Pertzov lab; Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg; Liad Mudrik
articles_hidden.abstract: Different individuals produce different gaze patterns while exploring the world. Here we examined whether these differences occur also when viewing a scene unconsciously. We reanalyzed the data collected in Lublinsky et al., 2025, looking for two types of individual differences; content-based individual differences, which depend on the visual stimulus presented, and content-free individual differences, which do not relate to the observed stimuli. In two experiments, 52 participants viewed scenes consciously and unconsciously, rendered invisible via Continuous Flash Suppression (CFS). We found reliable content-based individual differences in the conscious condition only, suggesting that unconscious processing of scenes does not evoke consistent patterns within individuals. On the other hand, we found consistent content-free individual differences in both visibility conditions. In the unconscious condition, these most likely reflect consistent gazing patterns on the CFS stimulation (i.e., the changing color patches). Yet these content-free measures showed differential strength for seen vs. unseen trials, thereby validating participants' subjective reports. These findings provides novel means to support a dissociation between conscious and unconscious processing under CFS, which is notoriously difficult due to methodological challenges.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding Stigmatization of Organic and Conventional Farmers: Occupational Taint, Dehumanization, and Perceived Burden
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas David; Gaétan Marinho; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Farmers face substantial physical and mental health risks, yet the role of public stigma toward agricultural groups remains insufficiently understood. This study examined stigmatization of organic and conventional farmers in France, using social distance as the main indicator of social rejection, and investigated whether it was associated with perceived vital forces and burdens, occupational taint, dehumanizing perceptions, and infra-humanization. A sample of 250 French participants completed an online questionnaire assessing perceptions of both organic and conventional farmers. Conventional farmers were evaluated less favourably than organic farmers across all stigma-related dimensions. However, partial correlation analyses showed that the same two dimensions remained robustly associated with social distance toward both groups: perceived burden and biologization. Item-level analyses of the perceived burden dimension further suggested that social distance was especially related to the perception that farmers benefit from collective wealth without sufficient contribution. Overall, the findings suggest mainly quantitative rather than qualitative differences between stigmatization of organic and conventional farmers: conventional farmers appear more strongly stigmatized, but social rejection toward both groups relies on similar social-perceptual pathways.

articles_hidden.title: Orthography Shapes L2 Stress PerceptionAcross Development: Evidence from L1 Mandarin Learners of Portuguese
articles_hidden.authors: Chao Zhou; Guilherme D. Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite growing evidence that written input shapes second-language speech learning, its role in suprasegmental acquisition remains underexplored. This study examines whether orthography facilitates lexical stress identification through syllable weight. Portuguese is well suited for this question because stress placement is strongly conditioned by syllable weight, which is transparently encoded in the writing system. A total of 186 L1 Mandarin speakers identified stress location in Portuguese pseudowords presented either auditorily or with accompanying written forms. Naïve listeners used syllable weight as a stress cue only when orthographic information was available, whereas experienced learners showed weight sensitivity from auditory input alone. For experienced learners, however, orthography did not further enhance weight sensitivity; instead, it biased responses toward the default penultimate- stress pattern. These findings suggest that orthographic effects change over L2 development, interacting with auditory cue weighting and distributional regularities in L2 stress perception.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Difficult to be a People Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing—meaning the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others—has gained a lot of interest in lay psychology. Only recently have scientific endeavors been devoted to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. Its three subscales (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) provided favorable item discrimination, widely dispersed item thresholds (even though the thresholds to obtain high scores were located at best at moderate levels), and ample levels of item information and reliability across the three latent trait spectra. These findings underscore that people-pleasing, as measured with the People Pleasing Scale, refers to an everyday rather than a clinical construct. As such, it is apt to be used to assess people-pleasing in studies across diverse areas of academic psychology and for applied contexts alike.

articles_hidden.title: Development and characterization of a standardized stimuli set of 240 famous faces in Quebec
articles_hidden.authors: Nastasia Maria Mitrikeski; Mélodie Leclerc; Zihao Geng; Maxime Montembeault
articles_hidden.abstract:
Famous faces are especially well suited to studying the semantic component of face processing because they carry a sense of familiarity shared across individuals. Recognizing famous faces is not only relevant to research, but it is also clinically informative. Famous-face recognition deficits are observed in prosopagnosia and neurodegenerative disease. They are differentially affected across dementia syndromes, making their assessment useful for differential diagnosis. Testing familiar face processing requires stimuli suited to a specific geographic and sociocultural context, which has led to the development of standardized famous-face databases in France, Great Britain, Spain, and Portugal. However, no such standardized set currently exists for the Quebec population. We therefore created a stimuli set of 240 locally and internationally known famous
people across four categories (politicians, singers, actors, and athletes), spanning different time periods and including famous people of different races, ethnicities, ages, and genders. Through an online survey on Qualtrics, adults aged 40 to 79 from Quebec are rating the famous faces on distinctiveness, familiarity, valence, and name frequency, alongside measures of famous face recognition, naming, knowledge, and agreement. Descriptive statistics were obtained for each famous face, and the standardized stimuli set will be available in open access once data collection is complete. Future directions include the development of new cognitive tests for face processing impairments, notably in neurodegenerative disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Meta-Analytic Evidence for an Ecological Account of the Relationship between Acculturative Stressors and Adaptation
articles_hidden.authors: Dinh-Hung Vu; Kinga Bierwiaczonek; Mike W.-L. Cheung; Rongtian Tong; Jonas R. Kunst; Nora C. G. Benningstad; Evita Willemiek van Duin; Karine Lindholm; Colleen Ward
articles_hidden.abstract: Acculturative stressors, reliably associated with poor migrant adaptation to receiving societies, are highly context-dependent. Yet, how context shapes the stressor-adaptation relationship remains poorly understood. In two pre-registered meta-analyses, we tested the moderating role of structural, cultural, and temporal factors in cross-sectional data (Study 1) and examined the temporal dynamics in longitudinal data (Study 2). Study 1 (k = 229, N = 66,409) modelled origin and receiving country contexts simultaneously to test specific migration routes. Structural factors, such as the receiving country’s poverty, inequality, and unemployment, intensified stressor-adaptation associations. Effects of cultural factors mostly concerned socio-cultural adaptation, most notably stronger stressor-adaptation associations when migrants moved from collectivistic to individualistic societies. For temporal context, longer residence in the receiving country was linked to weaker stressor-adaptation associations. Study 2 (k = 22, N = 8,555) validated the cross-sectional finding that stressor-adaptation associations attenuate over time: effects were stronger and reciprocal at earlier timepoints.

articles_hidden.title: Theorytopia: Psychological Science in 2050
articles_hidden.authors: Luiza Yuan; Denny Borsboom; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Jason Nak; Anne M. Scheel; Noah N'Djaye Nikolai van Dongen; Laura Francina Bringmann; Kyra Evers; Pritam Laskar; Willem Frankenhuis
articles_hidden.abstract: The year is 2050, and psychology has transformed into a theory-driven science—a Theorytopia. Drawing on initiatives and frameworks developed over the past decades since the Theory Crisis, three main advancements have made this transformation possible. First, specialization in theory construction within psychology ensures that theories are tested independently of those who propose them. Methodologies and training in theorizing have been strengthened, while new repositories, such as the “Garden of Living Theories,” promote cumulative record-keeping. Second, worldwide efforts consolidate robust psychological phenomena, reduce reliance on WEIRD samples, and systematize theoretical concepts. Measurement validation and studies probing context-dependency and auxiliary assumptions are now valued research directions in psychology, providing improved empirical bases for rigorous conceptual work. Third, stronger theories better serve the public. Computational modeling, tighter collaboration with stakeholders, better intervention design, new interfaces between science and the public, and the active inclusion of diverse perspectives are improving not just psychology’s societal impact, but also its epistemic value. In this paper, we describe what discussions, actions, and structural changes have led to these drastic improvements, and invite readers to participate in co-shaping the future of a psychological Theorytopia.

articles_hidden.title: Generative AI Use in Selection Testing: Applicant Perceptions, Behaviors, and Test Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Matt Brown; Michelle Martin-Raugh; Emily Gallegos; Michael Grossenbacher; Jessica Haig
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is potentially an effective tool for cheating unproctored internet tests (UIT). However, the practical threat posed by GenAI depends not only on its capabilities, but also whether applicants choose to use it and can do so effectively under real, high-stakes testing conditions. We conducted a series of large-scale surveys of US job applicants who completed selection test batteries in 2026 (n = 141,766) to observe the availability of GenAI assistance, decisions to use that assistance, and the extent to which its use yields higher test scores. Nearly half of applicants reported using GenAI during their job search (49%) but were more likely to use GenAI to help write resumes or to learn about jobs than to help during selection testing. Applicants who used GenAI during testing (9% of all applicants) scored lower on GMA (d = -0.28) and most personality traits (ds between -0.51 and -0.29). Effect sizes were consistent in magnitude and direction across job families, job zones, or AI adoption for work. Our findings suggest that the threat of GenAI on UIT depends not only on the capability of GenAI tools, but also on whether applicants choose to use them and can do so effectively under real testing conditions.

articles_hidden.title: The Effects of Group-Based Community Interventions on Social Reintegration of Marginalized Adults with Mental Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Thorup Dalgaard; jakob Kaarup Jensen; Jasmin Sami Adada; Maya Christiane Flensborg Jensen; Elizabeth Bengtsen; Mikkel Helding Vembye; Elizabeth Tipton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background 
Adults with mental illness who also experience social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, yet scalable interventions addressing both dimensions of recovery remain limited.

Aims 
To evaluate the effects of group-based community interventions on social reintegration and mental health among socially marginalized adults with mental illness.

Methods 
We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions delivered in OECD countries. Searches identified 28,980 records; 62 studies met the inclusion criteria and 49 studies, contributing 349 effect sizes, were included in the meta-analysis. Outcomes were classified as social reintegration or mental health. Meta-analytic models accounted for dependent effect sizes within studies.

Results 
Group-based community interventions improved social reintegration (g = 0.195, 95% CI [0.122, 0.268]) and mental health (g = 0.215, 95% CI [0.090, 0.340]) relative to control conditions, corresponding to effects approximately 2.3 and 1.4 times larger, respectively, than the typical improvements under treatment as usual. Effects varied substantially across studies and outcomes, while measured moderators explained little of this heterogeneity. Effects on social reintegration and mental health were positively associated. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses and showed little indication of publication bias. Nearly half of studies were preregistered and contributed approximately two-thirds of all effect sizes. Preregistered studies yielded smaller social reintegration effects than non-preregistered studies, although the average effect remained statistically significant and substantively meaningful.

Conclusions 
Group-based community interventions can improve both social reintegration and mental health among marginalized adults with mental illness, suggesting that they may support multidimensional recovery. Their potential value therefore extends beyond scalability and lower delivery costs to substantively meaningful improvements in outcomes. However, substantial unexplained heterogeneity indicates that benefits are unlikely to be uniform across populations, interventions, and settings.

What is already known on this topic
Adults experiencing both mental illness and social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, while existing systematic reviews on group-based interventions have largely focused on specific diagnoses, intervention types, or psychiatric symptoms.

What this study adds
Across 49 studies contributing 349 effect sizes, group-based community interventions produced positive average effects on both social reintegration and mental health. Effects in the two domains were positively associated, but substantial heterogeneity remained largely unexplained.

articles_hidden.title: From Probabilistic to Deterministic Missingness: When Predictive Mean Matching Breaks Down Under MAR
articles_hidden.authors: Kristian Kleinke; Henrik Gaisbauer
articles_hidden.abstract: Predictive mean matching (PMM) is usually considered a good alround imputation method that yields unbiased statistical inferences in many scenarios. A known drawback of PMM is that it imputes observed values and thus, by design, cannot make extrapolations beyond the range of the observed data. Nor can it make interpolations in regions, where the data are sparse. The purpose of the present paper is to further explore the breaking points of PMM and to provide applied researchers with a practical tool to diagnose if there are sufficient observed donor cases in all regions of the data space for PMM to work. In a Monte Carlo study with 752 conditions, we systematically varied the missingness mechanism from missing completely at random via probabilistic mechanisms of increasing selection sharpness up to a deterministic threshold. Under probabilistic selection, PMM was nearly unbiased even under relatively high missingness rates. When the outcome, however, was missing beyond a threshold (e.g., when a follow-up is administered only to those above a certain screening score), the slope in a bivariate regression model was attenuated by almost exactly the proportion of missing values, irrespective of the true effect, the sample size, and the number of donors. One noteworthy finding of our simulation was that confidence intervals tended to fail before point estimates did. A diagnostic computed from the observed data—the mean distance from each case to be imputed to its nearest potential donor—predicted coverage closely (ρ = −0.92). We provide an R function for this check and recommend running it before selecting PMM as imputation method in a given scenario. In situations where no suitable donors can be found, applied researchers should select other imputation methods (that can extrapolate).

articles_hidden.title: The Modulation of Mood Through Absorption in Music Listening
articles_hidden.authors: Bradley Austin-Keiller; Frank Russo; Karina J Linnell
articles_hidden.abstract: Music listening is widely used to regulate emotion, yet the listener-level processes underlying affective change remain under-specified. This longitudinal study examined musical absorption as one such process, testing a novel Musical Absorption Training (MAT) protocol designed to scaffold absorptive engagement. Adults aged 55 and older (analytic N = 49) completed 16 listening sessions over four weeks. Participants were randomly assigned either to eight sessions of guided MAT followed by eight unguided sessions, or to unguided listening throughout. Valence and arousal were rated before and after each session, state absorption after each session, and trait absorption (AIMS) at baseline, Session 8, and Session 16. Mixed-effects models showed that greater state absorption predicted larger within-session increases in valence and arousal, driven mainly by within-person fluctuations. MAT did not raise state absorption during the guided phase, but after guidance ended, absorption was preserved in the MAT group. Trait absorption increased over time without a significant Group × Time interaction; however, higher state absorption during the maintenance phase predicted higher trait absorption at study end. These findings identify absorption as a promising listener-level correlate of music-related mood change and offer preliminary evidence that structured attentional guidance may help sustain absorptive engagement across repeated listening.

articles_hidden.title: A Revolution in Search of an Estimand: On the Idionomic Proposal of Hayes et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Magnus Johansson; Matti Vuorre; Nils Olof Wilhelm Hentati Isacsson; Kristoffer Magnusson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Hayes et al. (2026) argue that clinical psychology is stalled by an “ergodic error”, the application
of group-level statistics to individuals, and propose idionomic analysis as the remedy. We agree
that pooled associations do not need to describe individuals and that treatment effects vary
between people, but the proposed remedy does not answer the clinical question. Personalizing
treatment is a causal problem, yet Hayes et al. never state which causal quantity, or estimand,
they target. Their evidence consists of observational within-person associations, which cannot
separate effects from confounding that varies over time. Applied to observational data, none of
the recommended methods can identify a causal effect. Non-ergodicity shows only that pooled
and individual associations may differ, not that causal effects do. The reported heterogeneity is
also questionable, in part because person-level estimates from short series are imprecise. The
reliability Hayes et al. cite against this concern describes person means rather than within-
person variation, and the statistics summarizing heterogeneity have not been adequately
checked against simulated data in which there is no heterogeneity. Designs that randomize
treatment within or between persons can target person-level and conditional effects, within
limits set by carryover and irreversible change. Rather than the proposed idionomic revolution,
clinical psychology needs to join the causal revolution, in which the estimand is stated before
the data are analyzed.

articles_hidden.title: Do God Primes Prime God? Converging Evidence Against the Efficacy of Experimental Religious Priming
articles_hidden.authors: Will M Gervais; Meara Geraty; Aiyana Koka Willard
articles_hidden.abstract:
How does religion change people? Religious priming has been used to scientifically ask this question for nearly two
decades, linking religious cognition to varied outcomes – especially prosociality. Priming research has proliferated
in the absence of direct evidence that religious priming tools work as implicitly assumed: by activating religious
cognition. Here, we evaluate this assumption. Across a bias-adjusted meta-analysis (k = 66) and two experiments
(total N = 2960), we report strong and converging evidence: 1) against the validity of the most commonly used priming
methodology, 2) against even overt primes’ abilities to robustly affect prosocial cognition or behavior, 3) against a
meaningful relationship between cognitive activation of religion and prosocial behavior; further, evidence was 4) in
favor of even ineffective primes nonetheless inviting participant suspicion. Combined, this suggests that the evidential
strength of existing priming research is likely overstated, with critical assumptions now contradicted by evidence.

articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing—meaning the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others—has gained a lot of interest in lay psychology. articles_hidden.title: Bounded rational world modelling
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel David Jones; Antonia Reul; Paul Rauwolf
articles_hidden.abstract: The effective navigation of complex environments requires forming and acting on memories of actions, states, and values; features collectively referred to as a 'mental model'. But what are the decision rules that shape world model acquisition? Dominant normative responses to this question characterise the decision about what information to engage with, and the fidelity in which to encode that information, in terms of cost-value optimisation. However, this is untenable in natural environments of any complexity. The current report presents new empirical support for a complementary characterisation of world model acquisition based on realistic assumptions about human decision-making. Across two pre-registered experiments, N=108 people explored a virtual machine in which combinations of action switches map to symbolic information with associated values. In experiment one, participants were incentivised to maximise value acquisition under costs, while in experiment two participants were incentivised to explore the machine without costs. Each experiment involved a test battery assessing participants' understanding of the machine. We show that varying value structure dramatically shapes world model acquisition - in particular, knowledge of low-value options is sparse under search costs. Search is affected by lapses in memory, and metacognitive awareness of learning progress is poorly calibrated with accuracy. Most importantly, comparison to optimal benchmarks suggests that shortfalls in human performance are attributable to satisficing against a subjective aspiration threshold and updating world models locally in light of the feedback elicited. These results demonstrate that noisy myopic satisficing is a core decision rule shaping world model acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: Nausea and disgust as aversive interoceptive signals in psychopathology.
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Bagley; Camilla Nord
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Disruptions in reinforcement learning are reliably seen across
psychiatric disorders. Yet the origins of reinforcement learning are in interoceptive
signals: we learn to pursue primary interoceptive rewards, such as calories, or avoid
primary interoceptive punishments, such as nausea. Interoceptive punishments may
drive diverse aspects of psychopathology, from enhanced disgust processing in
obsessive compulsive disorder to restricted eating behaviour in anorexia nervosa.

Aims: To determine the role of interoceptive punishments in psychopathology, we
tested a) whether the experience of the interoceptive punishment of nausea covaried
with psychiatric symptoms and b) whether learning about a close proxy of
interoceptive punishment—disgust—predicted psychopathology.

Method: In a large representative sample (n=308), recruited online, participants
completed a battery of questionnaires, on which we conducted a factor analysis, and
a learning task, to which we fit computational reinforcement learning models. This
enabled us to quantify both disgust-related and unrelated psychopathology as well
as reinforcement learning measures from disgust-based, fear-based and points-
based outcomes.

Results: Self-report measures of nausea were strongly and generally predictive of
psychopathology, unexpectedly spanning nearly all symptoms and syndromes. A
similar pattern emerged for self-reported disgust. This suggests that enhanced
experience of interoceptive punishment is a general feature of psychiatric
symptomatology. Additionally, a subset of questionnaires (contamination OCD,
blood-injury phobia and spider phobia) related to computationally-derived measures
of behaviour on a disgust-learning task, indicating a potential mechanism of
interoceptive punishment learning.

Conclusions: These findings provide insight into a previously-unexplored symptom
of mental health problems, nausea, and demonstrate a potential mechanism by
which aversive interoceptive learning may contribute to psychopathology, revealing a
new potential interoceptive treatment target.

articles_hidden.title: Contact first, protocols second: How to establish a therapeutic alliance in team-based care for severe mental illness according to mental health professionals?
articles_hidden.authors: Melina Tetzlaff; Jojanneke Bruins; Kurt van Houten; Stynke Castelein
articles_hidden.abstract: Intro: The therapeutic alliance (TA) is a well-established predictor of treatment outcomes, yet traditional conceptualizations are usually dyadic. For individuals with severe mental illness (SMI), contemporary care is primarily delivered in multidisciplinary teams, raising questions about how the TA is established when responsibility is shared across providers. Qualitative research on this topic remains scarce. Methods: We aimed to: 1) conceptualize the modern TA; 2) identify factors that facilitate TA development; 3) provide an initial exploration of a treatment team alliance; and 4) formulate practice-oriented recommendations for TA development. N=13 mental health professionals (MHPs), including peer support workers (PSWs), participated in in-depth, semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis, supported by iterative coding, researcher triangulation, member-checking, and peer-debriefing. Results: Participants described the TA as dynamic, reciprocal, and context-dependent and identified the relational component as its foundation. Key facilitators included genuine listening, authenticity, transparency, reliability, balanced professional boundaries, and collaborative decision-making. Protocolization, time constraints, and authority were identified as barriers. In team-based care, participants emphasized consistency, effective communication, and self-reflection among MHPs, and a designated point of contact for service users. Conclusion: Our findings emphasize the importance of establishing a connection before starting protocol-centric treatment.

articles_hidden.title: Detecting Response Styles in Visual Analogue Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik Vollbracht; Tanja Lischetzke; Mirka Henninger
articles_hidden.abstract: Response styles are prevalent in self-report data and may bias parameter estimates. While there are various approaches for detecting response styles in Likert-type data, models for visual analogue scales remain scarce. We propose a novel modeling framework that extends the beta item response model by Noel and Dauvier (2007) to jointly detect extreme response style, midpoint response style, and acquiescent response style. Estimated in a Bayesian framework using Stan, the model performed well in a comprehensive simulation study. Parameter recovery was primarily influenced by the number of (reverse-scored) items and the variance of response styles, whereas sample size had a negligible effect. The model’s practical utility is illustrated using empirical data (Kuhlmann et al., 2017), for which it demonstrated superior model fit compared to the original beta item response model. Overall, the proposed framework provides researchers with a principled approach to account for response styles in visual analogue scale data.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Distance Is Domain-Relative: Comparing Value-Based and Norm-Based Distances Using the Cultural Fixation Index
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Eriksson; Pontus Strimling
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers enter cultural distance, a single number, as a general-purpose control for cultural difference and use it to select study sites they hope are culturally distant. Both practices assume that the number is a stable property of a society pair, independent of the cultural content the items represent. We test that assumption using the cultural fixation index (CFst) of Muthukrishna et al. (2020), holding the estimator and societies fixed while varying content. Within the World Values Survey, distance matrices constructed from political and moral-religious value items share only about a quarter of their variance. Across domains, distance matrices built from value items and Global Study of Everyday Norms ratings share between about a tenth and a fifth of their variance, depending on the minimum sample per society. The low cross-domain agreement persists under controls for survey era, coding resolution, reliability, distance formula, and sample composition. Cultural distance is only defined relative to the content domain from which its items are drawn and does not reliably transfer to another domain. Researchers should name the domain from which a cultural-distance measure is constructed and match it to the research question.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
articles_hidden.authors: Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; Patricia Opondo; Juan David Leongómez; Yuto Ozaki; Zixuan Jia; Suzanne Purdy; Patrick E. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. Critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on new data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators (“Many Voices”), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles_hidden.authors: Leili Rouhi; Zuleykha Gasimova; Valerie A Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: Monitoring processes, such as confidence, are assumed to guide control processes, such as whether to change or persist with a response. Yet whether this monitoring–control link depends on the same working memory (WM) resources implicated in reasoning itself remains unclear. Fuzzy-trace theory (FTT) holds that reasoning relies primarily on low-effort gist representations and that errors arise when a salient but inappropriate gist interferes with the appropriate one. Drawing on FTT and the meta-reasoning framework the role of WM in reasoning, monitoring and control. Participants (N = 998) solved belief-bias syllogisms with and without conflict between validity and believability in a two-response paradigm. They gave an initial answer under a concurrent WM load, a response deadline, or both, followed by a confidence rating and a final answer. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined, and this decline was similar for conflict and non-conflict problems. Confidence was reliably lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems across all conditions, and confidence reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time regardless of WM constraints. Monitoring resolution, however, was low even without constraints. These results suggest that WM constraints impair reasoning generally but leave conflict detection and control sensitivity largely intact. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate their own correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a more general limitation of monitoring rather than a consequence of constrained resources.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Stoic Training on Fear of Negative Evaluation and Responses to Social-Evaluative Stress: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael William Lewis; Charles Kalarchian; Alexander MacLellan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Stoic philosophy has influenced cognitive and behavioral therapies, but Stoic training has received limited empirical evaluation. This preregistered randomized controlled trial examined whether Stoic training reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), improved broader psychological outcomes, increased Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and altered subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.

Methods: Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings. Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52). Seventy-eight subsequently completed a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST), of whom 66 provided usable electrocardiography data for the preregistered cardiac analyses. Before speech preparation, participants in the Stoic condition completed a five-minute Negative Visualization exercise, whereas control participants waited quietly.

Results: Relative to the active control, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining FNE when controlling for pretraining scores, b = −2.77, p = .016, adjusted d = −0.50, and higher posttraining Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale scores, b = 6.06, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.43. Exploratory subscale analyses suggested possible effects on Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness, although neither remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Between-condition effects on resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not significant. During the TSST, cardiac effects were contrary to prediction: Stoic training was associated with higher heart rate, b = 4.13, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.53, and lower heart rate variability, although the latter effect narrowly missed statistical significance, b = −0.17, p = .053, adjusted d = −0.49. Subjective distress and state-anxiety responses to the TSST did not differ significantly by condition.

Conclusions: Stoic training led to significantly greater reductions in FNE and increases in Stoic attitudes than an active control, whereas broader psychological outcomes did not differ significantly between conditions. These findings provide initial evidence that brief Stoic training may modify a cognitive vulnerability relevant to social evaluation while engaging the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate. The unexpected cardiac effects may reflect the broader training, the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered before the stressor, or their combination, highlighting the need to disentangle the cumulative and acute effects of Stoic practice and determine how the timing and context of Negative Visualization influence responses to social-evaluative stress.

articles_hidden.title: Are two words seen as one object? How age-of-acquisition affects the recognition and naming of pictorial representations of compound words
articles_hidden.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif
articles_hidden.abstract: Adults recognize objects learned in childhood (e.g., "unicorn") faster than those learned later (e.g., "taxes"). This phenomenon is known as the Age-of-Acquisition (AoA) effect. The integrated account proposes that this effect stems from higher demands on semantic processing or arbitrary input-output mappings. To investigate this, 48 British English-speaking students completed an object decision task and a spoken picture naming task using 150 compound words. Compound words were selected because their mapping to multiple morphemes requires increased semantic processing. In addition to individual task performance, we calculated a subtractive measure (naming latency minus object decision latency) for each item per participant. Results showed that early-acquired objects were identified and named more quickly than late-acquired objects. The analysis of the subtractive measure also revealed significant AoA effects. These findings suggest that the influence of AoA and semantic predictors is more pronounced in picture naming than in object decision. This supports the representation account, indicating that the AoA effect is rooted in semantic and phonological representations. Furthermore, the robust AoA effect observed in the subtractive analysis bolsters the mapping account, suggesting the effect also resides in the connections between these representations. Overall, these results align with the integrated account of the AoA effect.

articles_hidden.title: Word Frequency and Regularity in Reading and Spelling: Task and Item effects
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Burt
articles_hidden.abstract: Reading and spelling tasks were compared on a common word set with different groups of university students assigned to each task. In Experiment 1, words varied over 5 levels of normative frequency and each group performed speeded lexical decision (LDT), speeded spelling recognition (correct vs. incorrect classification) or (unspeeded) dictation. The results revealed frequency effects on both lexical processing and decision processes. In Experiment 2, words varied in spelling-sound regularity and each group performed LDT, speeded spelling recognition, name if a word, or dictation. Irregular pronunciation had effects on accuracy in reading and spelling tasks, whereas, when orthographic typicality was controlled, irregular spelling affected only dictation accuracy. In the two experiments there were substantial item-by-item associations in accuracy and latencies over the reading and spelling tasks. The results indicate a common effect of the quality of lexical representations over tasks, together with task-specific effects associated with decision processes and the deployment of spelling-sound connections.

articles_hidden.title: Differential Effects of Types of Momentary Social Support on Mood and Anxiety in Patients with Depression
articles_hidden.authors: Annalena Jachnik; Martin Weiß; Julian Gutzeit; Fabian Rothbauer; Sebastian Walther; Grit Hein
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Social support is a multidimensional construct that includes emotional, esteem, and informational support, as well as instrumental support, referring to tangible assistance, and negative forms of support. While patients experience these types of support in their daily social interactions, the specific effects of momentary received support types on psychopathology remain understudied. Therefore, this study examined the effects of multiple types of social support on depressive mood and state social anxiety using high frequency Ecological Momentary Assessment. 
Methods: Data was collected from patients diagnosed with affective disorders and current moderate to severe depression, as well as from control participants (N = 68) using smartphone-based assessments over five consecutive days. Specifically, participants reported on social interaction characteristics, the type of received support, as well as their mood and anxiety levels based on six survey prompts per day. 
Results: Results indicated that receiving emotional support was associated with lower depressive mood, while esteem support was associated with lower depressive mood and state social anxiety. In contrast, informational support showed opposite effects. 
Conclusions: These findings underscore the potential of social support in alleviating the core symptoms of clinical depression; with specific types of support being particularly beneficial. Thus, targeted application of social support types hold promise for interventions in depression.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Group Differences in Psychopathology Networks: A Slow–Fast Perspective on Context and Symptom Activation
articles_hidden.authors: Kyuri Park; Denny Borsboom; Michael Lees; Leonie Elsenburg; Gabriela Lunansky; Karien Stronks; Johan Bollen; Mary Nicolaou; Vítor V. Vasconcelos
articles_hidden.abstract:
Groups differing in social and economic circumstances often differ markedly in depressive symptom levels while their estimated symptom-network structures show few clear differences. Null results in network comparisons are interpreted as if indicating that the two groups' symptom systems are the same. However, it only indicates that no difference is detected in the interactions between symptoms. How readily symptoms become present, and how that may depend on the contextual conditions under which symptoms are observed, is rarely compared. Building on a slow--fast perspective, we conceptualize depressive symptoms as a relatively fast-changing system embedded in more persistent social, economic, psychosocial, health, and lifestyle conditions that shape symptom activation.

Using a cohort of 23,689 adults from Amsterdam, we illustrate this perspective with depressive symptoms measured by the PHQ-9 and a composite index of slow-layer contextual conditions, which we call {\em Slow Risk Load} (SRL), capturing persistent socioeconomic, psychosocial, and health-related conditions. Participants with High SRL showed substantially higher depressive symptom levels than those with Low SRL. A standard Network Comparison Test did not detect an overall difference in network structure between the groups, although global strength was modestly higher in the High SRL group.

Ising models, which separate how symptoms co-occur from how readily each becomes present, indicate that activation is higher under high SRL for eight of nine symptoms, and model comparison consistently favored group-specific activation over group-specific interactions.

The slow--fast perspective reframes group network comparisons as a problem spanning multiple time scales in which symptom-network structure, symptom activation, and contextual conditions should be considered jointly. It places symptom-focused and context-focused interventions at different layers of the same coupled system rather than in competition.

articles_hidden.title: Resting-State Functional Connectivity in Antipsychotic-Naïve First-Episode Psychosis: A Systematic Review of Network Alterations and Preprocessing Heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Ayla Ihsan; Ather; Joaquim Radua
articles_hidden.abstract:
Resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) abnormalities are central to characterising brain network dysfunction in first-episode psychosis (FEP), yet biomarker development remains limited by an incomplete understanding of connectivity heterogeneity. This systematic review synthesised 75 studies investigating RSFC in antipsychotic-naïve FEP across five functional network domains and one developmental subgroup. Antipsychotic-naïve FEP was consistently associated with hypoconnectivity within the default mode, salience, frontostriatal, cerebello-thalamo-cortical, and hippocampal networks. Exploratory analyses examined whether global signal regression (GSR) and motion-correction stringency were associated with differences in reported connectivity direction. Motion-control stringency showed no significant association with connectivity direction, indicating that the hypoconnectivity finding was not attributable to motion-related artefact; GSR use was strongly confounded with geographic origin, precluding independent assessment of its association with connectivity direction. Notably, no included study employed within-study preprocessing sensitivity analyses, and cross-national harmonisation efforts remain minimal. Future research should prioritise within-study GSR sensitivity analyses, establish test–retest reliability and external classifier validation for RSFC biomarkers, adopt harmonised preprocessing conventions, and systematically explore sources of directional heterogeneity across preprocessing strata to enable robust cross-national biomarker synthesis.
Keywords: Connectomics; global signal regression; motion artefact; thalamocortical dysconnectivity; salience network; default mode network.

articles_hidden.title: Prediction-error tolerance: Error attribution as the hinge between inquiry and the self
articles_hidden.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Kazuhiro Hayashi; Norihiro Sadato
articles_hidden.abstract: Close to one in three early-career researchers reports elevated psychological distress, at rates varying little across disciplines, genders and career stages. The standard explanation attributes the burden to the conditions of academic work; its rival prescribes resilience. Neither says what a condition does to a researcher who cannot yet tell whether an unexpected result reflects the phenomenon, the instrument or her own competence. A prediction error has no address until a researcher gives it one: by the Duhem–Quine thesis it may belong to the object of inquiry, the method or the context of evaluation, and logic does not decide which. We define prediction-error tolerance as the capacity to keep treating discrepancies as operable questions while holding uncertainty open, and identify its core operation, error-attribution separation, as the point at which two costs are decided together. When an error is routed to the self instead of to its address, the researcher’s well-being is damaged and the error is lost to inquiry; the adaptations that follow (safe questions, discarded anomalies, work subdivided to fit the measure) are those metascience explains by incentives alone. The two costs, we propose, are effects of one regime with a shared mediating step. We distinguish the construct from ten neighbours, fix the error episode as the unit of measurement, and state six predictions with the observations that would defeat each, including one that would leave the incentive account standing and ours not. An environment that returns errors with an address protects the person and the inquiry together.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting Memberships from Memory.
articles_hidden.authors: Luigi Grisoni
articles_hidden.abstract: Neural representations are commonly described as mappings between target variables and patterns of neural activity. A central challenge is to specify not only what the brain represents, but how representational content is organised and constrained across contexts. Here, the concept of Representation of Membership (RoM) is proposed as a perspective on representational organisation. RoM assumes that cognitive representations are shaped by the elements they contain and by the membership structures linking those elements to broader semantic, functional, and contextual domains. The same element may belong to multiple structures and play different roles within them, with particular memberships becoming relevant according to context, task demands, or prior knowledge. Within RoM, prediction reflects the dynamic activation, weighting, and refinement of learned membership structures, constraining which continuations, features, interpretations, or responses become more likely. RoM thus links neural representation, memory, flexibility, and prediction through the context-sensitive organisation and updating of membership structures.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond an Ethos or Inflexible Checklist of Research Practices: Grounding Open Science in a Biomedical Research Ethics Framework
articles_hidden.authors: P. Priscilla Lui
articles_hidden.abstract: The well-documented reproducibility problem facing psychological science has driven rapid growth in open science infrastructure and practices over the past decade. Despite most researchers broadly endorsing transparency as a virtue, actual practice adoption remains uneven and lags far behind the stated support. Three issues explain the value-practice gap: (1) general ethos does not motivate and guide actual practice use within context, (2) open science is often misconceived as a one-size-fits-all, all-or-nothing mandate applied agnostic to different research questions, methods, or populations, (3) insufficient attention to relational transparency relative to procedural transparency, thus inadvertently alienating psychological researchers who use qualitative and participatory methods. Currently, researchers are left without a principled framework to decide what, when, and how to implement specific practices in any given investigation. A critical step is translating the transparency ethos into a comprehensive set of ethical principles and benchmarks that can guide eventual open science practices. Drawing on Emanuel’s biomedical research ethics framework, this article maps open science practices onto eight established ethical principles. Examples are offered on how these principles and related benchmarks motivate specific, contextually appropriate practices. The systematic ethics framework offers researchers a principled basis for building local capacity to engage with open science practices.

articles_hidden.title: An Analysis of Flavor Distribution and Consumer Perception On Color In Life Savers Neon Gummies
articles_hidden.authors: Shriyans Tiwari; Aarush Jain
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the influence of artificial coloring, flavor naming, and  package design on consumer preference of the gummy. Although previous research has examined a product's packaging or a product's color, our study combines marketing and psychological factors to understand what appeals to the consumers. In this experiment, a survey was conducted with over one-hundred participants, asking them their preferred gummy color, flavor name, and whether or not they liked the packaging. In addition to this, the frequency and distribution of the colors was measured from eight packages of Life Savers gummies. Results revealed that Cherry Lime Splash was the most appealing flavor name, suggesting that combinations of exotic flavors appeal most to the consumers. Red emerged as the most appealing flavor color to consumers, while blue appeared most frequently in the package. These findings emphasize that both visual appeal and flavor naming significantly influence consumer decisions. Additionally, blue appearing the most was surprising, as this didn’t correlate with consumer preference. Ultimately, it is recommended that companies replace the artificial dies used to make the colors appealing, with natural alternatives such as beet juice, turmeric, and spirulina. These colors will help the gummies maintain strong visual appeal, while avoiding the usage of artificial dyes. Future research should examine whether natural colors would match or surpass artificial colors in terms of consumer preference.

articles_hidden.title: Conversation as data: Extracting features from naturalistic conversation datasets
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Templeton; Luke J. Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: In this chapter, we outline important considerations for designing and analyzing conversation studies. We first advocate for the use of representative designs to ensure that datasets adequately reflect the complexity inherent in conversation. We then focus on how behavior in conversation recordings can be quantified through a process of feature extraction, and discuss strategies to assess the validity of feature extraction pipelines. Finally, we discuss analytical considerations specific to working with conversation data. Being able to rigorously collect, operationalize, and analyze natural conversation data will lead to robust results that the entire field can build upon, advancing our understanding of exactly how conversation allows us to achieve our social goals.

articles_hidden.title: A systemic approach to self-harm in schools in Poland – a policy brief
articles_hidden.authors: Lea Satala; Daria Biechowska
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-harm among young people is a significant public health concern in Poland, while schools remain an underused setting for its early identification and prevention. Despite existing mental health initiatives and regulations, the Polish education system lacks uniform, systemic procedures for responding to self-harm, resulting in fragmented and unequal support across schools. This policy brief examines the scale and consequences of self-harm among young people, the current regulatory and institutional framework and evidence from school-based interventions in Poland and internationally. It argues that schools are particularly important for early intervention because most young people who self-harm remain in regular contact with school staff. The brief recommends a scalable, systemic intervention consisting of three complementary elements: (1) a short universal online training course for all school staff, (2) a uniform procedure for responding to self-harm and (3) a clearly defined pathway for referral to specialist support. The proposed training would strengthen staff competencies in recognising warning signs, conducting supportive conversations and directing students to appropriate services. Rather than introducing extensive new regulatory obligations, the proposal uses existing institutional mechanisms and recommends integration with the National Health Programme, professional development and staff onboarding. By establishing a common minimum standard of response, while accounting for institutional and resource constraints, the proposed approach offers a feasible first step towards a broader whole-school model of mental health support and self-harm prevention in Poland.

articles_hidden.title: A short-form decision-making task preserving value-based choices and their relationship to apathy in older adults
articles_hidden.authors: Dorothée Morand-Grondin; Madeleine Sharp
articles_hidden.abstract: Apathy, or diminished motivation, is increasingly understood as reflecting biases in value-based decision-making. The Everyday Choice Task offers an ecologically grounded setting for investigating this relationship. In this task, older adults rate everyday activities on 19 different value attributes, and then make choices between pairs of activities. Prior analyses of these value attributes recover three main value dimensions (effort, reward, and obligation) that significantly predict choice behavior, while overweighting of effort during choice is selectively associated with apathy. In this study, we tested whether a brief version of the task, inquiring about these three dimensions directly rather than using the full set of attributes, would preserve relationships between value, choice, and apathy observed using the original instrument. Older adults (n = 110) completed both the original and brief versions of the task in a randomized order, along with the Apathy Motivation Index. Ratings of effort, reward, and obligation derived from the original and brief versions of the task were strongly correlated. In both versions of the task, ratings of effort, reward, and obligation significantly predicted choice, and greater apathy severity was associated with a selective overweighting of effort. These findings support the use of the brief Everyday Choice Task as an efficient measure of value-based decision-making in future research.

articles_hidden.title: Validity, Diagnostic Accuracy, and Feasibility of Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality for Mild Cognitive Impairment
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Antonia Ioakeimidou; Myrto Dimakopoulou; Christina Anastasopoulou; Maria Roussou; Petros Roussos; Chrysanthi Nega; Ion Beratis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Immersive virtual reality (VR) adaptations of neuropsychological tests change how participants respond and must be validated in each clinical population. We evaluated the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze version of the paper-and-pencil Trail Making Test (hereafter, TMT) that records completion times and wrong-target selections automatically, in older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
Methods: In this case–control evaluation, 84 adults aged 60–89 years (42 with clinically diagnosed MCI, 42 healthy comparison participants) completed the TMT-VR, the TMT and the Mini-Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (M-ACE), with pre- and post-exposure cybersickness ratings. Planned analyses examined feasibility, convergence, group differences and diagnostic accuracy for all 26 TMT-VR scores against their TMT counterparts and the M-ACE, with demographic adjustment, multiplicity correction, bootstrap validation and education-matched sensitivity analysis.
Results: All participants completed both TMT-VR parts, and cybersickness ratings decreased over the session. Part B completion times correlated positively across formats within both groups. Participants with MCI were slower and made more wrong-target selections on TMT-VR Part B but not Part A. Score for score, the TMT-VR matched the TMT on Part B completion time and discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B, total and B−A error scores and every Part B-specific derived score; these effects persisted after demographic adjustment and widened in the education-matched subsample. The TMT's advantage lay in Part A completion time, and its error scores carried little discriminatory information. With education equalised, the TMT-VR B−A scores gave balanced operating characteristics and approached the M-ACE, which every TMT score remained below. The M-ACE discriminated more accurately than any single trail-making score of either format.
Conclusions: The TMT-VR is a feasible, well-tolerated adaptation with convergent validity against the TMT and known-groups validity for MCI. Because it discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B-specific and error-based scores that carry the test's executive demand, it emerges as the preferable Trail Making Test format within neuropsychological batteries for MCI; whether it adds diagnostic information beyond global screens such as the M-ACE must be established in consecutive clinical referrals, together with age- and education-stratified normative cut-offs.

articles_hidden.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
articles_hidden.authors: Brian W. L. Wong; Arthur G. Samuel; Efthymia C Kapnoula
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Referential Social Processing in Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder: Advancing Theoretical Precision and Clinical Insights with Model-Based Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Carly A Lasagna; Jacob Kraft; Michael D. Nunez; Takakuni Suzuki; Tyler Grove; Stephan F Taylor; Ivy Fei Tso; Timothy Joseph Pleskac
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) often misjudge whether social cues, like eye contact, are meant for them, which can fuel symptoms and functional impairment. These difficulties appear to stem from disruptions in how social information is dynamically processed (“evidence accumulation”). We used neurocognitive joint modeling to investigate which neural signals shape evidence accumulation during gaze perception and whether these brain-behavior links help explain disrupted self-referential social processing.

Methods. Leveraging EEG data from N=99 SZ, BD, and healthy controls (HC) during a self-referential gaze perception task, we built joint drift-diffusion models characterizing how different trial-level EEG features translated to evidence accumulation and behavior. Joint models were compared against each other (and models using task-averaged EEG or behavior only) for their ability to predict task behavior and relevant clinical dimensions, including paranoia, functioning, and cognition. We examined whether the best-performing model differentiated patients and HC.

Results. The best-performing joint model explained evidence accumulation through trial-level fluctuations—not task averages—in two neural signals: CPP and frontal midline theta, implicated in subjective deliberation/certainty and top-down modulation, respectively. Less reliable translation of trial-level CPP signals to evidence accumulation impaired gaze perception in SZ and BD. Mapping how trial-level theta dynamics translated to evidence accumulation captured paranoia and functioning better than behavior or task-averaged neural metrics alone.

Conclusions. Model-based approaches that embrace the within-person variability of neural signals may reveal more nuanced, clinically relevant perspectives on the pathophysiology of SZ and BD than those using task-averaged brain activity or behavior alone.

articles_hidden.title: Structural Equation Modeling with Causal Discipline: A Practical Tutorial from Regression and Mediation to Latent Variables and Growth Models in R and Mplus
articles_hidden.authors: Subir Hait
articles_hidden.abstract: Structural equation modeling (SEM) makes it easy to draw paths, estimate latent-variable models, and decompose associations, but those conveniences can blur three distinct questions: what statistical parameter is being estimated, what construct is being measured, and what additional assumptions would justify a causal interpretation. This tutorial organizes SEM around that three-layer distinction. Using one synthetic educational dataset, it moves from regression and path analysis through mediation, confirmatory factor analysis, latent-variable SEM, measurement invariance, longitudinal measurement models, and latent growth curves. Parallel examples in R using lavaan and Mplus show how the same model is represented across software. The mediation section makes the statistical-versus-causal distinction concrete: it derives the linear product-of-coefficients decomposition, shows when it can identify a natural indirect effect under stronger assumptions, and uses a residual-correlation sensitivity analysis with a known-truth simulation. Measurement-error attenuation, partial invariance, longitudinal latent means, and conditional growth models show why better statistical fit or richer latent-variable structure does not by itself create causal identification. A frozen reproducibility bundle supplies the data-generating process, truth files, software syntax, benchmark estimates, and independent numerical checks. The intended audience is graduate students and applied researchers who know regression and want a practical route into SEM without treating an arrow in a fitted model as evidence of causation.

articles_hidden.title: Working Memory and the Effectiveness of Written Corrective Feedback on Production Accuracy of the English Definite Article
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Nowbakht; Thierry Olive
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated the role of working memory (WM) in the effectiveness of direct, indirect, and metalinguistic written corrective feedback (WCF) on the production accuracy of the English definite article among pre-intermediate EFL learners. One hundred and thirty-five learners (72 female, 63 male) performed four picture-composition tasks and one argumentative essay transfer task, received WCF on their definite article errors, and rewrote their compositions accordingly. WM was measured using a first-language Operation Span Task (OSPAN). Results showed that WM predicted the effectiveness of metalinguistic and direct WCF at both immediate and delayed post-tests but did not predict the effectiveness of indirect WCF. Metalinguistic WCF produced the highest accuracy gains, which were maintained at the delayed and transfer assessments; direct WCF also outperformed indirect WCF. The findings are discussed in relation to cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988; Sweller et al., 1998)—which accounts for how WM constraints shape learners' differential responses to instructional feedback of varying explicitness—and Schmidt's (1990) Noticing Hypothesis and cognitive models of writing (Hayes, 1996; Kellogg, 1996; Olive, 2004).

articles_hidden.title: Low family income and behavior problems in early childhood: Is family stress the causal mechanism?
articles_hidden.authors: Gülbin Şengül-İnal; Nicolai T. Borgen; Eric Dearing; Henrik Daae Zachrisson
articles_hidden.abstract: The Family Stress Model (FSM) provides a causal theory for how a family’s economic situation influences children’s behavioral outcomes through increasing income-related stress on parents, existing research on FSM is overwhelmingly correlational. We compared between-family FSM associations—the analytical approach typically used in cross-sectional and longitudinal FSM studies—with within-family FSM associations. The latter provides a more stringent causal test by eliminating bias from time-invariant confounders and unobserved between-person heterogeneity. We used longitudinal data (N=80,349) on maternal distress, relationship satisfaction, and child externalizing and internalizing behavior problems, assessed when the children were 18, 36, and 54 months from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa). For household income, we used registry data. In both between- and within-family models, lower income was associated with more behavior problems, with total effect sizes being approximately two to three times larger in the former models. The proportion of indirect effect explained by family stress mediators was sizable in the between-effects model. In contrast, the within-effect model showed no indirect effect of family stress mediators. These results are consistent with the concern that between-family estimates of the FSM are confounded by unobserved factors that vary across families.

articles_hidden.title: Large Language Models for Test-Enhanced Learning: A Tutorial and Proof of Concept
articles_hidden.authors: Ariana Modirrousta-Galian; Daryl Yu Heng Lee; Frederic Dick; Eva Lash; David Shanks
articles_hidden.abstract: Practice tests improve retention of studied information and enhance learning and retrieval of new information (test-enhanced learning; TEL). In five preregistered studies (total N = 623)—four online randomized experiments and one correlational classroom study with final-year psychology undergraduates—we examined whether large language models (LLMs; Gemini and ChatGPT) can generate practice tests that promote TEL and whether this use of LLMs can be feasibly incorporated into a classroom setting. LLM-generated multiple-choice tests with fixed feedback did not improve 2-day recall of a TED Talk relative to a control (Studies 1 and 2). In contrast, LLM-generated short-answer tests with personalized feedback significantly improved 7-day recall of an educational video relative to rewatching it (Studies 3 and 4), regardless of whether final test format matched that of the practice test. In the classroom study, participation in fortnightly LLM-generated short-answer tests (with personalized feedback) on lecture content was positively associated with graded assessment performance, and students’ attitudes towards this use of LLMs were generally favorable. Overall, we demonstrate that LLMs can substantially reduce the practical burden of implementing TEL, while maintaining sufficiently good question quality and enabling automated personalized feedback, and that this approach can be feasibly deployed in an undergraduate psychology class.

articles_hidden.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
