articles_hidden.abstract: Current research supports that parenting practice contributes to individual differences in preschoolers’ self-regulation (SR). Dynamic systems theory suggests that the link between parenting and child SR may be bidirectional and family-specific. Taking a dynamic systems perspective, this study examined the daily bidirectional link between parenting practices and preschoolers’ SR and the family-specific holistic dynamic patterns. Thirty-nine families took part in a 100-day daily diary study in the United States. Using dynamic structural equation modeling, we examined the autoregressive and cross-lagged effects of daily parental responsiveness, negative reactivity, and child self-regulation. Autoregressive and cross-lagged effects were estimated as random slopes, allowing the dynamic effects to vary from family to family. On average, parental responsiveness predicted future SR, and SR predicted future negative reactivity. Significant heterogeneity was identified, indicating that the bidirectional links between parenting and SR were family-specific. Considering autoregressive and cross-lagged effects holistically, all families showed a tendency to return to their equilibrium states, defined by their personal means of responsiveness, negative reactivity, and SR. Among the 39 families, 19 families had a mutually influential connection between negative reactivity and SR, and one family had a mutually influential connection between responsiveness and SR. The rest of the families did not show a mutually influential pattern between parenting and child SR. The findings highlighted the importance of considering heterogeneity in the holistic within-family processes. The effectiveness of future interventions should be considered family-specifically and as changes in family dynamic patterns.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring a dreaming population: multilevel temporal organization in 75,000 dream reports
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander V. Lebedev
articles_hidden.abstract:
Dream reports exhibit reproducible organization at multiple scales. We analyzed >75,000 reports from four platforms: 30,241 reports by 5,524 Dreamseer users and ~45,000 from DreamBank, Reddit r/Dreams, and the Sleep and Dream Database. Within reports, emotional valence declined from beginning to end. Forward and reversed trajectories were distinguishable in all five corpus-language samples with a screening instrument (AUC 0.647–0.667) and four of five after sentence-level rescoring with the primary sentiment model.

The effect survived contributor-level inference and seven controls for ending-related material. Shuffling sentence order eliminated the mean descent while preserving lexical content, localizing the effect to sequence. Matched first-person waking accounts, fiction, and encyclopedic prose also declined, showing that downward movement is not dream-specific. However, on the endpoint estimand, Dreamseer and DreamBank declined more strongly than waking narratives (all q < .001); after standardization by within-document sentence-valence dispersion, they also exceeded all three human comparators (9/9 contrasts, q ≤ .018), with approximately two- to five-fold greater descent. Separation was less consistent for whole-trajectory slope. The hypothesized failure of emotional resolution at the ending was unsupported: the difference was concentrated earlier, with dreams beginning near neutral and then declining.

At population scale, Friday reports were lighter than Monday reports in English (β = +0.024, p = .008), but this did not replicate in Russian, was uncorrected, and partly reflected who reported. Nightmare-content variance increased before 12 downturns (Kendall’s τ = +0.236), surviving four of five surrogate tests but not a window-length block bootstrap; autocorrelation did not increase. We treat this as a prospective hypothesis, not evidence of critical slowing down. Low intrinsic dimension and a percolating semantic “continent” also appeared in matched non-dream prose, whereas non-narrative prose fell outside the connectivity range shared by all narrative corpora.

Weekly affect and content showed no robust entrainment to market, media, search, attention, or cultural indicators, constraining detectable direct societal coupling at this temporal resolution. At COVID-19 onset, explicit pandemic vocabulary increased ninefold (+4.68 percentage points), exceeding all 44 placebo-in-time cutoffs (empirical p = .022), showing that the stream could register a major societal event.

Together, these findings demonstrate collective structure without sustained interpersonal synchrony. Macroscopic organization emerged despite absent average-night convergence and a thin unexplained tail of unusually cohesive nights, while trajectory, calendar, variance, and event-related observables operated through partly independent channels.

articles_hidden.title: Infants’ learning of tones and VOT contrasts in the lab
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles_hidden.abstract: Infants likely home in on the speech categories in the ambient language(s) by attending to the acoustic cue distributions present in the input, but direct experimental evidence for this remains scarce. Young infants’ discrimination of /d-t/ and Mandarin Chinese tones T2-T4 was assessed over the course of a repeated exposure-test pro- cedure. In addition to being the first to document the emergence of perceptual categories through repeated testing of the same infants, this study suggests that perceptual learning through acoustic cue distributions could also account for the development of lexical tone perception.

articles_hidden.title: Kinematic encoding of the speed-accuracy trade-off in approach/avoidance decisions when facing social threats
articles_hidden.authors: Rocco Mennella; Julie Grezes; Matteo Sequestro; Morgan Beaurenaut
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceiving social threats, especially expressions of anger, increases the speed of both action selection and execution. However, it remains unclear how individuals balance speed with achieving desirable outcomes, such as threat avoidance, under these conditions. To investigate this trade-off between decision’s speed and accuracy, we examined the kinematics of finger-reaching movements using a "go-before-you-know" paradigm. Participants chose between two empty outer chairs in a waiting room. Two central chairs were occupied by either two individuals with neutral expressions or one neutral individual and one threatening individual. The threatening individual expressed anger or fear at one of four intensity levels. The results showed that social threats generally invigorated action decision, as high-threat trials elicited faster movements, which correlated with more direct trajectories compared to neutral trials. However, when participants chose to avoid angry individuals, the most frequent response, movements followed more central trajectories, compared to when they approached angry individuals. These findings suggest that while social threats generally invigorate action selection and execution, the accumulation of evidence for the decision can be temporarily prolonged to enhance the likelihood of a favorable outcome, such as threat avoidance. We propose integrating these results with recent models of action decisions under perceived urgency to advance understanding of threat-related decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Rescripting suicidal mental imagery in young people: A pilot study of feasibility, acceptability and safety
articles_hidden.authors: Lianne Schmaal; Georgie Paulik; Zamantha Munoz; Laura van Velzen; Pemma Davies; Martin Mitrevski; Eleanor Bailey; Phoebe Gleeson; Lisa Incerti; Samantha Galea
articles_hidden.abstract: Suicidal mental imagery – vivid, intrusive mental images of suicide or death - is common among young people experiencing suicidal ideation and may increase risk of suicidal behaviour, yet interventions directly targeting these images are lacking. We conducted a single-arm pilot study evaluating the feasibility, acceptability and safety of a brief, therapist delivered imagery rescripting intervention targeting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery in help-seeking young people aged 16–25 years with mood disorders and current or recent suicidal ideation. Fourteen participants were recruited; 12 were eligible for the intervention and 11 (92%) completed treatment and follow-up. The recruitment target (N=25) was not met, largely due to service disruptions and clinician capacity constraints. Acceptability and safety criteria were met: 73% reported that sessions were not distressing, none felt less safe following treatment, and no participant showed increased suicidal ideation from baseline to follow-up. Two serious adverse events occurred but were judged unrelated to the intervention. Exploratory analyses showed reductions in suicidal-image frequency, realness, compellingness, intrusiveness and distress, alongside a 52% reduction in suicidal ideation severity. Our pilot study indicates that directly rescripting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery showed encouraging short-term safety and acceptability signals in young people, supporting evaluation in a larger randomised controlled trial.

articles_hidden.title: Recovering Within-Family Lagged Effects of the Discordant Sibling Random Intercept Cross Lagged Panel Model on Sibling Panels
articles_hidden.authors: Yongseok Lee; Robert Duncan; Kristine Marceau
articles_hidden.abstract: The Discordant Sibling Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (DS RI-CLPM) integrates the sibling-comparison design with the Random Intercept-Cross Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) to separate shared family-level confounding from sibling-specific processes, and stable heterogeneity from within-child dynamics. Despite its empirical work, its performance relative to conventional longitudinal models remains untested. Using Monte-Carlo simulations, we compared the DS RI-CLPM against a wave-specific discordant sibling model, CLPM, and RI-CLPM, evaluating relative bias and root mean squared errors (RMSE). The results showed that the DS RI-CLPM generally recovered the within-family cross-lagged effect and standard errors across most manipulated conditions. However, it exhibited substantial bias and higher RMSE when unmeasured child-level time-varying confounding was present. Thus, the DS RI-CLPM is effective for examining sibling-specific within-family cross-lagged effects while controlling for stable or family-shared confounders, but it is insufficient when unmeasured child-specific time varying confounding is plausible.

articles_hidden.title: File drawer report: Testing for spontaneously perceived joint affordances in an object-based compatibility task
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad; Simon Laham; Natalie Sebanz
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence from joint action research suggests that a suite of spontaneous cognitive and perceptual processes underpins our ability to coordinate with others. We tested whether people spontaneously perceive affordances (or action possibilities) for the dyad when a co-actor is present. To test this hypothesis, we asked participants to complete an object-based response time task either alone (individual condition) or while seated next to a partner who completed the complementary task (joint condition). Participants in both conditions made unimanual go/no-go keypresses to objects that afforded either a bimanual (e.g., a laundry hamper) or unimanual (e.g., a bucket) grasp. In total, we conducted seven experiments (total N =293). An initial experiment revealed an affordance × task interaction effect on response times, such that responses to bimanually graspable objects were faster in the joint than in the individual condition. However, several follow-up experiments failed to replicate this finding, providing no overall evidence for spontaneously perceived joint affordances.

articles_hidden.title: Towards an Integrative, Interdisciplinary, and Multidimensional Approach to Curbing Epistemically Suspect Beliefs: A Commentary on Bronstein et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Magdalena Adamus; Jais Adam-Troian; Maria Chayinska
articles_hidden.abstract: In this commentary, we endorse the recent call by Bronstein et al. (2026) to open a polyphonic debate and bring clinical psychology into the dialogue on the nature, causes, and consequences of epistemically suspect beliefs. We concur with the authors’ call for creating an integrative approach that would triangulate findings across different disciplines in a much-needed attempt to harmonise knowledge about individual, situational, and structural factors that contribute to the endorsement of epistemically suspect beliefs. Using economic anxiety as a model case, we then show how the integration of clinical insights could inform innovative, cost-effective, and scalable intervention programmes. Finally, we call for careful consideration of the risks associated with incorporating the clinical perspective, particularly the potential pathologisation of epistemically suspect beliefs and stigmatisation of those who endorse them, as well as the need to carefully distinguish delusions from ill-informed beliefs and rational suspicions.

articles_hidden.title: Missing Pretest–Posttest Correlations in Pretest–Posttest–Control Group Designs:  A Practical Trade-Off for Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Wilhelm Liebenow; Valentin Emslander; Thorben Jansen; Oliver Lüdtke
articles_hidden.abstract: Pretest–posttest–control group (PPC) effect sizes incorporate baseline information but require the pretest–posttest correlation for sampling-variance estimation, which is frequently unavailable in primary studies. This creates a practical trade-off: retaining baseline information requires an assumption about repeated-measures dependence, whereas using posttest-only effect sizes avoids this requirement but discards available baseline information. The present study used a simulation to evaluate whether missing correlations can be replaced by constant assumed values while maintaining acceptable variance calibration, and complemented the simulation with reanalyses of three published meta-analyses to illustrate the consequences for meta-analytic effects. Across 2,160 design conditions, we examined the sampling variances of two pretest-informed estimators (dppc1  and dppc2). Performance was evaluated in terms of coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals and standard-error ratios. Across the fixed-correlation conditions, coverage declined from .97 to .83 for dppc1 and from .97 to .79 for dppc2 as the assumed correlation increased from .20 to .80, with corresponding standard-error ratios declining from 1.31 to 0.70 and from 1.32 to 0.68. Misspecification was asymmetric: overestimating the true correlation produced anti-conservative standard errors and undercoverage, whereas underestimating it generally produced conservative inference. Across the empirical examples, pooled PPC estimates were comparatively stable across correlation assumptions, whereas ignoring baseline information produced larger shifts in several pooled effects.  Based on these findings, we provide practical guidelines for handling missing pretest–posttest correlations, emphasizing a hierarchical use of study-specific information, external evidence, and transparent sensitivity analyses when constant assumptions are required. An accompanying Shiny app supports these analyses: https://lliebenow.shinyapps.io/ppc-rho-sensitivity-explorer/.

articles_hidden.title: Predictors Associated with Early Career Researcher Wellbeing: A Systematic Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Fletcher; Amber Tout; Talar Moukhtarian; Tabitha Jackson; Chloe Mitchell; Elena Riva; Carla Toro; Marie Sams; Sotaro Kita
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Early Career Researchers (ECRs) are integral to the academic ecosystem, representing a critical window for mental health promotion and early intervention within the higher education workforce. Their wellbeing is influenced by various factors that can either support or hinder healthy professional and personal development. This systematic scoping review maps and narratively synthesises current literature to understand predictors of ECR wellbeing, with the aim of informing upstream strategies for prevention and mental health promotion. 
Method: A systematic search was conducted across Web of Science, PsycINFO, and EBSCO (inception–May 2024). Of 2,577 records retrieved, 68 articles (69 independent studies) were included after screening.
Results: Seventeen distinct predictor clusters were identified and grouped by who has the most agency over them: 1) ECRs, 2) labs and departments, 3) institutions, 4) the sector, 5) all levels of agents combined. Frequently explored predictors included personal characteristics (i.e., age, gender), supervisor support and work-life balance, while depression, anxiety and stress were the most frequently measured outcomes.
Discussion: This review highlights both systemic and modifiable risk factors of occupational and psychological distress among ECRs. By identifying key drivers of wellbeing, this review offers actionable insights for developing early, targeted interventions at multiple levels. Investing in preventative and promotive strategies during this formative career stage may not only protect the wellbeing of ECRs but also foster healthier, more productive and sustainable academic environments.

articles_hidden.title: Potential Agency in the Absence of Actual Motor Control? Ownership-dependent Judgments in the Rubber Hand Illusion
articles_hidden.authors: Hélène Vanborren; Fleur Touzard; Matthew Longo; Loïc Paul Heurley; Brouillet Thibaut
articles_hidden.abstract: We define potential agency as the explicit judgment that one could have made an artificial hand move had one intended to do so. We asked whether participants would report potential agency for an artificial hand they had no means of controlling, and how such reports varied with body ownership. In a within-subject static rubber hand illusion (RHI) paradigm, 104 participants received synchronous and asynchronous visuo-tactile stimulation while their real hand remained hidden; neither the real nor the artificial hand moved, and no sensory consequences of voluntary action were available. After each induction, participants rated ownership of the artificial hand and potential agency towards it; proprioceptive drift was also measured. Synchronous stimulation produced the expected RHI pattern, with higher ownership and greater proprioceptive drift than asynchronous stimulation. Potential agency ratings were also higher following synchronous stimulation. Across conditions, ownership was positively associated with potential agency, but this association was stronger under synchronous stimulation. In the synchronous condition, ownership accounted for 56% of the variance in potential agency. Critically, on the −3 to +3 scales, the model-estimated probability of positive endorsement (mean potential agency rating ≥ +1) increased from 10% at ownership 0 to 88% at +3. Reanalysis of a comparable static RHI dataset showed a convergent ownership-dependent pattern. These findings extend the study of the ownership–agency relationship beyond executed actions and their sensory consequences: even in the absence of actual motor control, experienced ownership was closely related to whether the artificial hand was judged to be available for voluntary movement.

articles_hidden.title: Bodily Rhythms Bias Temporal Decisions Through Dissociable Neural Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Srishti Mittal; Kayser Christoph
articles_hidden.abstract: Being able to judge time accurately is central to behavior. Yet, judgements of time are shaped by factors such as attention and arousal, and hence our physiology. We studied the relation between cardiac and respiratory states and categorical judgements of sub-second intervals in humans. We asked whether these states relate to specific biases in time judgements and how they reflect in neurophysiological (EEG) signals. Thirty participants categorized tones of 450 to 600 ms duration as short or long, while we recorded 128-channel EEG, ECG, and respiration. Participants' reaction times were linked to cardiac and respiratory rates as well as respiratory phase. Systematic biases in interval categorization were predicted by heart rate and respiration rate. The physiological variables were not predictive of response accuracy, hence reflecting biases in time judgments rather than being tied to sensory precision. We then used multivariate EEG analysis to dissect neurophysiological signals related to interval duration and participants’ choice and modelled the influence of the physiological states on these. The respiration phase was linked to multiple EEG signals during a trial, while heart rate was predictive of choice-related signals carried by EEG components shortly before the response. This shows that cardiorespiratory states are systematically associated with the transformation of temporal information into categorical decisions, supporting an embodied account of time perception in which time perception fluctuates with ongoing physiological states.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Validity Argument for Automated Assessment from Transcript and Video Data
articles_hidden.authors: James Soland
articles_hidden.abstract: Automated assessment of psychological constructs from interview transcripts and video data has seen rapid technical development, yet the field lacks a systematic psychometric validity framework for interpreting scores from such measures. This paper applies Kane's interpretive/use argument structure alongside the five sources of validity evidence specified in the \textit{Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing} to automated transcript- and video-based assessment, using clinical assessment of depression as the primary illustrative case. We distinguish two design approaches --- item-based scoring, in which large language models (LLMs) rate explicit, theoretically derived items, and end-to-end embedding or classification approaches --- and examine how one could accrue validity evidence for each across the five sources. We argue that the field has concentrated almost exclusively on evidence based on relations to other variables (convergent validity against self-report criteria) while leaving response process and consequential evidence largely unaddressed. Further, we argue that construct validity evidence is often dismissed too quickly, especially for end-to-end approaches. Both evidence sources require fundamental reconceptualization for automated behavioral measures, and we propose reinterpretations suited to this context. Although the analysis centers on depression, the framework applies broadly to any construct assessed from passively collected video or transcript data. Implications for the design of future validation studies are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Person-Specific Symptom Networks From Brief Narratives: Development and Initial Evaluation of the Narrative-to-Network (N2N) Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Vogel; Carla Paulus; Julian Reichert; Jonas Tesarz; Stefanie Jungmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Person-specific symptom networks formalize which problems characterize an individual and how those problems are perceived to influence one another, making them increasingly relevant for individualized case conceptualization, treatment planning, and personalized psychotherapy. However, existing approaches typically rely on structured causal assessment or intensive longitudinal data, both of which can increase assessment burden. We developed and initially evaluated the Narrative-to-Network (N2N) framework for deriving directed person-specific networks from brief spoken narratives in which individuals describe their psychological difficulties and perceived relations among them in their own words. Following a development phase (N = 22), an independent evaluation sample (N = 50) completed a narrative assessment and a Perceived Causal Networks (PECAN) assessment. Narratives lasted approximately three minutes. Manual coding showed relatively high agreement for node identification (Dice = .76) and edge direction conditional on a shared relation (agreement = .81), with lower agreement for edge presence (Dice = .62). Narrative-derived and PECAN networks showed partial but incomplete convergence (mean Jaccard = .29). Most problems identified in narratives were also identified through PECAN (62.6%), whereas only 36.7% of PECAN problems appeared in the corresponding narratives. Despite containing substantially fewer problems and relations, narrative-derived networks were perceived as highly representative; among participants with complete ratings (n = 39), mean representativeness scores were 33.26 for narrative-derived networks and 34.10 for regulated PECAN networks, with no statistically significant difference (p = .527). Narrative node count was positively associated with psychological distress both concurrently (ρ = .34) and at follow-up (ρ = .40). These findings provide initial evidence that structured person-specific symptom networks can be reproducibly derived from brief prompted spoken narratives and may offer an economical, complementary representation of individuals’ difficulties.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Rules of Thumb: Empirical Sample Size Requirements for Detecting Institutional Effects in the context of Therapist Effects
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Segundo Pena Loray; Björn S. Siepe; Miriam Ina Hehlmann; Anne-Katharina Deisenhofer; Robin Anno Wester; Julian Rubel
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Multilevel modelling of therapist effects (TE) and institutional effects (IE) is standard in psychotherapy research, yet empirical sample-size guidance is scarce for TE and virtually absent for IE. Existing recommendations rely on rules of thumb from two-level designs that vary widely across sources and do not extend to three-level structures. We aimed to provide empirically derived design recommendations for reliably detecting TE and IE in three-level psychotherapy studies. Methods: We conducted a fully factorial Monte Carlo simulation crossing six design factors: true TE, true IE, patient allocation (balanced vs. unbalanced), patients per therapist, therapists per institution, and number of institutions. This yielded 52,488 unique conditions, each with 1,000 replications. For every condition we fitted a three-level random-intercept model and derived parametric bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for both intraclass correlations, evaluating bias, RMSE, coverage, and statistical power at three pre-registered thresholds. Results: Detecting TE was feasible across a wide range of realistic designs, requiring as few as 10 to 40 total therapists for moderate effects (TE ≥ 0.05). Detecting IE, in contrast, was strongly constrained by the number of institutions: no design with fewer than four institutions reached 80% power at the primary threshold, and adequate detection of small to moderate IE (≤ 0.20) required at least five institutions with substantial within-institution sampling. Conclusion: Reliably detecting IE imposes qualitatively different design requirements than TE, particularly regarding the minimum number of institutions. We provide cutoff tables and a Shiny application to support empirically informed sample-size decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding Creativity in Human–AI Collaboration:  How Cognitive Strategies and Student Profiles Relate to Students’ Creativity
articles_hidden.authors: Kim van Broekhoven; Marian Hickendorff
articles_hidden.abstract: Creativity is widely recognized as a critical competency for addressing the complex challenges of the twenty-first century. At the same time, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how students learn, think, and solve problems in higher education. In human-AI collaboration, this study first identified students’ cognitive strategies in GenAI-supported contexts, and examined the relationship between the cognitive strategy used and the creativity (i.e., originality and quality) of each idea. Second, this study identified latent profiles of students’ cognitive strategy use, and their relationship with creativity. Using a novel process-oriented theoretical framework and a combination of deductive and inductive analyses, six cognitive strategies were identified: repeat, unmediated, experiential, conceptual combination, semantic, and assumption reversal. A laboratory-based observational study involving 146 undergraduate students showed that constructive cognitive strategies (conceptual combination and semantic) were more frequently associated with highly original ideas than active cognitive strategies (unmediated and experiential), whereas no differences were found for idea quality. Furthermore, latent profile analysis identified four distinct profiles of human–AI collaboration: Largely Independent Thinkers, AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers. Although the profiles did not differ in their average originality, they differed significantly in their average quality. Students classified as AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers produced ideas of higher quality than the Largely Independent Thinkers. These findings demonstrate that the way students cognitively engage with GenAI shapes their creativity and provide insights for fostering effective human–AI collaboration in higher education.

articles_hidden.title: Packaging Psychological Theory: A New Standard for Reusable Computational Models
articles_hidden.authors: Kyra Evers; Lourens Waldorp; Eiko I Fried; Fred Hasselman; Denny Borsboom
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological theories are increasingly expressed as computational models to improve their rigour, robustness, and testability. Yet in the absence of shared standards for distributing such models, researchers often rely on idiosyncratic code formats. This creates large heterogeneity in the accessibility, quality, and intelligibility of models, making implementations difficult to reproduce, interpret, or extend. As a consequence, computational models are rarely reused, creating a vast space of isolated models with little effort towards theoretical integration. To address this challenge, we propose a new standard: computational models representing psychological theory should be distributed as software packages (e.g., in R, Python, or Julia). Packaged models should be openly available and licensed for reuse, documented and tested, checked by automated workflows, and preserved with a persistent identifier. Unlike static code archives, packages are tools made for users, with a familiar and engaging interface. Their format accommodates different programming languages, modelling frameworks, and stages of model development, giving authors substantial flexibility in how models are formalized and implemented. We illustrate the packaging standard with affectOU, an example R package implementing a psychological theory of affect dynamics. Our proposed standard draws on established infrastructure and best practices from software engineering to improve model quality and reproducibility. Adopting this standard would lower the cost of verifying and reusing computational models for authors, reviewers, and readers alike. In our view, improving model reusability is not optional but essential for cumulative progress in psychological theory.

articles_hidden.title: Crossmodal Congruency Affects Sensitivity but not Speed in Auditory–Tactile Go/NoGo Tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Andonovska; Ben Godde
articles_hidden.abstract: Crossmodal congruency and interference influence perception and action depending on modality, congruency, and task constraints. This study investigated auditory–tactile interactions using a Go/NoGo paradigm to dissociate effects on response speed (reaction time, RT) and perceptual sensitivity (d’). Participants performed a frequency discrimination task in which high- and low-frequency auditory tones (1000 vs. 500 Hz) and tactile vibrations (100 vs. 70 Hz) served as Go and NoGo signals across five conditions: unimodal auditory (A0), unimodal tactile (T0), auditory targets with tactile distractors (At), tactile targets with auditory distractors (Ta), and a combined condition (AT). In the crossmodal conditions, participants attended one modality while ignoring the other, and distractors were either response-congruent (both stimuli signaled the same response) or response-incongruent (the two modalities signaled different responses). Modality significantly affected performance, yielding particularly slow RTs and reduced d’ in the tactile-target condition containing auditory distractors (Ta). Crossmodal congruency robustly altered sensitivity, showing higher d’ for congruent than incongruent trials, particularly for tactile targets, but did not reliably influence RT. No evidence for multisensory facilitation emerged in the combined condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between speed and sensitivity in auditory–tactile processing, consistent with accounts where crossmodal congruency primarily limits or enhances the quality of perceptual evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Complex coordination through partner choice in baboons (Papio papio)
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Claidière; Constantin Montel; Tatsuya Kameda; Yohsuke Ohtsubo; Joel Fagot
articles_hidden.abstract:
Coordination is a cornerstone of social life, enabling individuals to achieve collective goals and maintain group cohesion. In non-human primates, coordination can rely on flexible partner-dependent strategies, but the interplay between these strategies and partner choice remains poorly understood. Here, we introduced a complex anti-matching coordination task to a group of Guinea baboons (Papio papio), requiring individuals to select a different stimulus from their partner to be rewarded. We compared their performance with a previously studied matching task, where selecting the same stimulus as their partner was rewarded. While baboons adapted to both tasks, increasing their success rate over time, we found little evidence of partner-dependent strategies. Instead, they primarily relied on partner choice: individuals reorganized their social interactions to engage with compatible partners, avoiding those with conflicting strategies. This reorganization was particularly pronounced in the anti-matching phase, where partner choice was critical to maintain high performance.
Our results demonstrate that, when possible, baboons prefer partner choice over partner dependent strategies to solve coordination problems. This highlights the importance of social flexibility and individual differences in shaping coordination outcomes, offering new insights into the cognitive and social mechanisms underpinning flexible cooperation in non-human primates.

articles_hidden.title: From Epic to Applied Psychology: A Conceptual Mapping of Sanskrit Psychological Constructs and Their Contemporary Relevance
articles_hidden.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles_hidden.abstract: This conceptual paper examines whether four Sanskrit epic constructs hold structural resonance with four established areas of psychological science. It responds to a growing interest in integrating Indian Knowledge Systems with psychological theory, extending that integration into underexplored epic material. Sanskrit's own literary and grammatical heritage has long been recognised in linguistics and aesthetics; this paper asks whether its psychological vocabulary deserves comparable recognition. Following a conceptual-article design (Theory Synthesis), the paper pairs dharma saṅkaṭa with moral cognition, tapas-nirvṛtti with self-regulation, rasa with affective science, and karma yoga with motivation theory. Four criteria—definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity—guided construct selection. Constructs were drawn from named episodes in the Mahābhārata, Kumārasambhava, and Buddhacarita, rather than from Sanskrit thought treated generally. Each pairing shows meaningful structural alignment without collapsing into a single unifying model. Applied implications extend to education, therapy, policy, and Gen-Z digital burnout, illustrating the pairings' contemporary relevance. Each pairing was illustrated through a textual episode and a contemporary vignette, grounding abstract resonance in concrete cases. The paper offers four testable propositions for future empirical validation. It also proposes a shared vocabulary bridging Sanskrit psychological thought and contemporary science, without claiming either tradition anticipated or exhausts the other.

articles_hidden.title: Stronger together? Examining the buffering effects of same-ethnicity partners on experiences of discrimination among sexual minority men of color
articles_hidden.authors: Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Joel Michel Le Forestier; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Jane Cao; Aki Gormezano; Tin D. Vo; Milada Dvorakova; Joseph Cox; Nathan Lachowsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Group membership and social connections play important roles in protecting people from stigmatized groups against the effects of discrimination on mental health. However, because people can belong to many groups, they may find themselves in situations where they experience stigmatization from others with whom they also share a stigmatized identity. We examine these intersectional experiences with a subsample of sexual minority men of color from a larger cohort study focused on sexual minority men’s health and wellbeing in Canada’s three largest cities (N = 314, nvisits = 725). We examine (i) whether experiences of racism from other sexual minority men and homophobia from other people of color affects the types of partners people seek out and (ii) whether having partners from a similar ethnoracial background protects against the effects of discrimination on mental health. We found that neither racism from other sexual minority men (including sexual racism) nor homophobia from people of color affected whom participants sought out as sexual partners. Having more partners of the same ethnoracial background had mixed protective effects. The effects of racism from sexual minority men (but not sexual racism) on mental health were attenuated among participants who reported more ethnoracial ingroup partners. However,  having more partners exacerbated the effects of homophobia from other people of color. These effects were limited to partners of the same race or ethnicity, and not to partners of color in general. These findings highlight the importance of attending to intraminority intersectional experiences and nuances of the effects of group membership across different forms of stigma.

articles.title: Distributional Validity of a Korean Synthetic Persona Panel: Evidence From the Korea Media Panel Survey
articles.authors: Howard Kim; Keun Tae Cho
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) personas are proposed as survey respondents, yet validation outside English-speaking contexts is scarce. We evaluate how well a Korean synthetic persona panel used to condition Gemini 3.5 Flash and EXAONE reproduces digital and artificial intelligence (AI) service-use distributions of the Korea Media Panel Survey. About 8,000 personas per model answered eight service-use items and eight attitudinal constructs; responses were compared with weighted survey estimates. The overall mean absolute error (MAE) was 14-19 percentage points (pp), with binary item-mean correlations of 0.70-0.91 across waves. Segment error across five axes was 14-18 pp, with between-group signed-error ranges of 49.6/34.7 pp (Gemini/EXAONE; 39.5/31.2 without the non-comparable teen cells). Errors were model-specific: an age stereotype (Gemini) versus an acquiescence-consistent level bias (EXAONE). Generative-AI overestimation was consistent with temporal misalignment; short-form underestimation was framing-sensitive and persisted under randomized order (both shown for Gemini). Post-hoc holdout calibration on 30% of the real data, with the correction form selected inside the calibration set, cut cell MAE from 18.3/15.1 to 4.9/4.4 pp, yet direct estimation from that subsample was more accurate than the calibrated panel (3.6 pp), a synthetic-informed shrinkage estimator beat its real-only counterpart by at most 0.7 pp, and the correction did not transfer competitively across waves. The calibrated panel kept an advantage only below roughly 250-860 real responses (at most 2.3 pp over a real-only shrinkage estimator) or, for one model, on unobserved segments. In this setting, synthetic panels are not survey substitutes; their value is diagnostic.

articles.title: Making Place for Health and Good Life: Tourism at the Intersection of Philosophy and Public Health
articles.authors: Fulvio Longato; Patrick Rina; Christian Josef Wiedermann
articles.abstract: Tourism is increasingly promoted as a resource for health, and destinations market the well-being their landscapes are said to afford; yet the notion of well-being invoked where tourism and public health meet requires further specification, as the fields that converge there do not necessarily use the term in the same sense. The conceptual analysis clarifies well-being by distinguishing its psychological dimensions from its philosophical characterisation in terms of human flourishing, and frames health from a salutogenic perspective. Human flourishing and salutogenesis intersect particularly through meaningfulness and the ways persons engage with what places make possible. Drawing on the phenomenology of the tourist experience and on the literatures of therapeutic landscapes and restorative environments, the paper argues that places contribute to health through multiple and potentially interacting pathways involving characteristics of settings, activities and experiences, and their social and environmental contexts. Embodied pathways further show the interconnection of experiential and bodily dimensions of health. The paper draws out implications for public health and participatory destination design. Alpine tourism destinations provide a suitable context in which these relationships can be examined empirically.

articles.title: A Reader’s Guide to the Rubin Report
articles.authors: John Levi Martin
articles.abstract: This was written for those readers of the Rubin report who are outsiders to the discipline of sociology, and look to this report as a guide to the state of this field.  Given the publicity this report has received, it would be reasonable for them to imagine that there is warrant for its claims.  There have been many responses to this report, but (as far as I know) none that have simply focused on whether she actually marshaled evidence to support her arguments, and whether she correctly represents her sources.

articles.title: Observed Shifts in the Health Equity Research Landscape: Results of a National Survey of Health Equity Researchers April-July, 2025
articles.authors: Clair Kronk; Sima Rabinowitz; Denise Milstein; Devin Madden; Nita Vangeepuram; Dinushika Mohottige; Timnit Berhane; Andrew Maroko
articles.abstract:
Objectives. To assess changes health equity researchers have made or anticipate making to their research in the context of the current federal administration’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusion. 
Methods. We shared an electronic survey link with health equity researchers at academic, non-academic non-profit, non-academic for-profit, and governmental institutions in the U.S. between April and July 2025. 634 responses were received; 381 completed. The survey assessed demographics, occupational and institutional characteristics, perceptions of job security, experiences of stress, collaborations, censorship, and funding sources. 
Results. A large majority of respondents (96.6%) reported having made or anticipated making changes to their health equity research. Changes included: using different language (83.7.%), adapting or altering research questions (56.4%), pivoting to new health equity topics (49.6%), developing new health equity projects (50.4%), seeking new collaborators (31.0%), stopping health equity research activities (18.9%), and withdrawing from existing collaborations (8.9%).
Conclusions. A significant number of health equity researchers have made or anticipate making fundamental changes to their research. These changes have critical implications for health equity research, public health, research teams, and the communities most impacted by this work.

articles.title: Patient-reported experience as audit evidence: a new perspective on governance in integrated care
articles.authors: Ilona Ogurcova
articles.abstract:
Patient-reported experience can identify problems in integrated care, yet feedback alone does not show whether organisations address them. This Perspective argues that experience data can inform internal audit evidence and person-centred healthcare governance when their quality, context and interpretive limits are examined. Developed within the author's doctoral research programme, the argument draws on a purposively selected set of scientific publications and official documents; it does not report a literature review or analyse the programme's empirical datasets. The conceptual method compares the purposes and units of patient-experience measurement, SCIROCCO integration maturity assessment, value-based healthcare implementation assessment and professional internal audit. An illustrative crosswalk then connects five coordination and participation concerns with contextual domains, candidate audit questions, corroborating information and management follow-up. The proposed cycle moves from patient-defined priorities through evidence evaluation to accountable action and repeated assessment of experience. It preserves management ownership of controls and distinguishes a reported concern from a demonstrated organisational failure. Neither the crosswalk nor the combined framework has been empirically validated. Patient involvement, feasibility assessment and comparative evaluation are needed to establish usefulness, burden and effects. The contribution is a testable governance proposition, not evidence of improved clinical outcomes or economic value.
Keywords: patient-reported experience data, internal audit, audit evidence, integrated care, SCIROCCO maturity model, healthcare governance, person-centred care

articles.title: Informing Instruction During Educational Disruptions: A UTAUT-Informed Mixed-Methods Study of Grade 11 Students' Evaluations of YouTube for Oral Communication Learning
articles.authors: Jo Michael Llamelo
articles.abstract: Educational disruptions can require students to rely on supplementary digital resources when ordinary classroom interaction is restricted. This study examined how 26 Grade 11 students enrolled in Oral Communication at a private senior high school in Legazpi City, Philippines, evaluated YouTube during emergency remote teaching in Academic Year 2020-2021. A convergent, cross-sectional mixed-methods survey used 17 six-point Likert-type items organized through UTAUT-informed domains, each paired with an open-ended prompt. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, while 442 written explanations were analyzed through deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis and integrated with their corresponding ratings. Domain means were generally favorable, ranging from 4.48 for behavioral intention to 5.08 for facilitating conditions. Internal consistency was strong for performance expectancy (α = .82) but weaker for the other domains (α = .37-.65), so domain-level results were interpreted cautiously and alongside item-level and qualitative evidence. The qualitative analysis produced 28 substantive codes synthesized into five cross-domain patterns: controllable multimodal explanation supported comprehension; YouTube expanded explanatory options but required active selection; educational value depended on content and presenter quality; access was flexible but infrastructure-dependent; and acceptance was pragmatic and supplementary rather than substitutive. Across 442 rating-explanation pairs, 75.3% were congruent positive and 15.4% were qualified or mixed. The findings suggest that students valued YouTube primarily as a flexible supplementary resource for clarification, review, and continuity rather than as a replacement for teacher-led instruction. Notably, connectivity and infrastructure concerns remained visible even among participants selected for online readiness, underscoring the distinction between nominal readiness and reliable access.

articles.title: Adolescent Online Leisure, Media Literacy, and Emotional Distress from Online Victimization: Evidence Across Fifty Countries and Economies
articles.authors: Yunqi Wang; Yan Ruth Xia; James A. Bovaird; Maria Rosario T. de Guzman; Paul Springer; Xiaoran Sun
articles.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has accelerated adolescents’ engagement in online activities. However, research on adolescents’ technology use and mental health often overlooks the complexity of online behaviors and the role of media literacy without examining specific mechanisms. This study addresses the gap by analyzing survey data from 295,843 adolescents aged 15-16 years across 50 countries and economies from Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) collected in 2022, examining the relations among adolescent online leisure, media literacy, and emotional distress from online victimization. Structural equation modeling results revealed that both adolescents’ online leisure and media literacy are positively associated with their emotional distress from online victimization experiences, such as exposure to unwanted content. Findings provide important implications for research, theories, and practices, highlighting an urgent need for parenting practices and interventions to promote adolescents’ media literacy and digital skills to navigate the online environment and mitigate online risks.

articles.title: Empirical Reasoning About FOI Request Delays in the European Union
articles.authors: Jukka Ruohonen
articles.abstract: Freedom of information (FOI) is a human right and an important concept for the transparency and accountability of governments and public administrations. It is also essential for democracy. Despite a long research lineage on FOI laws and their use by citizens, existing empirical knowledge is still limited regarding the inner workings of FOI requests. This limitation applies particularly to the European Union (EU) and the documents possessed by its various institutions. To help at addressing this limitation, the paper presents a few empirical observations about FOI requests in the EU context. By using a dataset containing 500 requests made between 2022 and early 2023, the insight presented cover the EU institutions targeted, the requesters making FOI requests, and particularly the bureaucratic delays in handling of FOI requests. According to results based on a regression analysis, the bureaucratic delays vary according to both the EU institutions and the individual requesters.

articles.title: Responsibility to Prepare: From Individual Security to Collective Resilience
articles.authors: Paulus Damgaard; Jonas Toubøl; Lærke Høgenhaven
articles.abstract: In the context of heightened geopolitical tensions, European societies increasingly frame private crisis preparedness as integral to societal resilience. Once viewed as antisocial survivalists, preppers now offer insight into civil society’s role in prepar-edness. Drawing on a netnographic study of one of Denmark’s largest Facebook prepper groups (2015-2024), this article examines how the group members per-ceive responsibility for crisis preparedness across four periods: before COVID-19, during the pandemic, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and following the Danish government’s 2024 appeal for household preparedness. Findings reveal a dominant individualistic framing in stable times, but a shift towards collective understandings of responsibility following official communication during crises. The article con-tributes to sociological research on crisis preparedness by demonstrating how per-ceptions of crisis contexts and state communication shape preppers’ responsibility frames, challenging static portrayals of preppers as antisocial and highlighting how individualised practices of preparedness can evolve into collective orientations that complement state capacity.

articles.title: Your AI Knows Your Story. Should It Die With You?
articles.authors: Alexander Seifert
articles.abstract: Personal conversations with AI assistants increasingly contain memories, reflections, and records of changing judgment that may outlive their users. This commentary argues that selected exchanges could form a digital legacy: not a posthumous replica, but a personal testimony curated while the person is still able to correct it. Such legacies may be especially meaningful for people who wish to pass on their experience beyond their immediate family. Their creation, however, requires explicit consent, designated recipients, durable access, and a clear separation between the user's own words, the system's contributions, and any interpretations generated later. Whether such archives transmit wisdom or support bereavement remains an open question.

articles.title: Organising the Social Layer: How Organisational Paradoxes Shape Engagement in Cryptocurrency Communities
articles.authors: Annika Aebli; Fabienne Silberstein-Bamford; Joshua Silberstein Bamford
articles.abstract: Cryptocurrencies (crypto) and their underlying blockchain technologies are designed around the promise of collective organising without reliance on centralised authority, intermediaries, and hierarchical coordination. Yet sustaining collective participation in decentralised networks without conventional forms of coordination remains an organisational challenge. This study demonstrates that keeping participants engaged in crypto communities depends on continuous work within crypto’s social layer. Drawing on the organisational paradox lens and 26 semi-structured interviews with developers, team members, and regular users across four crypto communities, we show that sustained engagement depends on balancing organisational paradoxes rooted in communication, decision-making, and community development: technical discourse versus social-media-style interaction, decentralised participation versus centralised guidance, and scaling versus a sense of authentic community. Our findings suggest that continually balancing, rather than resolving these tensions is essential for engagement and community cohesion. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of decentralised organising by showing how collective participation can be maintained in organisational arrangements that seek to reduce reliance on conventional centralised structures. More broadly, we show that decentralisation does not eliminate the need for organising but relocates much of this work to the social layer of interaction, coordination, and community building, where contradictory demands must be continually negotiated to keep participation workable and sustainable.

articles.title: Mind the Gap: Elite Preferences for Redistribution and How they Differ from the Mass Public
articles.authors: Mogens K. Justesen; Marko Klašnja; Sara B. Hobolt; Robert Klemmensen
articles.abstract:
Increasing inequality has raised concerns over the disproportionate influence of the rich on public policies. Central to such concerns is the assumption that elite policy preferences are unified and differ significantly from the general public. We theorize economic elites as fiscal constituencies, highlighting intra-elite differences in policy preferences based on elite sources of affluence and therefore fiscal claims they face from the state. 
Employing high-quality administrative and survey data, including conjoint experiments, from Denmark, we compare tax and spending preferences in the general population with the largest samples to date of the top 1% by income and wealth. While elites are more economically conservative, they are not uniformly anti-redistribution; the asset-rich are less conservative than the income-rich; and their preferences often differ over tax policy. These findings highlight elite group differences based on their relation to the fiscal structure of the state and offer new insights into the micro-foundations of unequal representation in advanced democracies.

articles.title: Ranking Data in Political Science
articles.authors: Yuki Atsusaka; Shubhangi Singh
articles.abstract: Across scientific disciplines, researchers have used ranking data to study people's comparative judgments, preferences, and decision-making over a range of items. While existing data-sharing infrastructures in statistics and machine learning, such as PrefLib, offer a rich collection of ranking datasets, including those related to politics, they are not necessarily designed specifically to support cumulative research in social science. In this work, we introduce the first large-scale database of political rankings based on various studies from leading political science journals. Our first release covers 52 datasets from 27 original studies published between 2005 and 2025. Our database demonstrates notable variation in substantive topics and forms of ranking data that go well beyond canonical examples of candidate evaluations and value orientations, enabling researchers to perform comparative analyses, replication, reanalysis, methodological evaluation, and new substantive research with real-world political rankings. Along with validating our database, we illustrate it by replicating key findings in four selected studies, including those of multiple identities in American politics, the representation of Muslims in India, factional leaning in the Syrian civil war, and legislative accountability for affordable health care.

articles.title: Agreeing in Principle, Disagreeing on Policy: How Beliefs About the Gender Pay Gap Shape Fairness Concerns and Policy Preferences
articles.authors: Fabian Kalleitner; Jule Adriaans; Ole Brüggemann; Cristóbal Moya; Sandra Bohmann
articles.abstract: Willingness to reduce gender inequalities partly depends on whether people are aware of them and consider them unfair. Extending scholarship centered on inequality misperceptions, we focus on beliefs about the sources of the gender pay gap (GPG), experimentally varying people's ability to attribute pay disparities to women's choices. Preregistered survey experiments in the U.S. and Germany show that information about larger (vs. smaller) and within-job (vs. overall) GPGs independently increases awareness, raises perceived unfairness, and translates into general support for government action. Initially less-supportive groups (conservatives, men) showed some of the largest increases in general support. Yet, updated beliefs did not increase support for specific policies, such as pay transparency laws or gender quotas. These findings suggest that information campaigns can affect beliefs about GPG's size and sources, but even perceiving GPGs as unfair does not bridge the gap between abstract commitment to gender equality and concrete policy support.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: Heed the warning: how NATO can find and fill the gaps in its warning systems
articles.authors: Nikki Ikani
articles.abstract: Intelligence warning failures are too often viewed in binary: Either intelligence succeeded or it failed. In reality, often only segments of the warning chain collapse while others operate well. This Outlook paper treats warning success as a spectrum rather than as a pass/fail test in a new framework for warning performance. It illustrates the use through three recent case studies: the fall of Kabul (2021), Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (2022) and the Niger coup (2023). The decisive shortfall across all three cases was the failure to reconcile divergent NATO member state views into an operational consensus within NATO. There are practical solutions for integrating NATO capabilities to institutionalize rapid after-action reviews, conduct periodic divergence drill exercises, prepare contingency packages and further embed red team analyses.

articles.title: Detecting Inequality in Noisy Communication: Promises and Pitfalls of Large Language Models
articles.authors: Susanne Reinhardt; Jonathan J.B. Mijs; David Schieferdecker; Michael Vaughan
articles.abstract: How inequality is communicated shapes how it is explained, understood, and legitimated or contested. Yet studying these communicative processes at scale is challenging because inequality is multidimensional, often expressed implicitly and relationally, and context dependent. We argue that large language models (LLMs) shift, but do not eliminate, these methodological challenges. We trace the development from manual content analysis to rule-based computational approaches and machine learning to LLMs and assess how these methods combine conceptual alignment, semantic sensitivity, contextual sensitivity, and scalability. LLMs help relax some longstanding trade-offs between semantic sensitivity to meaning and scalability, thus promising more comprehensive analyses of established research questions and opening possibilities for comparative research across contexts. Yet untapping their full potential for research on inequality communication depends on addressing problems concerning conceptual validity, representation, comparative measurement, and substantive inference. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for rigorous LLM-based inequality communication research.

articles.title: Women and AI: A Large-Scale, Validated Mapping of Women’s Under-Represented and Under-Recognized Contributions to AI Research
articles.authors: Chiara Binelli; Elena Cossu
articles.abstract: Participation in AI research shapes which type of AI is built, whose societal needs it addresses, and how it is used in society. Despite increasing attention to gender diversity in AI, we lacksystematic evidence on the research topics, methods used, and collaboration structures associated with female AI researchers. This paper addresses this significant gap by developing the first large-scale, validated mapping of women’s contributions to both generative and non-generative AI research across data science and the main social science disciplines (economics, political science, and sociology). Using a sample of over 500,000 papers published between 2023 and 2026, we document three key findings. First, women are under-represented among academic AI authors across all four disciplines and recent years, and least represented in data science. Second, conditional on participating, women’s AI research is thematically distinctive: it is more applied, social and purpose-driven, concentrated in health, education and fairness, and, in data science, oriented towards using rather than building AI. Third, this distinctive work is heard less: conditional on working on the same AI topic women and men are cited equally, but the topics women disproportionately work on are themselves cited less, so women’s ideas receive systematically fewer citations. This voice gap is therefore a topic-composition penalty rather than a same-topic penalty, and it reduces efficiency by giving a distinctive, society-oriented research agenda too little voice in how AI develops.

articles.title: L’IA dans les élections municipales 2026 : Des usages qui appellent un regard nuancé
articles.authors: Antoine Marie
articles.abstract:
The municipal elections of March 15 and 22, 2026 constitute the first
French local election in which generative artificial intelligence has
massively entered campaign practices. This research brief offers a
balanced analysis of documented uses, distinguishing legitimate
applications (poster generation, programmatic chatbots, content
synthesis) from confirmed abuses (defamatory deepfakes, misleading
images, astroturfing). While these new technological capabilities raise
legitimate concerns for the integrity of democratic debate, we argue that
their impact must be put in perspective in light of the literature on the
limited effects of mass political communication and the actual
determinants of disinformation consumption. Rather than a
catastrophism that risks fueling generalized distrust, we advocate for an
approach grounded in media literacy and the strengthening of
professional journalism.

articles.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles.title: A New Era of Political Socialization? The Interplay Between Political Social Media Exposure, Conspiracy Thinking, and Political Distrust Among Dutch Younger vs. Older Generations
articles.authors: Tamar Montagne; Anouk Smeekes
articles.abstract: In recent years, populist radical-right parties (PRRP) have gained substantial electoral support in European countries, especially among younger voters. However, few studies have focused on the generational divide in PRRP voting behavior and the factors that explain why current younger generations are more likely to vote for PRRP. The current study addresses this research gap by examining whether generational differences in PRRP voting can be explained by variations in political social media exposure (PSME) and its indirect pathways through conspiracy thinking and political distrust, while accounting for the moderating role of anti-immigrant attitudes. Drawing on insights from developmental psychology, political psychology, and political science, we developed an interdisciplinary framework. We tested our expectations in the context of the Netherlands using data from the Dutch Parliamentary Election Study 2023, drawing on a sample of Dutch eligible voters. Results showed that current younger generations (Generations Y and Z) were more likely to vote for PRRP compared to older generations, partly explained by their higher PSME and subsequently, stronger conspiracy thinking and political distrust. Results further showed that the effect of conspiracy thinking on PRRP voting was particularly pronounced for respondents with low levels of anti-immigrant attitudes.

articles.title: Health-Related AI Information Seeking, Anxiety, and Professional Mental Health Service Use Among U.S. College Students
articles.authors: Tania Akter
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are becoming more widely used in students’ daily lives, yet little is known about how anxiety relates to college students’ use of generative AI for health-related information seeking. This exploratory study examined associations between anxiety, health-related generative AI information seeking, and professional mental health service use among U.S. college students. Survey-weighted logistic regression models were used to assess these associations. Results showed that higher anxiety scores were associated with greater odds of reporting health-related AI use. Among students who reported health-related AI use, higher anxiety was also associated with greater odds of professional mental health service use. Findings suggest that health-related generative AI use is an emerging behavior modestly associated with anxiety and may coexist with professional mental health help-seeking among college students.

articles.title: What is edtech for? A cross-national popularity index of educational apps
articles.authors: Lulu Shi; Basak Bozkurt
articles.abstract: Digitalisation in education is so far described through broad indicators such as market growth, venture capital investment, infrastructure provision, or device availability in schools and homes. While useful, these measures reveal little about for what purposes digital technologies are used in education, and how these purposes vary across national contexts and time. This article addresses these gaps by developing an education app popularity index based on daily top-200 education app rankings across twelve countries between 2017 and 2023: Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Norway, Poland, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Drawing on app metadata, education apps are categorised according to the services and functions they offer to understand for what purpose they serve. The ranking is then aggregated to analyse category prominence over time and across countries to understand popularity of education apps by category. The study makes three contributions. First, it provides a granular account of what educational apps offer, showing that the educational app landscape is not dominated by a single type of service but consists of a heterogeneous mixture of tutoring tools, management platforms, parent-facing communication apps and a range of apps supporting infomal learning. Second, it shows the popularity of different types of digital education services and how and their popularity shift over time. Third, it shows that these patterns vary across country contexts. Differences across countries point to that edtech usage is not only driven by individual preferences but by distinct institutional arrangements and cultures. Lastly, this study also advances a methodological approach for understanding the realities of edtech deployment by using Google Play Store data, the world’s largest app market in terms of content volume.

articles.title: Autonomy, Adolescents, and Artificial Intelligence
articles.authors: Michael J. S. Beauvais
articles.abstract:
In this essay, I explore the potential implications of adolescent use of AI assistants on the development of adolescents’ capacities for autonomy. Thinking through these issues from the perspective of first principles is, I believe, needed in order to sharpen our understanding of some of the issues AI assistants pose for young people. A clear analysis will suggest which legal or policy prescriptions should follow. 

I first give an overview of adolescent use of AI assistants, noting their popularity and the variety of use contexts. Drawing upon the work of Catriona Mackenzie, I then outline a relational conception of autonomy that conceives of autonomy as having three distinct dimensions: self-determination, self-governance, and self-authorization. The precision of Mackenzie’s conception allows us to more carefully consider how different uses and contexts of technological use can affect individuals’ capacities for autonomy. Using this three-dimensional conception of autonomy, I propose three potential interventions for law and policy: thinking beyond harms, substantive privacy protections, and autonomy impact assessments.

articles.title: Press freedom shapes the link between mainstream and social media use for news and climate change understanding: evidence from 30 countries
articles.authors: Laurent Cordonier; Didier Witkowski; Florian Cafiero
articles.abstract: A recent meta-analysis examining the relationship between individuals’ information behaviour and their views about climate change found that, on average, using social media and other user-generated online sources was more strongly associated with science-consistent climate beliefs than using mainstream media. The present study, however, investigates whether these associations vary across countries depending on the level of press freedom, as mainstream journalism is better able to foreground scientific expertise and challenge misleading climate claims when operating freely, whereas social media may provide a partial alternative to constrained domestic mainstream coverage. Accordingly, mainstream media use was hypothesised to be more positively associated with science-consistent climate beliefs and knowledge in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, while the opposite pattern was expected for social media use for news. The analysis draws on a survey of 23,500 respondents in 30 countries. Within each country, survey-weighted models estimated associations between mainstream and social media use for news and four outcomes: belief in the existence of climate change, belief in its anthropogenic nature, belief in its negative consequences, and climate change knowledge, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Overall, mainstream media use was more often positively associated with science-consistent beliefs and knowledge than social media use. Cross-national analyses then tested whether these country-specific associations varied with press freedom, controlling for socioeconomic development. For each outcome, the association with mainstream media use was more positive in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, whereas the association with social media use for news showed the opposite cross-national pattern. These findings suggest that mainstream media generally contribute more to public understanding of climate change than social media, especially where press freedom is greater, while social media may play a partial compensatory role where domestic journalism is constrained.

articles.title: Researcher well-being as a leading indicator in research-funding governance: A system dynamics exploration of top-down versus bottom-up allocation
articles.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Satoshi Sano
articles.abstract: Governments face a recurring dilemma in dividing public research funding between top-down, competitive, mission-oriented programmes and bottom-up, investigator-led institutional grants. This research note presents an exploratory system dynamics model that endogenizes researcher motivation, conceived following self-determination theory as a slow-moving stock of psychological capital, within the feedback structure linking funding allocation, research outputs, and societal returns. Simulation experiments across three policy scenarios reveal a consistent time-asymmetric pattern. First, accelerating the shift toward competitive funding produces an earlier but lower peak in societal returns, followed by sustained decline. Second, shifting toward bottom-up funding restores motivation but opens a transition valley in returns whose depth grows with transition speed. Third, delayed corrective reallocation exhibits hysteresis: once motivation is depleted, even aggressive reallocation requires roughly two decades before returns recover. One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis indicates that these qualitative patterns persist across the tested parameter ranges, while the level of long-run returns proves highly sensitive to the weight placed on discretionary research time, around which the baseline system undergoes a regime shift. The model implies that researcher well-being functions as a leading indicator of research-system health, preceding declines in publication-based lagging indicators. We derive three testable propositions and outline an agenda for empirical calibration, beginning with a national baseline survey of researchers being launched in Japan. For funding governance, the results imply that monitoring leading indicators and pacing allocation transitions matter as much as choosing the allocation ratio itself.
