articles.title: Provisioning for human needs at low resource use: institutional lessons from Cuba, Costa Rica and Ecuador
articles.authors: Chirag Dhara; Gustav Cederlöf; Viviana Cordero; Carolina Mauri; Tannya Pico; Soumyajit Bhar
articles.abstract: In the pursuit of sustainable development, Global South countries face the challenge of advancing wellbeing without breaching environmental limits. A central question for development policy is what institutional and policy configurations can deliver high levels of human need satisfaction at low ecological cost. We address this through structured comparative case studies of Cuba, Costa Rica and Ecuador: three middle-income countries achieving health and educational outcomes comparable to  higher-income nations with considerably lower environmental impacts, while also differing widely on the political-economic spectrum. Situating them within a social provisioning framework, we analyse the exogenous endowments, external conditions, structural-institutional configurations and concrete policies that account for their performance. Five cross-cutting patterns emerge across otherwise divergent political contexts: 1. sustained public investment in health and education, protected from fiscal volatility even during economic crises has been the foundational mechanism of needs satisfaction among all three; 2. periods of institutional stability have been preconditions for transformative legislation; 3. land tenure reform and food system restructuring have functioned simultaneously as instruments of ecological governance and social equity; 4. organised civil society has proved facilitative for sustaining provisioning gains across political transitions, although in Cuba such organisation has occurred within the politicised framework of the state; and 5. low energy and material throughput has been induced at least partly by resource constraint rather than by design. For the Global South, these cases offer a spectrum of configurations that can enable the satisfaction of human needs at moderate levels of affluence.

articles.title: Living Arrangements, Going Outdoors, and Well-Being Among Older Persons: Examining Their Associations in a Swedish Population
articles.authors: Jeanette Melin; Marie-Louise Möllerberg; Marit Preuter; Kristofer Årestedt
articles.abstract:
Aim: This study examined associations between living arrangement, frequency of going outdoors, and well-being among older persons in Sweden, with particular attention to their interaction.
Methods: Community-dwelling older persons (n = 1,727) across nine Swedish municipalities participated in a cross-sectional survey. Well-being was assessed using the Older Persons’ Well-being Scale (OPWELLS). Linear regression models examined associations and interactions.
Results: Living alone was associated with lower well-being compared to cohabiting, whereas going outdoors more frequently was associated with higher well-being. The association between living arrangement and well-being differed by outdoor frequency.
Conclusions: Frequency of going outdoors was strongly associated with well-being irrespective of living arrangement. However, the association between living alone and well-being varied with outdoor frequency. Thus, living alone should not be considered an isolated indicator of lower well-being in older age and highlights the importance of considering living arrangements within the broader context of older persons’ everyday lives.

articles.title: ‘Intersectionality in the Mind’: Applying an Intersectional Lens to the Study of Lay Perceptions of Inequality
articles.authors: Margherita Cusmano
articles.abstract: Research on lay perceptions of inequality has typically examined economic, gender, and racial inequalities separately and treated social positions additively. Using migrants as a case study, this study employs an intersectional lens to investigate perceptions of inequality. Drawing on interviews and group discussions with 47 participants, the analysis shows, first, that individuals framed different inequalities as interdependent, showcasing what I term ‘intersectionality in the mind’. Second, their intersectional social positions informed how they understood broader patterns of inequality. These findings demonstrate the value of intersectional approaches in analysing the complexity of lay perceptions of inequality. This study points toward methodological and conceptual developments that can better capture both how people cognitively link inequalities and how intersecting social positions inform these perceptions.

articles.title: Systematic Evaluation of Nation-State Propaganda in LLM Outputs
articles.authors: Kevin T. Greene; Jacob N Shapiro
articles.abstract: The rapid growth and usability of AI is creating new risks to information quality, including the possibility that chatbot responses spread propaganda from state-backed influence campaigns. There is little systematic evidence regarding how frequently LLMs spread such narratives when responding to user queries. Previous attempts to assess these risks rely on small numbers of evaluation questions, use opaque query construction procedures, and fail to account for key sources of uncertainty in model responses. We address these gaps with an automated, reproducible pipeline that samples documented state-backed propaganda and news items, programmatically generates evaluation questions, and audits LLM-generated responses. We evaluate whether five prominent models: (1) reproduce arguments aligned with documented Kremlin propaganda narratives; (2) present the Kremlin perspective on events without providing corrective context; and (3) cite known propaganda outlets. We find substantially lower rates of propaganda-aligned responses and propaganda-source citation than prior small-sample work would suggest. These risks are particularly rare for questions resembling ordinary information searches about Ukraine. Our approach enables systematic comparisons across models and issue areas, supports ongoing monitoring, and could be extended to many other hotly-debated topics.

articles.title: Delisting and dispersal: author communities before and after removal from Scopus
articles.authors: Marek Deja
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Delisting removes a journal from an index but not its authors. This study asks whether cohorts disperse or share destinations and whether concentrated inflow is associated with receiving journals' subsequent delisting.

Design/methodology/approach: The analysis reconstructs interval-valued delisting dates from successive Scopus lists, assigns delisted event clocks to matched cohorts, and compares destination overlap with margin-preserving, opportunity-structured, and matched-observed benchmarks. A six-month-landmark discrete-time hazard model handles right censoring and competing exits.

Findings: Delisted-journal output averaged 66.7% below the post-event reference path. For 121 cohorts, median observed-to-expected overlap was 2.40 under the opportunity-structured benchmark. Across 55 matched sets, delisted cohorts overlapped 10.6 percentage points less than references (95% CI [-0.14, -0.07]), a gap that predated delisting and was smaller but present on venues new to the author. An exploratory hazard analysis showed a positive in-sample association between concentrated inflow and receiving journals' subsequent delisting, but extensive censoring and short follow-up preclude a stable magnitude claim.

Research limitations: Delisting is non-random; estimates are descriptive contrasts, benchmark deviations, and conditional in-sample associations.

Practical implications: Synthetic benchmarks establish residual cohort structure; matched observed cohorts test whether it is event-specific.

Originality/value: The study provides a two-stage design for event-specific concentration claims. Pairing a constrained randomisation with matched observed cohorts reversed the substantive conclusion.

articles.title: What the World Studies, Invents and Reports About Urban Heat
articles.authors: Narendra Kumar
articles.abstract: We assemble 20,422 scholarly papers on urban heat islands (1990–2025), read the 17,101 that carry an abstract sentence by sentence, and join them to 96,726 news articles (2021–2025), 4,123 patent families, 14,576 recorded heat incidents, registers of companies, funding rounds and government funding events, and the annual accounts of Indian companies. Eight results stand out. (1) The field grew about 9 times faster than the scholarly literature as a whole, and in 2015–2019 titles naming "extreme heat" overtook those naming "heat island". (2) Of 2,409 papers that attribute urban heat to a cause, 48% name urbanisation and land-use change; attribution to anthropogenic heat fell from 18.4% to 7.7%. (3) Research and news describe different problems: at equal text length, 28% of research openings raise mitigation against 1.6% of news leads, while 22% of news leads are forecasts or warnings against 1.4% of research. (4) They also describe different places: China accounts for 31% of the research and 2.3% of English-language coverage, and Delhi receives 7.4 times the coverage its research share would predict. (5) Invention has outrun science: patent families for cool and permeable pavements grew 12-fold in a decade against 2.4-fold for the research on them. (6) Across 194 studies the median reported cooling from urban trees is 2.0 °C (air temperature 2.0 °C, surface temperature 2.9 °C). (7) Between 2021–22 and 2024–25 news coverage moved from the hazard to the people exposed: workers, schools, the elderly and hospital patients each rose 1.4- to 2.4-fold as a share of heat articles while wildfire and drought fell by about half and climate change — raised in about one article in ten — fell by a quarter. (8) The market record is thin: 140 of 5.05 million companies state a heat or cooling purpose, and recorded capital is $2.7 billion of cooling-infrastructure finance against $48 million of venture funding; larger Indian cooling companies grew revenue 25% a year over three years against 16% for Indian companies generally. Every cause category extracted from the research was tested against an independent second reader; three failed, and no result reported here rests on them.

articles.title: Theravada Buddhism in Contemporary China and Its Followers
articles.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles.abstract:
This paper studies the influence of Theravada Buddhism in contemporary China, with a 
focus on the seven ethnic minorities that share a considerable presence of Theravada Buddhism. 
It also considers the populations of Theravada Buddhists among the seven ethnic minorities, as 
well as from another 49 official-recognized ethnicities. It discovers that the Theravada Buddhist 
population increases from 1.3868 million in 2010 to 1.4519 million in 2018 and is expected to 
grow to 1.4786 million by 2027. The present study finds that the Dai ethnicity is not only 
essential for spreading Theravada Buddhism to other ethnicities but it also has the largest 
Theravada Buddhist ethnicity in China, which represents more than 72% of the total Theravada 
Buddhist population. Finally, it discloses that the seven ethnicities each have their own forms of 
folk religions with their faith showing a mix of folk religion with Theravada Buddhism.

articles.title: When Digital Exposure Meets Everyday Buying: Understanding Consumer Behaviour in FMCG
articles.authors: Rithik Bhattacharjee
articles.abstract: Consumers today may discover a product on social media, encounter it repeatedly through digital advertising, and still make the final purchase from a neighbourhood store. This study explores the relationship between digital exposure and everyday consumer behaviour in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector. Using a consumer survey dataset containing 26 usable responses, the study examines purchase frequency, purchase channels, exposure to social-media promotions, reported influence of online advertising, customer satisfaction, and recommendation intention. The findings show that social-media exposure is relatively common, while reported influence of online advertising is more mixed. Traditional retail remains important, with kirana stores and supermarkets accounting for most reported purchase channels. Mean satisfaction was 3.92 out of 5 among respondents with valid satisfaction scores, while recommendation intention was predominantly positive. Exploratory statistical analysis did not identify a statistically significant association between online-ad influence and recommendation intention (χ² = 0.26, p = 0.61), nor a statistically significant relationship between satisfaction and recommendation intention (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.21, p ≈ 0.31). The findings suggest that digital visibility should not automatically be interpreted as behavioural influence. Consumer decisions appear to involve a broader combination of digital communication, product experience, purchasing convenience, availability, and customer service. Given the small and youth-concentrated sample, the study is exploratory and does not claim population-level generalizability. The paper highlights the need for larger and more diverse studies examining how digital engagement interacts with the wider FMCG consumer journey.

articles.title: The City Multiple: Comparing Geographies of Digital Visibility across Google Maps, Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok
articles.authors: Reza Ardekani Shaker; Justus Uitermark
articles.abstract: Digital platforms have become key geospatial infrastructures through which cities are discovered, experienced, and evaluated. Whereas the extant literature has often focused on single platforms or assumed an undifferentiated platform urbanism, we know very little about how different platforms produce distinct geographies of urban visibility. To address this lacuna, we examine the spatially differentiated regimes of visibility that emerge when platforms mediate urban environments. In doing so, we distinguish between three dimensions of platforms’ geographies of digital visibility: (1) spatial inequality—how each platform distributes visibility across places; (2) spatial articulation—how platform visibilities map onto local urban geographies; and (3) spatial representation—the kinds of places and content that achieve visibility on each platform. Combining computational, geographic, and interpretive methods, we analyse how 6,682 eating and drinking establishments in Amsterdam are represented on TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps, and Facebook, and find strikingly weak correlations between their visibility on the four platforms. We find that each platform produces distinct structures of unequal visibility, with algorithmic-discovery platforms concentrating visibility more intensely than review-based systems. Neighbourhood-level analyses further show that platform-specific spatial articulations correspond to the gentrification and touristification of specific areas. Our findings contribute to the literatures on digital geography and platform urbanism by demonstrating that digital platforms generate multiple instantiations of the same city.

articles.title: Why Politicians Retweet: News Trustworthiness, Emotion, and Partisan Asymmetry in Elite News Sharing among US Congress Members
articles.authors: Apeksha Shetty; Esther Simmendinger; Jula Lühring; Annie Waldherr; David Garcia; Hannah Metzler
articles.abstract: On social media, politicians' retweets can determine which claims gain visibility in online and in wider political debate, yet the factors associated with these retweeting decisions remain poorly understood. Combining natural language processing measures of emotional tone and partisan cues with politician-level characteristics, we analyze the retweeting behavior of United States Members of Congress between 2021 and 2023 using multilevel logistic regression models. Using all news-related retweets during this period, paired with a negative sample of non-retweets, we examine how tweet content and legislators' ideological extremity predict the amplification of tweets linking to more and less trustworthy news domains. We find that partisan identity is a stronger predictor of retweeting than other factors. While politicians generally preferred retweeting content with links to trustworthy sources, this preference weakened when tweets contained party-related references. Anger and fear predicted higher retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political opponents, while anger predicted lower retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political allies. Furthermore, ideology conditioned how politicians responded to news trustworthiness: among Republicans, increasing ideological extremity was associated with weaker preference for trustworthy sources, with the most ideologically-extreme Republicans being especially likely to retweet tweets with links to less trustworthy domains. Together, these results suggest that politicians use retweets to reinforce partisan boundaries between 'us' and 'them'. This identity-centered pattern to retweeting explains how information from less trustworthy sources gains traction in polarized digital environments.

articles.title: Examination of the News-Finds-Me Perception as an Expanded Bifactor Construct
articles.authors: Toby Hopp
articles.abstract:
Within the mass and political communication literatures, the news-find-me (NFM)
perception has been increasingly used to explain the democratically deleterious implications of a
reliance on incidental, socially mediated news contact. Despite these efforts, there does not
currently exist a consistent means of measuring the NFM construct. This study developed an
expanded NFM measure and evaluated it using a latent bifactor model specification. The results
suggested that a bifactor-(S·I 1) specification fit the data in a plausible manner, and, therein, that
there exist research scenarios where the use of such an approach may confer benefits to
researchers.

articles.title: Staying Connected: Methodological Insights for Developing Panel Surveys with People Experiencing Homelessness
articles.authors: Caroline Teague; Aryaa Rajouria; Yuanxi Li; Brandon Morande; Hugo Aguas; Nathalie Williams; Jerald Herting; ihsan kahveci
articles.abstract:
Longitudinal research on people experiencing homelessness remains rare due to
challenges in sustained contact, digital access, and institutional trust. This study draws on
three focus groups conducted between September 2024 and January 2025 in King
County, Washington, to explore how to tailor contact modes in longitudinal surveys with
persons experiencing homelessness to improve retention and reduce attrition. Participants
highlighted major barriers to digital contact, including inconsistent access to phones and
service, charging stations, and two-factor authentication. Email was preferred for its
stability. Participants emphasized the need for transparent, scheduled communication and
flexible incentives, such as Cash app. We conclude with a summary of practical
suggestions to improve survey design and discuss how our findings from one particular
setting can be extended more broadly around the country and world.

articles.title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
articles.authors: Mihai Alexandru Bîclea
articles.abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

articles.title: The Substitution Trap: Development Aid and the Composition of Government Spending in Indian States
articles.authors: Krishna Vadlamannati; Roberto Iacono
articles.abstract: The question of whether aid supplements or substitutes government spending has long been debated in public finance literature. Building on Vadlamannati and Iacono (2026), who examine how development aid affects discretionary fiscal transfers to Indian states, we address a distinct fiscal question: how does aid exposure affect the composition of subnational government expenditure? Using panel data for 30 Indian states over 1979-2019 (41 years) and an instrumental variable strategy addressing potential endogeneity, we find that greater exposure to aid is associated with a lower share of capital expenditure and a higher share of revenue expenditure. This pattern is consistent with substitution of externally aided projects for domestically financed spending. The effect however varies systematically with electoral incentives. In states with greater electoral competition, aid is more strongly associated with capital expenditure, suggesting that electoral incentives can encourage state governments to channel external resources towards visible capital investments. Our findings extend the evidence on fiscal consequences of aid in India from the allocation of intergovernmental discretionary transfers to the composition of state government expenditure. Our findings reveal that the developmental effects of aid depend not only on how resources reach subnational governments but also on how governments subsequently allocate them.

articles.title: Migration–Citizenship Trajectories and Institutional Incorporation: Long-Term Mental Health Consequences
articles.authors: Nan Zhang
articles.abstract: Migration does not necessarily produce equivalent changes in institutional membership. This study examines how geographical mobility and institutional citizenship unfold jointly across adulthood and whether differentiated pathways of institutional incorporation are associated with long-term mental health. We analysed longitudinal data from 8,297 adults aged 60–80 in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020). Sequence analysis reconstructed joint trajectories of rural–urban residence and institutional citizenship (hukou) between ages 15 and 60, which were linked to depressive symptoms (CES-D-10) using multilevel growth-curve models. Substantial inequalities emerged across migration–citizenship trajectories and persisted throughout later life. Rural–urban migrant workers retaining rural hukou, historically associated with more restricted access to urban social rights and protection, had depressive-symptom levels comparable to lifelong rural residents, whereas trajectories involving urban hukou were associated with more favourable outcomes. Longer migration duration was associated with modestly lower depressive symptoms among women, while the estimated association was essentially flat among men. The findings demonstrate that geographical mobility does not necessarily entail institutional incorporation and that the long-term consequences of migration depend on how geographical and institutional mobility are configured across adulthood.

articles.title: Data visualization: Spanish results in PISA across  waves by parental educational attainment
articles.authors: Manuel T. Valdés; Fabrizio Bernardi
articles.abstract: Using Spanish PISA microdata from 2003–2025, we analyze performance trends in mathematics and reading by parental educational attainment. Results show a steady decline in scores among students from highly educated families, starting as early as 2012 in mathematics and 2015 in reading.

articles.title: The Influencer I’ll Vote For: Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok
articles.authors: Marcos Echevarria-Eirea
articles.abstract: TikTok, and social media generally, continue to rise as important spheres of political communication and information. Mapping how political elites use these platforms thus remains consequential to our understanding of the political arena. However, due to its relative infancy, we have yet to thoroughly study these patterns on TikTok across countries. In response to this shortcoming, this paper introduces Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok (MPPTikTok), a dataset of TikTok accounts for national MPs and parties across 17 Western democracies, comprising over 2,190 usernames. Using these to collect ≈260,000 posts, I then describe the supply of content (presence and posting activity) and the engagement it receives across party families. Both radical party families are proportionally more present, post more, and receive more engagement than the Mainstream. The Radical Left leads most clearly in proportional presence and posting activity, while achieving engagement levels comparable to the Radical Right, with differences between them depending on the metric.

articles.title: Calibrating Synthetic Respondents: A Within-Persona Experiment on Public Reactions to Protest in Turkey
articles.authors: MEHMET FUAT KINA; Helin Yaren Ekmen
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents, yet the inference pipeline that turns a persona into a response is rarely calibrated for the population and outcome it is applied to. This study makes population- and outcome-specific calibration the research task itself. Using a nationally representative survey in Turkey as the benchmark, we construct persona-conditioned synthetic respondents for all 2,615 survey participants and search a structured space of persona content, sampling strategies, temperatures, model backbones, and prompt framings. Calibration is assessed against two held-out outcomes that carry the response structures on which social movement research typically rests, a rare binary measure of protest participation and a five-point attitude item, and the selected protocols differ between the two. We then run a within-persona synthetic experiment that places the same protest for Kurdish-language education in a political opportunity and a political threat context. The threat context lowers simulated movement legitimacy and willingness to attend, and the simulated contrasts differentiate by political orientation, ethnicity, and education in the directions theory anticipates. Calibration is a precondition for reading synthetic experiments, not a robustness check appended to them.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: The Politics of Threat Construction: Securitisation as a Site of Contestation in Georgia’s Public Sphere
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili; Zinaida Bechná; Kornely Kakachia
articles.abstract: Moving beyond studies on contemporary security challenges posed by information manipulation, economic coercion, and military pressure, this article problematises the securitisation of foreign interference narratives by political leaders through the case of Georgia (2023–2025). The analysis draws on 325 social media posts by high-level officials and ten in-depth interviews with civic actors resisting state narratives. It relies on securitisation theory to (1) examine how political elites frame domestic actors as instruments of the Western interference despite the country’s constitutionally anchored pro-European orientation and overwhelming public support for EU integration, and (2) explore how counter-securitisation unfolds among civic actors. The findings reveal a structured securitising narrative grounded in sovereigntist logic, invoking historical memory, identity threats, and conspiracy framings to delegitimise civic actors as rootless and foreign aligned. However, rather than generating stable audience acceptance this securitising move triggers counter-securitisation as civic actors contest the proposed threat hierarchy, reframe Russia and democratic backsliding as primary dangers, and additionally mobilise performative resistance through street protest. The analysis highlights the agency of civic actors who simultaneously occupy the positions of securitised subjects and a segment of the audience and complements post-structuralist understandings of the securitisation as a co-constitutive and iterative rather than a linear process.

articles.title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
articles.authors: Mitchell Sanders
articles.abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

articles.title: Distributed Citizenship in Local-Oriented Online Communities: A Behavioral Repertoire of Civic Roles Across 50 North American City Groups
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: Local-oriented online communities increasingly serve as informal spaces where residents exchange local knowledge, discuss public issues, and encounter local news. Yet existing research often treats these communities as digital third spaces, with less attention to how civic labor is distributed among participants. This study understands these communities as components of local information infrastructures, examining how civic roles are distributed by analyzing year-long data from 50 highly active North American city subreddits in 2024. Focusing on 43,263 sustained users, we combine media-domain matching, LLM-assisted topic classification, latent profile analysis, and qualitative case comparison. The analysis identifies six behavioral civic roles: National News Commentators, Platform-Native Political Discussants, Local Civic Respondents, Cross-Scale Media Brokers, Local News Brokers, and Peripheral Generalists. The findings show that local-oriented online communities function as local information infrastructures which depend on uneven but complementary forms of resident participation.

articles.title: Multiracial young adults’ experiences of Whiteness as a wage and tax
articles.authors: Monica Heilman
articles.abstract: Debates persist on the racial position of multiracial Americans, namely whether this population will “become White” or not. However, the premise of this question is predicated on a monoracial paradigm of race that cannot fully account for the experiences of multiracial individuals. Multiracial experiences with Whiteness, including ways they conform to and confound monoracial expectations, have the potential to reshape our understandings of racial constructions, boundaries, and futures, particularly considering shifting racial demographics. One necessary precursor toward these insights lies in the distinctions between how multiracial and monoracial individuals experience Whiteness. Drawing on thirty-seven in-depth interviews with multiracial young adults with White ancestry in the Midwest, I argue that multiracial individuals experience Whiteness as a wage (privileges) and a tax (costs). Like monoracial Whites, multiracial individuals viewed as White can receive public and psychological wages, yet these wages are offset by an inseparable “racial tax,” which is predicated on the contingent and exclusive nature of Whiteness. These results underscore the utility of calling attention to the monoracial structure, as well as recognizing and theorizing beyond its limits.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond compensation: Climate politics, mobilization, and transformative statecraft
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Braun; Leah Downey
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments have pursued decarbonization through a combination of subsidies for capital and compensation for people. Political scientists have identified the compensation of those who incur losses from climate policies as the the central challenge in building green coalitions and achieving a just transition. However, a decarbonization path aimed at limiting global warming to 2 degrees Celsius entails transformative change for virtually everyone. We argue that, under such conditions, a compensation-based approach reduces green backlash to pocketbook concerns; citizens to bundles of fixed preferences; and evaluation to policy-by-policy assessment. Proposing to move beyond compensating existing preferences, we contend that transformative statecraft reshapes preferences through political mobilization. From this perspective, a technocratic approach—focused on calculation and compensation—constitutes a binding constraint on green statecraft. We defend this mobilization-based approach against the objections of manipulation and deprivation of freedom and suggest that a democratic version of transformative statecraft is possible.

articles_hidden.title: Language Replacement and Individualism: Linguicide as a Measurable Cultural Variable
articles_hidden.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-cultural research has linked grammatical features, especially the obligatory use of subject pronouns, to national individualism, but such links are hard to separate from language family, wealth and history. This study treats colonial language replacement as a measurable variable and asks whether colonized countries whose majority home language became a European colonizer's language are more individualist than colonized countries that kept their own. Using a 55-country dataset and a validated individualism index (Akaliyski et al., 2025), I compare 10 replaced-language and 9 retained-language countries, controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure. Replacement was associated with 12.1 points higher individualism (95% CI [8.0, 16.2]). The association was larger where English, which requires overt subject pronouns, did the replacing (17.5 points) than where Spanish or Portuguese, which allow pronoun drop, did so (11.4 points), though the difference between the two was not statistically significant (p = .10). The replacement association persisted when census-based settler population share was controlled, and settler share showed no independent association. This test rests largely on a single case: Ireland, where the population remained and the language shifted, scored with the English-speaking settler states. Within Ireland (N = 3,057), residents of areas where more Irish was spoken in 1911 placed less weight on self-direction values today, while present-day daily use of Irish showed no association. Within Latin America, Indigenous language retention was inversely associated with individualism, but this could not be separated from national wealth. Replacement was not associated with autism prevalence once diagnostic capacity was controlled. I argue that language replacement offers a direct, measurable proxy for linguicide and a route for testing claims about language and selfhood.

articles_hidden.title: From volume to care: an ethic of aver cura for tourism and host-community well-being
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Josef Wiedermann; Patrick Rina; Harald Pechlaner; Fulvio Longato
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose. This paper proposes an ethic of care — aver cura — as an integrative concept for destination development that connects two disconnected uses of "care" in tourism scholarship and specifies how the concept can be observed and measured.
Design/methodology/approach. The paper is conceptual. It synthesizes tourism studies, public health and the ethics of care, and illustrates the argument through the single case of Meran, South Tyrol, a historic alpine health resort.
Findings. Tourism research invokes care as an ethos, while public health and health tourism treat care as provision; the two seldom meet. An ethic of aver cura, built on caring for self, others and place, integrates them and reframes success from volume to sustaining visitor, resident, worker and landscape together. Civic trust, distinct from commercial destination trust, is the operational core through which care becomes measurable.
Research limitations/implications. The six propositions are conceptual and untested; they set a future agenda for comparative and longitudinal research.
Practical implications. Destinations would shift from volume metrics to civic-trust and community indicators and to recurring deliberative governance.
Social implications. The approach foregrounds the well-being of residents and tourism workers alongside that of visitors.
Originality/value. The paper offers an integrative concept of care that bridges ethical and public-health registers, distinguishes civic from commercial trust as its measurable core, and grounds care in a destination's own formative logic rather than importing it from outside.

Preprint of a manuscript currently under review at the Journal of Tourism Futures (Emerald). This is the submitted version and has not been peer-reviewed.

articles_hidden.title: "How do I survive the next 12 hours?": Disability and lived experiences of extreme heat in the UK
articles_hidden.authors: Hollye Kirkcaldy; Annayah Miranda Beatrice Prosser; Keren MacLennan; Christina Demski
articles_hidden.abstract: As extreme heat becomes a more frequent consequence of climate change, understanding how marginalised populations experience it is critical for adaptation. Disabled people are routinely categorised as ‘at-risk’, yet research largely quantifies heat risk at population level, leaving lived dimensions of heat experience for Disabled people under-explored, particularly in the UK. Drawing on theories of ableism and psycho-emotional disablism, this qualitative study asks how Disabled people in the UK experience extreme heat and what shapes their capacity to adapt. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 27 self-identified Disabled adults across the UK between July and September 2025 and analysed data using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Across three main themes, participants depict heat as an actively disabling environmental condition which erodes capacity, diminishes identity, exposes ableist assumptions in adaptation and is mediated by material and structural conditions across housing, care and urban infrastructure. Current adaptation frameworks contain significant blind spots, including the temporal and psycho-emotional dimensions of heat harm, and are, in some respects, actively harmful for Disabled people. Addressing this requires a fundamental interrogation of whose knowledge informs the design of heat adaptation policy in the UK.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Load and Moral Strain: Situational Demands and the Experience of Carrying Them
articles_hidden.authors: Chase Crossno
articles_hidden.abstract: People often recognize that something morally significant is happening before they can name what they are experiencing. Existing vocabulary, including moral distress, moral injury, moral residue, and moral resilience, describes important forms and consequences of moral difficulty. This paper develops an analytic distinction among moral demands, moral load, and moral strain. Moral demands are the morally significant claims, obligations, risks, or consequences present in a situation. Moral load names how those demands bear on a particular person through roles, relationships, commitments, foreseeable consequences, and available agency; moral strain names the internal experience of carrying that load. Load is therefore neither a property of the situation alone nor a subjective reaction to it. Prior uses of moral load have addressed moral sensitivity, clinical decision-making, and moral deliberation. The contribution here is a relational architecture that separates situation-level demands, person-specific load, and internal strain. Demands, tasks, authority, resources, and support may be redistributed, thereby changing the load borne by particular people; support may also alter strain even when underlying load remains. Consequences including moral residue and moral injury can generate new obligations and shape later load and strain, making the relationship recursive rather than linear. Implications for education, team practice, and research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Efficiency, Elasticity, and Disruption: A Mechanistic Framework for Socio-Technical System Transitions
articles_hidden.authors: Vitor Miranda de Souza; Diogo Figueirinhas; Brian D. Fath; Fredrik Nilsson
articles_hidden.abstract: Efficiency improvements are persistently accompanied by demand expansion and increased resource throughput, systematically undermining sustainability strategies in operations and supply chain management. While existing explanations rely on behavioural assumptions or empirical correction factors rather than structural accounts, this paper develops a first-order mechanistic formulation of efficiency-induced demand expansion, introducing system elasticity εsys as a structural property of socio-technical configuration. Building on and generalising Ayres and Warr’s framework, we derive the service relationship S ∝ η^(ε_sys−1) and its resource corollary R ∝ η^(ε_sys−2), establishing two sustainability thresholds: ε_sys > 1 for service expansion and ε_sys > 2 for absolute resource growth. Two independent empirical cases – the 19th-century steam engine and contemporary computing – yield ε_sys ≈ 3.5, consistent with the backfire condition. The formulation reframes the operational challenge from governing resource efficiency to governing service elasticity.

articles_hidden.title: Post-growth policies and business transformation: A mixed-methods expert assessment of perceived relevance
articles_hidden.authors: Josefine Henman; Manuel Suter
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines how different policies are perceived by researchers regarding their relevance in supporting the transformation of traditional businesses toward reducing ecological footprints, securing well-being, and increasing social equity. While post-growth scholarship has discussed a wide range of policy proposals, their implications for business transformations remain underexplored. To address this gap, the study combines a quantitative survey of 1,734 sustainability policy researchers with qualitative focus group discussions with post-growth business scholars. The survey results indicate that the majority of policy instruments are perceived as at least moderately relevant for supporting a business transformation towards post-growth. Descriptive analyses show that respondents with a degrowth work-orientation tend to perceive the instruments as more relevant than growth-indifferent or green growth-oriented respondents, with differences particularly pronounced for more structurally disruptive interventions. The qualitative analysis explores how post-growth business scholars perceive key tensions, barriers, and enabling conditions associated with three previously highly ranked policies: transitioning ownership structures, banning planned obsolescence, and introducing declining resource caps. Two central topics emerge from these discussions: the role of businesses’ profit orientation as a structural factor that may shape responses to policy interventions, and the importance of combining policies in order to address anticipated tensions and wider societal implications. The article bridges post-growth policy and business research by suggesting how different policy instruments and mixes may support business transformations in line with post-growth objectives.

articles_hidden.title: When Red Is - and Is Not - Blood: A Corpus-Assisted Cognitive-Semantic Analysis of Five Settler Australian Texts (1874-1907)
articles_hidden.authors: Nguyen Huynh Si Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates when the colour term RED is conceptually connected with BLOOD and when the two domains remain independent in settler Australian literary discourse. The data comprise five complete public-domain texts published between 1874 and 1907 by Marcus Clarke, Henry Lawson, Miles Franklin, Joseph Furphy, and Jeannie Gunn. The study adopts a corpus-assisted qualitative design combining full-text lexical retrieval, paragraph-level concordance reading, cognitive-semantic annotation, and counterexample analysis. A verified analytical set of 30 concordance contexts was assembled across the five texts to test explicit BLOOD-RED bridges against competing RED and BLOOD pathways; the set is deliberately criterion-based and is not treated as a frequency sample. Three direct bridge types are attested: blood-red compounding, blood as a colour comparator, and bodily circulation as a causal basis for visible redness. The same texts also provide systematic counterevidence to any general RED IS BLOOD equation. RED occurs independently in landscape, fire, flora, atmospheric description, and conventional idioms, while BLOOD extends independently to violence, personhood, descent, temperament, inheritance, vitality, and exploitation. The findings support an asymmetrical partial-overlap model: BLOOD can motivate RED, but RED does not entail BLOOD, and many figurative BLOOD constructions have no chromatic component. The analysis further shows that red soil, red gum, and comparable Australian landscape expressions cannot be classified as blood imagery without local lexical or causal co-activation. Methodologically, the study demonstrates the value of separating lexical semantics, metonymic motivation, metaphorical extension, and literary symbolism before cross-linguistic comparison.

articles_hidden.title: Geopolitical Influence & Peace: Tracking the trends shaping international relations
articles_hidden.authors: Sascha Nanlohy; Paulina Pijacka
articles_hidden.abstract:
This report asks whether the world has entered a "new Cold War" and what intensifying great power competition means for peace, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Using datasets including SIPRI, ICEWS, UCDP/PRIO, the Correlates of War and the Foreign Bilateral Influence Capability (FBIC) dataset, it compares today's international system with the Cold War and post-Cold War periods.

Geopolitical risk now exceeds Cold War levels and is nearing the peaks seen after 9/11. Global military expenditure reached a record US$2.43 trillion in 2023, the largest annual rise since 2009. Nuclear disarmament has stalled, and the UN Security Council has become less effective, with fewer resolutions passed and more vetoes since the 2010s. Bilateral sentiment between the US, Russia and China has deteriorated since 1995.

The current system nonetheless differs from the Cold War. It is multipolar and economically interdependent, although trade has plateaued at around 60 per cent of global GDP. It is also shaped by technological competition and global challenges such as climate change. The number of countries holding more than 10 per cent influence in five or more other states has almost tripled, from 13 at the end of the Cold War to 34 in 2024. This reflects the rise of middle powers such as Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, South Africa, Vietnam and Indonesia, alongside China and India.

For LMICs, competition for influence is intensifying, notably in the Sahel, West Africa, South Asia and South America. The US holds more than 10 per cent influence in 74 LMICs and China in 65. China is dominant in sub-Saharan Africa and the US in Latin America. Internationalised intrastate conflicts have increased nearly threefold since 2010. The Sudan and Syria case studies show how external backing for warring parties can prolong conflict and raise the risk of mass atrocities. Proxy wars also drove many of the Cold War's deadliest conflicts.

Economic pressures compound these risks. In 2024, 3.3 billion people lived in countries where debt interest payments exceeded spending on health and education. Aid is also shifting from multilateral to bilateral channels, which further constrains development and Positive Peace.

The report concludes that competition for influence can undermine local governance and divert attention from climate change, food insecurity and peacebuilding. A nuanced understanding of these dynamics is needed to support long-term stability and development in the developing world.

articles_hidden.title: No King, and Other Matters—America’s Perspectives in Mid-2026 on Democracy, Authoritarianism, and Election-Related Violence:  Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Garen J. Wintemute; Bradley Velasquez; Sonia Robinson; Krista Neumann; Shaina Sta Cruz; Aaron Shev; Daniel Joseph Tancredi; Elizabeth A. Tomsich; Mona A. Wright; Veronica Pear
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Political violence and the rise of authoritarianism are emerging threats to the nation’s health, stability, and future as a representative democracy. To inform and facilitate prevention efforts, we present new and updated findings on the public’s views on authoritarianism and its support for and willingness to engage in election-related and pro- or anti-government violence. 

Methods: Findings are from Wave 5, conducted May 15-June 15, 2026, of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of adult members of the Ipsos KnowledgePanel that was initiated in 2022. Findings are for the cohort as a whole and for subgroups defined by political party/Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliation. Year-to-year change for items included in 2025 and 2026 is estimated using mean change scores. Cross-sectional findings for 2026 are presented as weighted prevalences and item scores.

Results: The completion rate was 90.7%; there were 7,552 respondents. Nearly 90% of respondents continued to consider it very or extremely important that the US remain a democracy (change 0.01, 95% CI -0.00, 0.03). Agreement with expressions of authoritarianism was much less common; it decreased for the statement, “having a strong leader for America is more important than having a democracy” (change -0.04, 95% CI -0.07, -0.02) and others. In 2026, 2.1% (95% CI 1.6%, 2.7%) of respondents agreed strongly or very strongly that President Trump should be made king, but nearly half (47.7%, 95% CI 46.2%, 49.2%) agreed strongly or very strongly that he should be impeached and removed from office. 

There was little agreement with 5 actions the federal government might take in 2026 that employed violence to enforce its policies or suppress its critics in the US; the prevalence of strong or very strong agreement ranged between 4.4% and 9.6%. Across 12 items, there was very little agreement with actions—including violence—the federal government might take to subvert elections; strong or very strong agreement ranged between 2% and 4%. Willingness to commit violence was rare. For example, only 1.6% (95% CI 1.2%, 2.1%) were very or completely willing to use violence “to make sure that President Trump remains in office after his term ends.” Decreases from 2025 to 2026 in support for expressions of authoritarianism and for government-initiated violence were common across the spectrum of party/MAGA movement affiliations.

Conclusions: With national elections a few months away, Americans remained strongly supportive of democracy, did not endorse authoritarianism, and rejected the use of force by the current federal government to enforce its policies or subvert elections. They were deeply unwilling to engage in violence. These hopeful findings can inform and guide efforts to preserve democracy and prevent political violence.

articles_hidden.title: The Darkside of Collegiality: From Audit Culture to Participatory Taylorism
articles_hidden.authors: Abe Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: Cultures of shared governance in academia may appear as a noble tradition to be upheld and defended against the steady encroachment of audit culture. However, building upon recent interest in the ‘dark side’ of collegiality, this theoretically-motivated article proposes that the collegial ideal of collective and participatory decision-making now co-exist alongside performance metrics in an uneasy alliance that softens their surface-level opposition. Invoking the paradoxical concept of ‘participatory Taylorism,’ this study demonstrates that faculty engagement is essential to audit culture’s apparent staying power. Performance metrics survive by opening themselves to the demos, inviting robust debates about their composition and legitimacy – provided these dialogues stop short of contesting audit culture itself. In this sense, permissible modes of shared governance perform a type of ‘collegiality-washing,’ substituting a simulacra of participation for the real thing.  Moreover, because ‘participation’ is precisely the lever through which performance measures exert their influence, conventional oppositional strategies risk co-optation. In a university setting that demands constant engagement and actively recuperates dissent, resistance may take the form of withdrawal, silence, or even a more recent trend, ‘quiet quitting.’

articles_hidden.title: Effective Anti-Corruption Strategies for Public Organizations: Insights from Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
articles_hidden.authors: Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller
articles_hidden.abstract: Fighting corruption remains one of the most pressing management challenges in public organizations worldwide. While different organizational approaches to anti‑corruption exist, evidence of their effectiveness and the conditions under which they reduce different forms of administrative corruption remains limited. Drawing on a meta analysis and meta regression of 174 effect sizes from 34 empirical studies, this study shows that both integrity based and compliance based anti corruption strategies have a significant, positive, small to moderate effect on public organizations’ ethical performance, although their effectiveness varies across contexts. Compliance based strategies, particularly formalization and accountability mechanisms, are more effective in addressing multiple forms of administrative corruption, whereas integrity‑based strategies, such as ethical leadership, primarily reduce collusion, demonstrating that ‘one-size-fits-all’ approaches are ineffective. The findings highlight the conditional effectiveness of organizational anti‑corruption strategies and the importance of context‑sensitive ethics management. These findings carry important implications for public administration theory, research, and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Captured by the Ballot: Non-Partisan Judicial Elections and Democratic Erosion in Mexico
articles_hidden.authors: Brett Ryan Bessen
articles_hidden.abstract: Public tolerance for democratic erosion is often attributed to voter partisanship. Voters are thought to overlook undemocratic maneuvers to support the partisan in-group. Yet, backsliders  often disavow traditional parties and frame their reforms as non-partisan. I examine the role of voter partisanship in non-partisan elections, showing how elite manipulation of the information environment can generate partisan outcomes that facilitate backsliding—even when citizens prefer non-partisan outcomes on average. I examine Mexico’s 2025 judicial elections, pairing a conjoint experiment with an analysis of the electoral results. While the conjoint indicates that voters preferred independent judges, the electoral results indicate that government-aligned candidates on illicitly circulated voter guides (acordeones) received the most support, contributing to the partisan capture of the Supreme Court. Elite manipulation of the information environment and electoral incentives—rather than partisan preferences among the eligible electorate—were primary contributors to the court’s partisan capture.

articles_hidden.title: Adverse Outcomes Among Youths Admitted to Compulsory Institutional Care: A Swedish Matched Cohort Study
articles_hidden.authors: Amber L. Beckley; Fredrik Sivertsson; Sofi Oskarsson; Catherine Tuvblad; Peter Larm
articles_hidden.abstract: Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care represent a particularly vulnerable population with substantial behavioral, social, and health-related needs. However, evidence on their long-term outcomes relative to other high-risk youths, and on when adverse outcomes emerge following discharge, remains limited. We examined the characteristics of youths admitted to compulsory institutional care in Sweden, compared their overall and adulthood outcomes with matched youths from the general population and compulsory social care, and examined the timing of adverse outcomes following discharge. The Swedish Longitudinal Compulsory Care Study (SLCCS) includes all youths admitted to compulsory institutional care (CIC) in Sweden between 2000 and 2020 (n = 14,677), matched to youths from the general population (14,349 pairs) and compulsory social care (8,879 pairs). Analyses were stratified by sex and included descriptive statistics, fixed-effects regression, Cox proportional hazards models, and Kaplan–Meier analyses. Criminal behavior and substance use were the most common reasons for placement. The CIC group experienced poorer outcomes than both comparison groups overall and in adulthood. Compared with matched women from the general population, adjusted hazards of substance use disorder (HR = 7.83, 95% CI 6.07–10.10) and all-cause mortality (HR = 8.42, 95% CI 3.01–23.54) were nearly eightfold higher among women admitted to compulsory institutional care. Corresponding hazards among men were fivefold higher for substance use disorder (HR = 5.11, 95% CI 4.26–6.12) and threefold higher for all-cause mortality (HR = 3.11, 95% CI 2.02–4.77). Kaplan–Meier analyses indicated that mental health and substance use diagnoses were concentrated within the first five years following discharge. Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care face an elevated risk of adverse outcomes extending into adulthood, and the first five years following discharge may represent an important period for aftercare and support.

articles_hidden.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles_hidden.title: От «светоча нации» до «педагога-тирана»: как русскоязычные Telegram-медиа конструируют образ учителя, 2020–2025
articles_hidden.authors: Munira Vassilova
articles_hidden.abstract: Исследование анализирует, как профессия учителя конструируется в русскоязычном новостном Telegram-корпусе за 2020–2025 гг. Исходный архив был получен из открытого набора ResearchData.kz (dataset 233) и включал 653 170 публикаций; после ограничения периода осталось 551 880 сообщений. Лексический поиск по основам «учител*», «педагог*» и «преподавател*» дал 5 721 кандидата, после скрининга сформирован рабочий корпус из 5 256 размещений в 19 каналах. Семантическое кодирование выявило 4 440 содержательно валидных упоминаний и 816 нерелевантных совпадений. Кодбук, сформированный абдуктивно из литературы и повторяющихся паттернов корпуса, различает F0 — присутствие учителя без самостоятельного профессионального фрейма — и семь содержательных фреймов. F0 составляет 32,2% валидных публикаций. Среди содержательных фреймов наиболее распространены поддержка/инвестиции и уязвимость — по 15,1%; экспертность/агентность составляет лишь 6,2%. Это показывает, что медиа чаще говорят об учителе как об объекте поддержки, ограничений, регулирования или оценки, чем как о самостоятельном производителе профессионального знания. Временные различия невелики: доля экспертности/агентности возрастает с 3,8% в 2020 г. до 7,3% в 2025 г., а уязвимости — с 11,6% до 17,6%. Среди казахстанских источников медиа регионального охвата значительно чаще используют фрейм экспертности, а государственные — признание и поддержку; негосударственные чаще проблематизируют профессию и показывают уязвимость. Работа показывает, почему для анализа статуса профессии важно различать простую видимость, профессиональную репрезентацию и распределение символической агентности.

articles_hidden.title: Resistance to Backsliding: The Role of Democratic Conceptions
articles_hidden.authors: Noam Gidron; Yotam Margalit; Lior Sheffer; Itamar Yakir
articles_hidden.abstract: We examine who mobilizes against democratic backsliding, focusing on mass protests against the judicial overhaul advanced by the Israeli government in 2023. As contemporary subversion of democracy is often driven by governments that won an electoral majority, we posit that protesting against the government's actions requires people to have a thick conception of democracy that goes beyond majority rule. Drawing on panel data collected before and after the overhaul's announcement, we show that citizens vary substantially in their conception of democracy, and that a thick conception not only predicts protesting against backsliding but also moderates the role of other key factors in mobilizing against democratic erosion. The findings highlight the role of small-d democrats in safeguarding democracy.

articles_hidden.title: What the Balkan Barometer Can and Cannot Rank: A Measurement Audit of the Western Balkans' Flagship Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles_hidden.abstract: The Balkan Barometer, annual since 2015 with roughly 1,000 face-to-face interviews in each of six Western Balkan economies, is cited across the region as what its citizens think. We evaluate it as a measuring instrument from the Regional Cooperation Council's own released microdata for 2023 to 2025, within a total survey error frame. The published percentages reproduce from the microdata (440 of 444 cells within one point). Of the fifteen pairwise economy differences on each of thirty 2025 headline items, 71 percent are resolvable at a design effect of 2.0, but only 40 percent of adjacent-rank pairs are: six points is the least difference at which two economies of 1,000 can be told apart. The WB6 figure is an unweighted mean of six economies whose populations differ tenfold; under population weights it moves by 6 to 12 points on the most-quoted items, including EU membership (64 versus 58 percent in 2025). Of twenty-three headline series present in all three editions, four are comparable throughout; between 2024 and 2025 the changed series moved by 14 points on average against 6 for the stable ones. The 2025 institutional battery is scalar invariant once two cells are freed, police in Kosovo* and courts in North Macedonia; with them freed, Kosovo*'s raw-score lead disappears and the top three economies cannot be separated. The two published editions score 16 of 32 on a documentation checklist built from what the ESS, the Eurobarometer and the AAPOR Transparency Initiative publish routinely; precision, comparability and limitations score zero. We report two database errors and a file anomaly for correction, and close with the four things a technical report would need to contain.

articles_hidden.title: Social Networks and Unequal Income Returns to Education: Gender Differences and Cross-National Context
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; Emmi Mäkeläinen; Aki Koivula
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines how social networks are associated with unequal income returns to education and whether these associations vary by gender and across national contexts. Using data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 from representative samples in 15 countries, the study analyses the interrelations between educational attainment, social ties, and personal income. The analyses distinguish both the status of social contacts and the type of ties to the upper middle class, while also examining variation by gender and country-level income inequality. The results show that access to upper-middle-class contacts is associated with wider educational differences in income, and that close ties, especially family members, relatives, and close friends, are more strongly associated with income than weaker ties. These patterns also vary by gender, with educated men’s income more strongly associated with upper-middle-class ties than educated women’s. In addition, educational differences in the association between social networks and income are more pronounced in countries with higher levels of income inequality. The study contributes to research on social stratification by showing that income returns to education are socially embedded and also vary by gender and national context.

articles_hidden.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles_hidden.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles_hidden.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The Electoral Costs of Exclusion: Women’s Candidate Placement and Party Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Iris E. Acquarone; Alba Huidobro
articles_hidden.abstract: Political elites continue to behave as if including women in electable positions is electorally risky, despite growing evidence of voter support for gender-inclusive representation. This paper advances a theory of the electoral costs of exclusion, arguing that continued exclusion can become electorally costly when parties fail to adapt to changing electoral responses to women's representation. Using data from Spanish local elections (2003-2019) and a difference-in-differences design, we show that parties increasing women's representation in electable list positions gain votes and seats relative to parties that do not; this divergence coincides with gains among parties increasing women's representation and losses among those maintaining or reducing it. These consequences grow over time and are strongest where inclusion is voluntary rather than quota-mandated. Our findings challenge the idea that underrepresentation persists because inclusion fails electorally, pointing instead to a changing electoral constraint some elites may fail to recognize: exclusion has become costly.

articles_hidden.title: Still Secularizing: Cohort Replacement, Rebound, Overreporting, and Gender Convergence in a Pooled Analysis of Eight National Surveys
articles_hidden.authors: David Eagle; Joshua Gaghan
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent reports claim young men in the United States are becoming more religious. This would signal an end to the longstanding pattern of cohort-driven declines in religiosity. Pooling young-adult trends within eight national surveys measuring affiliation, attendance, salience, prayer, and biblical literalism, we find no measure shows a credible increase among young men, and the youngest cohort is no more religious than its predecessor was at the same age. The gender gap is narrowing because women are secularizing faster, not because men are returning, which likely reflects gender-based ideological realignment. Religiosity has rebounded from its pandemic trough, but not credibly past pre-pandemic levels, and the gap between self-reported attendance and time-use diaries has widened. Intense religious identity is also declining across cohorts. Variability between surveys, a post-pandemic rebound, and growing measurement drift are all confounding patterns of religious change. Cutting through the noise, cohort replacement continues to organize American religion.

articles_hidden.title: Daily Dynamics of Urban Racial Segregation in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Cody Arlie Reed
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines racial segregation changes across the day and week to assess three perspectives in urban sociology: social isolation, compelled mobility, and cosmopolitanism. I link mobile phone tracking data collected on 18 days in January 2020 to 2020 Census data on the racial composition of estimated home tracts. Using the Theil multigroup segregation index, I estimate hourly racial segregation in 18 large U.S. commuting zones. Racial segregation is highest overnight, declines during weekday work hours, and is generally higher on weekends than weekdays. These patterns are most consistent with the compelled mobility perspective, under which lower racial segregation is expected when residents travel beyond their neighborhoods to access employment and other resources. Relatively high weekend racial segregation offers only weak support for social isolation. Friday and Saturday nights and the following early mornings have lower racial segregation than Wednesday at the same hours, offering clearer partial support for cosmopolitanism. Although the data do not identify why people travel, they show that the clearest declines in racial segregation coincide with the workday. Measuring racial segregation across hours and days thus helps distinguish theoretical accounts of how racial segregation persists or diminishes beyond residential neighborhoods.

articles_hidden.title: The Promise: A Breakthrough for Social Science
articles_hidden.authors: Bruno Sérgio Dias Oliveira
articles_hidden.abstract:
[SSRN has the latest version of this preprint at https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4982428 ] 

Sociology has long wrestled with theoretical fragmentation, hindering a unified understanding of social life. This paper unveils the General Social Theory of Compromises (G-STOC), a bold framework that reimagines social phenomena through the lens of promises and their reciprocal arrangements, termed compromises. G-STOC posits that all social interactions — whether mundane exchanges or transformative societal shifts — hinge on promises, broadly defined to include not just explicit pledges but also tacit expectations, norms, and imposed duties. These promises knit together into compromises, forming the essential fabric of social relationships. The theory advances several key insights: (1) social behavior springs from actual and virtual agency, with virtual agency rooted in anticipated promises; (2) emotions like anger and disappointment reveal breaches of these promises, highlighting their omnipresence; (3) compromises unify individual actions with broader social influences; and (4) sociological insight arises from tracing these compromises across time. Emphasizing the future-oriented nature of social action, G-STOC sidesteps perennial debates like agency versus structure, offering a potent, streamlined tool to decode human interactions. This paper urges scholars to engage with G-STOC, testing its potential to revitalize social science and deepen our grasp of society’s complexities.

articles_hidden.title: Health system and hospital utilization in Chile, 1952–2020: trends, reforms, and inflection points
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective. To collect and analyze longitudinal data on hospital discharges in Chile between 1952 and 2020, both at the national level and within the public subsystem. Patterns of change were identified in relation to the following key institutional milestones: the Curative Medicine Act of 1968, the creation of the National Health Services System in 1979, and the implementation of the Universal and Guaranteed Access Reform in 2005. Methods. A first-of-its-kind time series was constructed using official sources from the Ministry of Health and institutional documents. Indicators were calculated for the total number of discharges, discharge rates per thousand population, and comparisons with the United States. The analysis included exploratory graphics and construction of segmented regression models. Results. Hospital discharges rose steadily, with two periods mirroring robust expansion of the private sector: between 1982 and 1987 and between 2006 and 2019. Public provision of hospital services slowed or decreased with the 1979 reform and with the 2005 reform, although not with the 1968 reform. Conclusion. This study provides empirical evidence on the long-term trajectory of Chilean hospital services and confirms a structural contrast between the country's major health system models and the differences in their reforms. It also underscores the need for long-term information to analyze the impact of health reforms.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Inference in the CLS Cohort Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Liam Wright; Georgia D Tomova; Martin Nejedly; George Ploubidis; Richard J. Silverwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Correlations between variables in cohort and other observational studies do not necessarily indicate causal effects and may instead reflect bias due to confounding, sample selection processes, or measurement issues.
