Thankfully, multiple statistical methods, frameworks, and research designs have been developed that – when used judiciously – can aid making causal inferences with observational data. This is especially the case with CLS’s cohorts, which have several properties (e.g., longitudinal assessment and rich and varied data collection) that that can make the assumptions of these methods more plausible or provide ample opportunities for each method’s use. In this guide, we provide an overview of the possibilities for causal inference in CLS’s cohorts. Specifically, we: (1) provide background on the problem of causal inference in observational data, (2) detail the attributes of CLS’s cohorts that can support causal inference, and (3) outline an extensive set of methods and research designs that – assumptions permitting – can be used to estimate causal effects in CLS’s cohort data, illustrating each with existing applications and highlighting opportunities for further work.

articles_hidden.title: FRAGMENTED GOVERNANCE AND THE FAILURE TO EXECUTE URBAN PROJECTS: THE LARGO DA BATATA COMPETITION (2001-2022)
articles_hidden.authors: Leticia Takeda Lodi
articles_hidden.abstract: Architecture and urban design competitions are often defended as democratic selection mechanisms, yet many fail during implementation. This article argues the failure stems from fragmented governance: semi-autonomous sectoral authorities operating without a coordinating hierarchy. Through a 21-year documentary analysis of the National Competition for the Urban Reconversion of Largo da Batata (São Paulo), comparing the winning, basic and executed projects (2001-2022), we show each authority discharged its mandate competently, yet the absence of coordination fragmented the outcome. This mechanism, pockets of micro-regulation practices, moves the debate from describing competition failure to explaining it, with implications for governance research.

articles_hidden.title: What influences the time to reach a tenured university professorship? Insights from machine-learning
articles_hidden.authors: Jasmin M. Kizilirmak; Frauke Peter
articles_hidden.abstract: The race to professorship is influenced by many factors, ranging from individual achievements to systemic structures. Prior research has underscored the significance of aspects such as academic productivity, institutional affiliations, and personal choices in shaping academic careers, but comprehensive analyses in specific contexts remain limited. The last two decades have seen strategic shifts within the German academic system, most notably with the introduction of junior and tenure-track professorships intended to offer a more secure career path. Yet, uncertainties persist regarding the determinants of career trajectories to tenured university professorship. Addressing this gap, this paper uses unique and novel longitudinal data of German professors to elucidate the various pathways to professorship. Based on a sample of individuals who successfully secured full university professorship, we estimate comprehensive models using machine learning to determine relevant factors that predict the time needed to reach this position. Key correlates are obtaining a habilitation, having held positions with leadership responsibilities, and disciplinary fields.

articles_hidden.title: Social Exclusion, Institutional Support and the Perceived Criminal Involvement of Waste Pickers: Evidence from a Stakeholder Survey in Rawalpindi–Islamabad, Pakistan
articles_hidden.authors: rabail ghazanfar
articles_hidden.abstract: Informal waste pickers (rag-pickers) are among the most marginalised urban groups in Pakistan, yet they are often linked in public debate to petty crime, substance use and sex work. This study surveys 300 frontline stakeholders (78 police personnel, 175 NGO staff and 47 other residents) in Rawalpindi and Islamabad to examine which offences they attribute to waste pickers and how these perceptions relate to perceived social exclusion and perceived support from government and NGOs. Substance use (80%) and prostitution (79%) were the offences most often attributed; murder rarely (5%). Perceived social exclusion was strongly associated with perceived criminal involvement (r = .73, p < .001), while perceived institutional support showed a weak negative association (r = -.17, p = .004). In a regression model (R2 = .53), exclusion was the only significant predictor (beta = .75); the association of support with criminal involvement operated indirectly through lower exclusion (indirect effect = -.23, Sobel z = -5.27, p < .001). The findings suggest that support reduces perceived criminality only insofar as it reduces exclusion, and argue for inclusion-oriented policy: integrating waste pickers into municipal waste systems, making social protection reachable, and protective rather than extractive policing. Based on the author's MPhil thesis (National Defence University, Islamabad, 2020).

articles_hidden.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS
articles_hidden.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles_hidden.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles_hidden.title: Analysis of the Social System in Post-Capitalist Society
articles_hidden.authors: 周勇
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to enhance productivity is pivotal in determining the success of a social system. Beyond scientific and technological advancements, productivity primarily hinges on workers' production enthusiasm and labor quality, the scale of production within each unit, and the pattern of resource allocation. Under given productive forces, the scale of production per unit is determined by the rate of exploitation imposed by owners upon laborers. As productive forces advance, new production models emerge. To boost productivity, the rate of exploitation diminishes, elevating the political and social standing of the populace, thereby giving rise to new social formations. Undifferentiated human labor constitutes the origin of goods value, while interest and capital gains represent the outcome of value distribution. Goods prices in the market are primarily determined by supply, with the labor value of goods serving as the equilibrium point of supply—thus constituting the market's equilibrium price. The labor theory of value can explain the Equity Risk Premium Puzzle. The higher the automation level of enterprises, the lower the value of goods, and in the long run, the lower the profits of enterprises. After the highly developed productive forces in capitalist society, the vast majority of industries will become low-profit public infrastructure services, making it difficult for private entities to continue operating. Public ownership will replace private ownership. The future social structure will be a “communist society” characterized by public ownership and distribution according to need as the mainstay, supplemented by private ownership and distribution according to work under a free-market economy. In the historical development toward communist society, there exists no so-called transitional stage of socialist society. In this communist society the state will persist, giving rise to a united human government where selfless dedication becomes the socially advocated moral standard. Under current productive forces, public ownership impedes both productive and economic development. Marxism is mistaken about the reasons and timing for the inevitable collapse of the capitalist system. Contemporary society faces issues such as welfare systems, nationalization, unified currencies, and China's economic and political structures.

articles_hidden.title: The Vanishing Mutual Citation
articles_hidden.authors: Maayan Matsliah
articles_hidden.abstract: Mutual citation – a pair of publications that cite each other – provides a simple measure of reciprocation linkage within scientific literature. Such pairs arise because papers are not published in strict sequence: authors often cite each other's preprints and working papers, add citations during revision, and sometimes publish related papers together. Using OpenAlex citation data from 1975 to 2023, we ask two questions: how has the rate at which papers reciprocate citations changed over five decades, and are interdisciplinary papers reciprocated less often than non-interdisciplinary papers? Contrary to both expectations, reciprocation declined sharply rather than rising with improved discoverability of scholarly work, and interdisciplinary papers did not reciprocate less than non-interdisciplinary papers. Mean mutual citations per paper fell by ~88% and the pooled mutual-citation rate fell by ~95% between 1975 and 2023. Papers citing three or more fields (interdisciplinary) exceeded the reciprocation rates of papers citing one or two fields (non-interdisciplinary) across a central band of six reference-count deciles (10-46 references, accounting for approximately 58% of the corpus), reciprocating up to 17% more. The two groups converged at 47-64 references (a 0.6% gap, non-interdisciplinary papers slightly ahead), and non-interdisciplinary papers reciprocated up to 28% more at the shortest and longest reference lists (3-9 and 65-5,000 references).

articles_hidden.title: Assessing and identifying special protection needs among refugees in the EU: Overview and Synthesis of Evidence and Policy Recommendations
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Nutsch; Maren Hintermeier; Andreas W. Gold; Clara Perplies; Nils Robson; Veronika Wiemker; Till Bärnighausen; Sven Rohleder; Kayvan Bozorgmehr
articles_hidden.abstract: The EU’s Reception Conditions Directive requests member states to identify special protection needs among asylum seekers and refugees, but assessment practices remain inconsistently implemented across Europe. We systemically searched scientific and grey literature and synthesised evidence of 81 eligible documents to identify recommendations for assessing special protection needs and their implications for policy and practice. The evidence indicates that vulnerability, which may necessitate special protection, is multidimensional, intersectional, and dynamic. This requires early, continuous, and multimethod assessment rather than one-off screening. Effective assessment systems combine standardised procedures with individualised assessment, referral pathways, and multidisciplinary collaboration. We identified 51 screening tools, however, no single tool was universally accepted and used, highlighting that implementation depends less on individual tools than on coordinated, person-centred systems supported by rights-based documentation, informed consent, and secure information sharing. These findings provide evidence-informed directions for strengthening assessment of special protection needs systems across the EU.

articles_hidden.title: An Assessment of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report on Sociology
articles_hidden.authors: Julian Go
articles_hidden.abstract: The Sociology portion of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report (VWUR) claims to have studied the discipline of sociology and asserts that sociology’s search for truth has been compromised by what the author calls “politicization.” I find that the VWUR’s claims are unsubstantiated and based upon fundamental errors. The problem is not lack of data but rather that the author, Dr. Ashley Rubin, misunderstands and misrepresents the data she does have while failing to check her own biases. She mistakenly reads politicization into everything she sees, reaffirming a thesis she had already held before her supposedly impartial study without taking the appropriate steps to suspend her bias. The VWUR violates the very social scientific standards that it purports to defend while distracting us from other problems facing social science.

articles_hidden.title: Reassessing the Role of Offline Teachers in the Era of Online Learning: In the context of India’s National Education Policy 2020
articles_hidden.authors: Rakesh Kumar Pandey; Soniya
articles_hidden.abstract: India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisages a substantial expansion of higher education and identifies online education as an important instrument for increasing access. The assumption that online learning can simultaneously expand educational access and reduce instructional costs, however, requires closer examination, particularly when online courses are incorporated into regular undergraduate and postgraduate programmes. This paper examines whether such integration can sustain the completion rates and learning outcomes normally expected from regular classroom-based education. Drawing on reported completion-to-registration data from selected online education providers, a critical review of the literature on learner engagement and learning outcomes, and a conceptual analysis of different pedagogical approaches, the study examines the relationship between learner maturity, self-directed learning, teacher interaction, and instructional requirements. The analysis suggests that large-scale access to online content does not necessarily translate into comparable levels of course completion. It further argues that pedagogical approaches designed to enhance engagement—including blended learning, active learning, problem-based learning, and personalised instruction—require sustained interaction with teachers, mentors, or facilitators. The paper therefore questions the assumption that online education will necessarily reduce instructional requirements. It proposes a hybrid pedagogical model in which online learning complements rather than replaces classroom teaching for young learners, supported by structured facilitation and mentorship to sustain completion rates and learning outcomes. Despite their low completion rates, fully online courses may be particularly appropriate for mature, self-directed lifelong learners seeking flexible opportunities for continuous skill and knowledge development.

articles_hidden.title: A POLÍTICA DE EXPANSÃO ECONÔMICA SIMBIÓTICA PULSANTE DOS ESTADOS UNIDOS: MECANISMOS DE INFLUÊNCIA GLOBAL E EXPLORAÇÃO DE RECURSOS ESTRANGEIROS
articles_hidden.authors: Juliano Paniago de Alcântara
articles_hidden.abstract: O estudo propõe o modelo da “Política de Expansão Econômica Simbiótica Pulsante” para descrever a projeção de poder dos Estados Unidos como sequência recorrente de coerção, reestruturação e extração, e o submete a séries temporais, a um painel país×ano e a quatro estudos de caso (Iraque, América Latina, Ucrânia e Golfo Pérsico). Na série 2000–2024, a associação entre gastos militares e renda de investimento direto no exterior é, no longo prazo, absorvida pelo ciclo de renda mundial; em primeira diferença, a precedência dos gastos militares tem o sinal previsto e significância marginal. Em painel país×ano com cerca de oito mil observações, a presença militar americana associa-se a maior comércio e a maior participação americana nas importações do hospedeiro, sem precedência estabelecida. No Golfo, o acesso americano ao mercado iraniano colapsa após a ruptura de 1979 e as sanções subsequentes. Formaliza-se a “pulsação” como construto temporal falseável, distinto do smart power.

articles_hidden.title: Does Carbon Pricing Outperform Command-and-Control Regulation? Firm-Level Evidence from Korea’s Dual Regulatory Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Pyung Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: This study exploits South Korea’s unique dual-policy, in which an emissions trading scheme (ETS) and a command-and-control program (Target Management System, TMS) operate in parallel, to compare carbon pricing with prescriptive regulation at the firm level. Using a difference-in-differences design on firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2022, I find that ETS-regulated firms reduced energy use by 5.8% to 8.8% and carbon emissions by 7.3% to 8.5% relative to TMS firms, while effects on carbon intensity were not robust. These reductions were strongest in the more market-oriented phases of the ETS, which featured allowance auctioning and benchmark-based allocation, pointing to the importance of incentive-based policy design.

articles_hidden.title: Financial Sector Stability and Credit Growth in Nepal:  A Case Study
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: Nepal’s financial system has undergone waves of credit booms, especially in the pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic periods, which raises questions about the health of the banking sector. This paper examines the association between credit growth and banking sector health using secondary data from Nepal Rastra Bank and the International Monetary Fund. The World Bank for fiscal years 2016/17-2023/24. It is found that private sector credit grew at nearly 29 percent in 2016/17 and more than 27 percent in 2020/21, which far exceeded the overall economy’s growth rates. Credit boomed due to large remittance inflows, low real interest rates, and rapid expansion of bank outlets and digital products. Heavy lending to real estate, housing, construction, and import sectors. Consequently, the quality of banks’ assets declined as credit growth slowed down sharply in 2021/22. The non-performing loan ratio, which averaged between 1.2 and 1.8 percent during the boom years, rose to about 2.6 percent in 2022/23 and 3.7 percent in 2023/24. The capital adequacy ratio of banks dipped from 14.5 percent in 2016/17 to 12.8 percent in 2023/24. The study concludes that rapid credit growth, albeit beneficial for a short time, may pose significant financial stability risks if the lending environment worsens and credit becomes concentrated in a few sectors. The paper recommends enhanced risk-based supervision, countercyclical capital buffers, diversification of credit to productive sectors, improved governance, and enhanced capital markets to complement bank lending

articles_hidden.title: A New Approach to Addressing the Rampant Gun Violence in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: 周勇
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper identifies an ammunition ban is the only viable policy to fundamentally address the rampant gun violence. Such a policy would prohibit the private possession and circulation of ammunition and specialized components used in its manufacture, while allowing government-authorized and regulated commercial shooting ranges and hunting outfitters to possess ammunition and conduct lawful shooting activities. It would also permit the private collection of certified top-tier antique ammunition, and permits reloading enthusiasts to reload ammunition in government-authorized and regulated reloading workshops, while providing a service to deliver the reloaded ammunition to their designated commercial shooting ranges or hunting outfitters. The government subsidizes commercial shooting ranges, hunting outfitters, and reloading workshops, enabling them to offer their primary services free of charge to consumers. The new policy also repeals all existing gun control laws and regulations, allowing anyone to freely own and carry firearms, and to freely enter commercial shooting ranges, hunting outfitters, or reloading workshops without background checks. The new policy has a little impact on the firearms industry’s revenue and does not markedly increase the government’s fiscal burden. The new policy would not trigger large-scale illegal manufacturing, smuggling, or black-market trading of ammunition, the frequency of ammunition theft or diversion is extremely low. The new policy would eradicate gun violence while simultaneously protecting citizens' rights to freely own, carry, and use firearms, while also significantly reducing the cost of shooting for the public. As a result, the beneficiaries of the policy would far outnumber those who would be adversely affected, thereby securing support from the majority of the public. Strong public backing would not only smooth the policy’s passage through the House and Senate but also encourage the Supreme Court to reinterpret the Second Amendment, facilitating its implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Social Ecology and Diagnostic Visibility: A Cross-National Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Prevalence in 55 Countries
articles_hidden.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-national variation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence is commonly attributed to differences in diagnostic infrastructure and case ascertainment. We tested whether cultural individualism predicts this variation independently of detection capacity, and whether the result is robust to known limitations of Hofstede's widely used but methodologically dated Individualism Index (IDV). Using 55 countries (GBD 2019 ASD prevalence, World Bank GDP, an author-constructed diagnostic infrastructure index, Hofstede's IDV, and a recently validated individualism-collectivism index built from nationally representative survey data; Akaliyski et al., 2025), we found the raw individualism-ASD correlation is robust to measurement choice (Hofstede: r = 0.702; validated index: r = 0.624; both p < .001, n = 47 non-screening countries with both measures available). However, its apparent independence from detection capacity is not robust: partial correlations controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure remain significant with Hofstede's IDV (partial r = 0.30-0.39) but collapse to non-significance with the validated index (partial r = -0.14 to 0.09, ns), because the validated index correlates far more strongly with diagnostic infrastructure (r = 0.919) than Hofstede's IDV does (r = 0.818). The four mandatory-screening countries (Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan) exceed their IDV-predicted prevalence under both measures, though less dramatically using the validated index (1.57x vs. 2.84x), indicating measurement error in Hofstede's scores inflated the original screening-policy estimate. These findings show the bivariate cultural-prevalence association is genuine, but caution against treating it as evidence independent of detection capacity without testing robustness to cultural measurement choice.

articles_hidden.title: Using Hierarchical Models to Estimate Heterogeneous Effects
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua Alley
articles_hidden.abstract: Conditional theories are ubiquitous in political science, but standard interaction models cannot handle this proliferation of theoretically informed modifiers. This paper describes why, when, and how to use hierarchical models to encompass multiple sources of heterogeneity and regularize estimates. Doing so is simple, and starts with identifying the key sources of heterogeneity and grouping observations accordingly. Next, fit a hierarchical model with two linked regressions, one connecting treatment with the outcome, and another that models the treatment effects with potential sources of heterogeneity and partially pools group estimates. This captures systematic and random variation in heterogeneous effects, encompasses many interactions, and fits commonly used modeling frameworks, but regularization in this model breaks down if there are many small groups. I document these claims with a simulation analysis and reanalysis of a published study.

articles_hidden.title: The Dai People and Their Relationship with Theravada Buddhists in Yunnan: A Profile and Population Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles_hidden.abstract: Focusing on the Dai people of Yunnan, China, this study explores their demographics and Theravada Buddhist practices, examining their influence on neighboring ethnicities. It investigates how Theravada Buddhist temples serve as cornerstones of cultural identity and community cohesion, offering novel insights into the trajectory of Theravada Buddhism within Dai communities. The study employs two innovative approaches to estimate the Theravada Buddhist population in Yunnan and China. Firstly, it leverages data from the Pew Foundation survey conducted in neighboring countries. Secondly, it analyzes temple density in Xishuangbanna and Dehong. Both approaches converge on a figure of roughly 1.1 million Theravada Buddhists residing in Yunnan in 2016. Furthermore, the study estimates the total Theravada Buddhist population in Mainland China to be approximately 1.14 million in 2015 and 1.16 million in 2020. Significantly, the research reveals that the dominance of the Dai people within Theravada Buddhist communities comprised 87.7% of Theravada Buddhists in Yunnan. These findings shed light on the interplay among religious affiliation, temple density, and demographic profile, providing the religious landscape in Dai- dominated regions.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding
articles_hidden.authors: Helena Miton
articles_hidden.abstract: In many domains, human life has undergone dramatic changes—globalized exchanges, complex technological systems, large societies—that would both require and result from rapid cognitive change. In this work, I introduce the Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding Hypothesis, which posits that (1) human cognition is uniquely culturally evolvable because our cognitive processes rely on environmental resources that are largely culturally evolvable, and, as a consequence, (2) it is these specific cultural innovations, called cultural cognitive scaffolds (CCS), that are responsible for much of the rapid, recent changes in human cognition. Importantly, to achieve this effect, these cultural innovations must balance cognitive impact and cultural success. The historical expansion of exchange networks offers an ideal case to illustrate how diverse cultural innovations helped manage the high uncertainty associated with exchanges across larger physical and cultural distances, and a window into how cultural success can be achieved for different cultural innovations. Finally, this framework has important implications for our understanding of the uniquely open-ended character of human culture.

articles_hidden.title: Going Beyond the Method of Description from a Critical Realist View
articles_hidden.authors: Esha dey
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper draws on Margaret Archer's Morphogenetic Framework in a postcolonial political-economic context to examine narrative and biographical interviews from migrant households in a place named Kaliyaganj, West Bengal, in eastern India. It addresses a central methodological challenge in Critical Realism, which is regarding the move from narrative accounts of lived experience to the explanation of underlying causal mechanisms. To operationalise this, I have developed a process-based heuristic, the Trigger–Pathway–Feedback (TPF) process, which allowed me to sensitise the processual framework, followed by two more systematic analyses, which enable tracing disruption and reinforcement across migrant trajectories. By analysing recurring patterns, the study shows that migration instability is not a series of isolated events but a processual outcome of interacting structural constraints and reflexive adjustments. This gives rise to the concept of Reflexivity Traps and the formation of a conceptual subject figure, Flux Migrants.

articles_hidden.title: Evidence and Overreach in the Rubin and Commission Reports
articles_hidden.authors: Geoffrey T Wodtke
articles_hidden.abstract: The report on “The Status of Scholarly Standards in Sociology,” authored by Dr. Ashley Rubin, claims that sociology has been “compromised” by “politicization.” In particular, it claims that “institutionalized political commitments now influence the field’s norms, priorities, and evaluation of scholarship” (pg. 5) to such an extent that “we can no longer call sociology, as a field, a data-driven social science of society” (pg. 107). I agree that some of the phenomena Rubin identifies warrant concern and deserve serious consideration and reflection. However, my assessment of the report concludes that its broad diagnosis far outruns the proffered evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Agreeing in Principle, Disagreeing on Policy: How Beliefs About the Gender Pay Gap Shape Fairness Concerns and Policy Preferences
articles_hidden.authors: Fabian Kalleitner; Jule Adriaans; Ole Brüggemann; Cristóbal Moya; Sandra Bohmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Willingness to reduce gender inequalities partly depends on whether people are aware of them and consider them unfair. Extending scholarship centered on inequality misperceptions, we focus on beliefs about the sources of the gender pay gap (GPG), experimentally varying people's ability to attribute pay disparities to women's choices. Preregistered survey experiments in the U.S. and Germany show that information about larger (vs. smaller) and within-job (vs. overall) GPGs independently increases awareness, raises perceived unfairness, and translates into general support for government action. Initially less-supportive groups (conservatives, men) showed some of the largest increases in general support. Yet, updated beliefs did not increase support for specific policies, such as pay transparency laws or gender quotas. These findings suggest that information campaigns can affect beliefs about GPG's size and sources, but even perceiving GPGs as unfair does not bridge the gap between abstract commitment to gender equality and concrete policy support.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging the Four Exits: Using Free Tools to Empower Senior High School Students
articles_hidden.authors: Kian Anthony R. Dait
articles_hidden.abstract: Senior High School (SHS) in the Philippines was designed to prepare students for four possible exits: Higher Education, Employment, Entrepreneurship, and Middle-Level Skills Development. In practice, however, the college pathway remains more familiar to many students than the other options. This essay examines how existing free and publicly available learning resources can help make the four exits more practical and understandable for students. It considers resources such as the TESDA Online Program, open educational platforms, digital project portfolios, youth programs, entrepreneurship initiatives, and international learning opportunities. The discussion also draws attention to the limits of these resources. Free online learning does not automatically mean equal access, since students still need devices, internet connectivity, time, and guidance. The essay therefore proposes a connected approach in which students first identify a possible direction, determine the skills they need, choose relevant learning resources, apply what they learn, and document appropriate evidence of their work. Schools, teachers, guidance counselors, and local communities can support this process by helping students navigate existing opportunities rather than creating another separate system. The goal is not to encourage students to collect certificates, but to help them make informed choices and develop evidence that supports their next step after SHS.

articles_hidden.title: Human Circuits in Cold War Taiwan: RCA, Labour Governance, and the Developmental State
articles_hidden.authors: Ethan Chiu
articles_hidden.abstract: Industrial development depends on institutions that organise technological learning and govern production. In Cold War Taiwan, these institutions also shaped who could challenge industrial harm. Drawing on field research, interviews, legal records, and institutional histories, this article argues that Taiwan’s developmental capacity was selective. A paired history of RCA Taiwan and the separate RCA-ITRI technology transfer project shows how investment promotion and labour governance privileged officially selected industrial objectives over workers’ independent authority. Public sponsorship equipped semiconductor learning with personnel, facilities, and foreign knowledge. Labour administration, managed representation, and corporate control of hazard information restricted workers’ demands for protection. Pay, housing, and production routines made exposure difficult to avoid, while repeated inspections failed to secure compliance. Missing records, withheld information, and corporate restructuring then obstructed compensation claims. Workers and their supporters challenged these barriers by assembling legal, scientific, and archival resources. Their struggle places labour protection within the history of developmental capacity, alongside the acquisition of technology.

articles_hidden.title: Explaining historical persistence in Germany's electoral geography across 130 years: a cleavage-perspective on continuity in spatial patterns of party support
articles_hidden.authors: Leon Gawenda
articles_hidden.abstract: This article studies the long-run persistence of electoral geographies. Drawing on cleavage theory, I argue that spatial patterns of party support persist where cleavages remain politically salient and the social groups they mobilise stay in place. I evidence this argument for Germany, combining electoral and census data from the German Empire (1890–1912) and reunified Germany (2002–2021) at the municipality, county and electoral-district level. The spatial analyses reveal substantial continuity in the electoral geographies of the mainstream left and right. The analysis traces both to one source, the persistent spatial distribution of Catholics. Christian democrats continued historical strongholds of the Center Party where Catholics stayed concentrated, while the SPD persists as its mirror image in the non-Catholic space. Persistence therefore rests on the stability of the religious geography and cleavage, not on the class cleavage and the economic geography, which has changed markedly. The findings position cleavage-based persistence as a complement to cultural-transmission accounts of historical legacies, locating continuity in the ongoing mobilisation of stable social groups rather than in transmitted attitudes alone.

articles_hidden.title: When the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) is Full of Holes: The Child’s Right to Mental Health in Post-Conflict Sool and Sanaag
articles_hidden.authors: Guleid Ahmed Jama; Marieke Janne Hopman
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper aims to understand the situation of children’s mental health rights in Sool and Sanaag. We apply the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) model (Hopman et al. 2026) to a dataset of 85 research conversation conducted between May and November 2025 (40 children, 45 adults) in the two cities. A key finding from the research is that children’s mental health is not recognised as a distinct rights issue within the socio-legal orders applicable in the research area. Moreover, there is no clearly articulated or enforceable socio-legal obligation (from any socio-legal order) concerning the protection of children’s mental health. Nor do the socio-legal norms seem to establish specific remedial measures for children experiencing mental health difficulties. The language of rights is largely absent from people’s understanding of children’s mental health. Across clan, community, religious, and state normative orders, children are mainly seen through the family framework. The paper suggest that 1) children’s mental health should be seen as a children’s rights, 2) families, particularly mothers, and the community, should be engaged as key entry point for societal change, 3) space should be created for children where they can safely share their experiences and views at all levels, including the family, schools, community and post-conflict peacebuilding initiatives.

articles_hidden.title: Agreement Without Accuracy: Six Systematic Defects an LLM Annotation Study Could Not See in Its Own Reliability Statistics
articles_hidden.authors: Hon-Ren Lin
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers who use large language models as annotators are commonly asked to demonstrate reliability, and test–retest agreement under a fixed seed is the cheapest evidence. We report a study in which it was systematically misleading. Annotating 1,902 student UML class specifications under a fixed snapshot, seed and zero temperature, we compared three prompt configurations, each run twice. A three-stage pipeline appeared to raise answer-level agreement from .647 to .845, with chance-corrected agreement rising for every code and internal consistency satisfied throughout. Comparing per-code prevalence led us to inspect outputs; five systematic defects emerged: an instruction promising an input never supplied (wrong on 64.7% of its flags at κ = .971); a stage receiving element names stripped of the types it was to judge; residual error after repair; enumerated conditions firing outside their scope; and alignment tables stored without half of what they summarised. A sixth lay in our checking procedure: the audit rule we wrote agreed with a blind reading on only 67.5% of cases, and the twenty cases read to confirm it were drawn from its own output. A blind reading of forty random submissions, judged before any output was seen, is the study's only anchored estimate; under it our one reported repair cannot be shown to help. None was surfaced by a reliability statistic; those that altered the model's inputs or rules raised agreement by easing its task. Reliability from repeated runs should be accompanied by prevalence comparisons and a sample read blind, drawn independently of the detector.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding
articles_hidden.authors: Helena Miton
articles_hidden.abstract: In many domains, human life has undergone dramatic changes—globalized exchanges, complex technological systems, large societies—that would both require and result from rapid cognitive change. In this work, I introduce the Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding Hypothesis, which posits that (1) human cognition is uniquely culturally evolvable because our cognitive processes rely on environmental resources that are largely culturally evolvable, and, as a consequence, (2) it is these specific cultural innovations, called cultural cognitive scaffolds (CCS), that are responsible for much of the rapid, recent changes in human cognition. Importantly, to achieve this effect, these cultural innovations must balance cognitive impact and cultural success. The historical expansion of exchange networks offers an ideal case to illustrate how diverse cultural innovations helped manage the high uncertainty associated with exchanges across larger physical and cultural distances, and a window into how cultural success can be achieved for different cultural innovations. Finally, this framework has important implications for our understanding of the uniquely open-ended character of human culture.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying determinants of ecological footprints: A novel application of latent growth curve models (LGM)
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Beltrán-Hernández; Marcelo Lufin
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the determinants of ecological footprint growth trajectories in 112 countries (2004–2017) using latent growth curve models (LGM). Unlike traditional panel methods, LGM captures dynamic trends and country-level heterogeneity in environmental impact over time. The approach integrates economic, institutional, and socio-geographic determinants into a unified causal framework. Results indicate that economic complexity mediates the relationship between economic growth and ecological footprint, promoting technological innovation and sustainable practices. Higher economic complexity also partially offsets environmental impacts from increased fossil fuel consumption. These findings underscore the need for policies fostering innovation, economic diversification, and sustainable urban planning to mitigate environmental degradation.

articles_hidden.title: Determinants of the relationship between growth and CO2 emissions: A novel application utilizing bivariate latent growth curve models (BLGM) across European regions
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Beltrán-Hernández; Marcelo Lufin
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the key determinants shaping the dynamic relationship between economic growth and CO2 emissions in 220 European NUTS2 regions from 2000 to 2021, using a bivariate latent growth curve model (BLGM). Unlike traditional methods, the BLGM framework addresses a critical gap in modeling latent growth processes, variable interactions, and regional heterogeneity, significantly advancing previous methodologies. The approach integrates determinants of regional economic structures, energy consumption patterns, labor market characteristics, and educational attainment. The results highlight the crucial role of financial structure, spatial centrality, and educated development, offering insights for adaptive and effective regional climate and sustainability strategies and emphasizing the need for coordinated policies that integrate technological innovation, territorial planning, labor market diversification, and sustained investment in education.

articles_hidden.title: From Affective Experience to Mechanism: A Critical Realist Case Study Architecture Using Reflexive Thematic Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Varun S. Nair
articles_hidden.abstract:
Studying affective life qualitatively poses a known problem. Burnout, emotional labour, and slow shifts in teacher–class relations are real with measurable effects, yet not directly visible; we infer them from behaviour and language. Interpretation always mediates. How can we claim mechanisms without pretending to observe them?
This paper proposes a case-study architecture using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist frame. It integrates five usually separate elements: a multi-perspectival case design; abduction and retroduction as genuinely different inferences; systematic assessment of rival explanations; a procedure for sorting context from mechanism when they do not separate cleanly; and a hierarchy of claims calibrated to evidence. The combination yields what neither purely interpretive nor purely causal work can: fallible mechanism explanations that take meaning and causation equally seriously.
The argument is specified, not demonstrated. Two computational simulations provide proof of concept. The first distinguishes two known ground-truth mechanisms across 40 synthetic cases, with 80% overall recovery (95% CI [68%, 92%]; 85% and 75% per mechanism). The second adds a third rival—perceptual reconstruction, in which teacher behaviour is unchanged but students report change—and distinguishes all three across 60 synthetic cases, with 95% overall recovery (100%, 100%, 85%). The three-way test uses tighter noise parameters than the two-way, so rates are not directly comparable. Both test only one component and neither substitutes for empirical validation on real classroom data, which remains future work.

articles_hidden.title: Ideology on the U.S. District Courts: Reexamining Presidential and Senatorial Appointment Power
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas O. Howard; David A Hughes; Philip Warncke
articles_hidden.abstract: Unlike U.S. appellate courts, scholars of the American federal judiciary typically lack ideological estimates for district court judges that are derived directly from their behavior. Rather, scholars have primarily relied upon proxy measures based upon the preferences of a  judge's appointing president or those of home-state senators in the event senatorial courtesy is in effect. Nevertheless, senatorial courtesy is a norm, and norms can be broken. It remains an open question  whether home-state senators genuinely constrain the president when it comes to the ideological tenor of appointees to the district courts. We produce novel ideal point estimates for 1,680 U.S.~district court judges appointed between 1913 and 2009 based upon their votes in approximately 100,000 cases, in addition to contextual factors unique to judges and the process by which they were appointed. We map these ideal points into the Judicial Common Space and make them publicly available to American courts scholars. These ideal points differ meaningfully compared to previous proxy measures and improve predictive power in judge voting behavior. Importantly, despite a battery of statistical tests, we find that senatorial courtesy appears to play a minimal role with respect to the revealed preferences of U.S. district court judges compared to the role the president's ideology plays. If senatorial courtesy indeed constrains presidents in the separation of powers game, it is likely on some other, non-ideological dimension.

articles_hidden.title: Orange Cones and Urban Stress: A Population-Based Survey of 1,033 Residents in Greater Montreal
articles_hidden.authors: Emmanuel Stip; Marie Claude Delisle; Shekinah Martino; Charles-Édouard Giguère; Jean Caron
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background: Urban environments expose residents to recurrent low-intensity stressors, including traffic congestion, construction activity, noise, visual overload, disrupted mobility, and unpredictability. In Montreal, orange traffic cones have become an unusually prominent feature of the streetscape and a symbol of construction-related urban disruption. The terms “Montreal syndrome” and “conophobia” were previously proposed as heuristic concepts to explore the psychological significance of this phenomenon. Population-level data, however, have been lacking.
Objective: To examine the frequency of exposure to orange traffic cones among residents of Greater Montreal and characterize associated behavioural responses, emotional reactions, perceived effects on quality of life, and perceptions of their relevance to mental health and well-being.
Methods: A cross-sectional population survey was conducted in collaboration with an independent professional polling company using a general-population panel. A total of 1,033 adults completed a structured questionnaire assessing exposure to orange traffic cones and heavily marked construction zones, behavioural adaptation, emotional reactions, perceived impact on quality of life, and perceived relevance to mental health and well-being. Associations with sociodemographic characteristics were examined using Pearson chi-square tests.
Results: The most unexpected finding concerned perceived mental-health relevance: 56.1% of respondents considered the phenomenon, at least to some extent, a potential mental-health or well-being issue (16.0% “yes, definitely” and 40.1% “yes, to some extent”). Orange-cone exposure was frequent, with 44.1% noticing cones daily or several times per day, and 76.9% reported modifying their behaviour often or sometimes because of cones or heavily marked construction zones. On the multiple-response item, 51.4% of respondents selected slowing down as a precaution, 31.0% changing route or avoiding the area, 27.2% irritation, and 12.3% anxiety or worry. Overall, 67.6% rated the impact on quality of life at the midpoint or higher on a five-point scale. Several sociodemographic associations were observed, particularly for age, employment status, and parental status.
Conclusions: Repeated exposure to orange traffic cones and construction-related disruption is associated with measurable behavioural responses and perceived effects on quality of life in a substantial proportion of Greater Montreal residents. Particularly striking was that more than half of respondents themselves attributed potential mental-health or well-being relevance to the phenomenon. The findings do not establish conophobia as a discrete psychiatric disorder, but provide preliminary population-level support for a measurable dimensional construct of urban environmental stress, ranging from normal adaptation to potentially clinically significant distress.

articles_hidden.title: Bandura meets Feminism: Narratives That Normalize and Legitimize Intimate Partner Violence Through Moral Disengagement Mechanisms
articles_hidden.authors: Kaja Glomb; Martyna Sekulak; Andrew M. Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: This article undertakes a focused, thematic synthesis of interdisciplinary scientific literature to synthesize existing knowledge on how Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) is legitimized and normalized across diverse sociocultural contexts. Our analysis comprehensively covers physical, psychological, sexual, and controlling behaviours. The effect of this review is a novel hierarchical typology of narratives that frame and justify abuse, which are then analysed through the lens of Bandura’s eight mechanisms of moral disengagement (MD). The core argument proposes that the widespread persistence of IPV is sustained by a system of social coherence, not solely individual pathology. Legitimization operates hierarchically: fundamental societal ideologies provide the foundational Moral Justification, enabling the subsequent activation of individual MD strategies (specifically Dehumanization, Attribution of Blame, and Diffusion of Responsibility) by perpetrators. Crucially, the MD framework is extended to show that these narratives are also mobilized by external observers and social institutions to manage moral discomfort and maintain a predictable social order through defensive attribution and the Belief in a Just World. This model demonstrates that effective prevention must target the underlying cultural narratives and the hierarchical moral architecture that actively license these moral exemptions.

articles_hidden.title: The Rise of Competitive Authoritarianism in Israel: The Paradox of Uneven Competitive Authoritarianism
articles_hidden.authors: Oded Haklai; Andrew O'Donohue
articles_hidden.abstract: This article evaluates whether Israel crossed the line into competitive authoritarianism under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. To date, scholars and democracy indices disagree over whether prominent cases of autocratization, such as Israel, have crossed this threshold. One reason for these disagreements, we argue, is that there are varieties of competitive authoritarianism. We theorize that competitive authoritarian regimes vary in the degree to which they are uneven across dimensions of democracy and in their levels of repression and competitiveness. We then evaluate empirically whether Israel meets Levitsky and Way’s definition of competitive authoritarianism. We find that by Levitsky and Way’s criteria, Israel crossed the line into competitive authoritarianism after 2023 under Prime Minister Netanyahu, due to the government’s politicization of state institutions, harassment of independent media, and uneven media access. We further show that Israel’s competitive authoritarian regime is uneven, in that autocratization is more severe in some areas than others, and less repressive than many other competitive authoritarian regimes. This regime unevenness has led to Israel’s misclassification as a democracy thus far.

articles_hidden.title: Disaffording the Pedestrian: When Affordances Are Removed
articles_hidden.authors: orla fahey
articles_hidden.abstract:
Designing for pedestrian road safety is challenging. Designs need to work for a broad and diverse range of pedestrians, while also considering the needs of other vulnerable road users, such as cyclists. Pedestrians are ranked as the most vulnerable in the road user hierarchy and designing for those with protected characteristics is critically important for road safety designers.  One key challenge faced is designing the environment so that safety provisions can align with national and international goals to encourage people to walk or wheel more for health, economic and environmental reasons.

Doctoral research was undertaken to understand whether and how design can improve pedestrian road safety and used key study sites in London to investigate the relationship between safety affordances in public space and pedestrian safety.  One main finding was that often, during a redesign, safety features are removed. The consequences of these changes make it difficult for pedestrians to maintain their safety, particularly those with protected characteristics. Beyond potential physical harm, there are psychosocial impacts: people may avoid a route if they feel it is unsafe or leads to conflict in contested spaces which leaves pedestrians feeling unable to navigate a space confidently. These experiences are not routinely captured within road safety data, which focuses largely on KSI (killed or seriously injured) outcomes.

I have coined this phenomenon of removing an affordance a disaffordance.  The concept comes from over five years of doctoral research into pedestrian road safety in the UK, which focused on pedestrian-only study sites in London that had been redesigned as shared-space zones. Identifying safety affordances and disaffordances in the built environment helps to identify opportunities for broader and more systematic pedestrian participation in the design process. The research also developed GroundMap, a diagnostic approach for identifying and mapping affordances and disaffordances and anticipating the potential consequences of their removal.

At a broader level, the term disaffordance might be extended to identify other environments where the removal of an affordance has significant consequences. While this research applies the concept specifically to pedestrian safety, its wider application across other environments and domains is identified here as a direction for future work.

articles_hidden.title: The Unequal Toll of Loneliness on Electoral Participation: Longitudinal Evidence from The Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Marolla; Arturo Bertero; Cristiano Vezzoni
articles_hidden.abstract:
While declining turnout is often attributed to a lack of social integration, the political relevance of
subjective disconnection has only recently drawn scholarly attention. Using eleven waves of the
LISS panel in the Netherlands, we study how social and emotional loneliness relate to electoral
participation, net of objective social position and objective social integration. Lower self-reported
voting propensity is tied specifically to social loneliness, the perceived lack of a broader community
network, whereas emotional loneliness shows no independent association once the social facet is
accounted for. Separating stable between-person differences from within-person change, we find this
gap concentrated among citizens who are chronically high in social loneliness, while within-person
fluctuations show no association, indicating that the relationship is dispositional rather than situational
and consistent with a link between chronic loneliness and weaker voting habits. Crucially, the gap is
substantially narrower among citizens with greater education, political interest, and partisanship. The
participatory cost of loneliness is therefore unevenly distributed across the electorate, falling hardest
on citizens with the fewest civic resources.

articles_hidden.title: Lessons from History:  Historical WaSH Programmes and the Decline of Summer Diarrhoeal Mortality
articles_hidden.authors: Hannaliis Jaadla; Romola Davenport
articles_hidden.abstract: Using high-frequency historical data on mortality (weekly) and temperature (daily), we examine the puzzle of the late decline of infant diarrhoeal mortality in British and Irish cities. While mortality from other faecal–oral diseases began falling before the 1880s alongside investments in urban water supply and waste disposal, large summer epidemics of infant diarrhoea persisted until the 1910s. We analyse a large panel of towns spanning the period 1893–1930 to characterise the temperature-infant mortality nexus and to identify turning points in this relationship. Two-way fixed effects models reveal the roles of flush toilet provision, reductions in fly populations, and infant feeding practices in the decline of infant diarrhoeal mortality. Our findings indicate that preventing lethal summer epidemics among young children required coordinated improvements in both domestic and environmental hygiene.  We suggest that these findings provide historical support for contemporary calls for ‘transformative WaSH’ programmes.

articles_hidden.title: Monetary Policy Transmission in Nepal: A Study of How Central Bank Policy Rates Affect Bank Lending and Economic Activity
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract:
Monetary policy transmission, the mechanism through which the monetary policy of the central bank impacts bank lending rates and, by extension, the broader economy, is of great interest to policymakers. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the monetary policy transmission mechanism in the Nepalese context. It focuses on the interest rate pass-through channels and associated frictions in the Nepalese monetary policy framework. It uses the information published by NRB, the central bank of Nepal, as well as scholarly research and reports on the topic to perform the study. It highlights that the interest rate pass-through in Nepal is partial and delayed and discusses the reason why monetary policy transmissions in Nepal work as they do.
The paper starts with an introduction to the topic of monetary policy transmission. Then, it proceeds to discuss research questions and objectives, theoretical background, and methodological background. Finally, it presents data analysis and discusses the findings to reach final conclusions and recommendations.

articles_hidden.title: External Debt Sustainability in Nepal: A Case Study Based on Nepal Rastra Bank, IMF, and World Bank Data
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: External debt sustainability is a matter of great concern for many developing countries like Nepal since a part of the borrowed money is regarded as the liability that threatens to criticize the value of their local currency and increases their fiscal burden. This paper performs an analysis of the external debt indicators of Nepal and the risk of a debt distress using the information provided by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. According to the results, the total public debt in Nepal is expected to reach about Rs 2.97 trillion (USD 19.21 billion) by the end of fiscal year 2025/26, which is equivalent to 45.07 percent of GDP, as compared to 43.79 percent in the previous year. The external debt increased to about 25.3 percent of GDP from 20.6 percent, and that of domestic one remained at about 22-23 percent. Nepal still belongs to the countries with low risk of experiencing a debt distress, according to the joint World Bank-IMF Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA). However, the study highlights several vulnerabilities in the external debt of Nepal as the present value of the external debt-to-exports ratio exceeds the indicative threshold in the export shock scenario. The Nepali rupee has depreciated by around Rs 8 against the US dollar in the first seven months of FY2025/26, adding Rs 92.96 billion to the external debt of the country. Only around one-third of the capital budget has been spent, which implies that the borrowed money is used for sustaining the recurrent expenditure rather than capital spending. The paper concludes that Nepal’s debt is sustainable in the near term. However, the increasing vulnerabilities in the form of currency depreciation, inadequate revenue mobilization efforts and low efficiency utilization of the borrowed funds should be responded to in order to address long-term sustainability.

articles_hidden.title: Turning Ambition into Action: Lessons from the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan
articles_hidden.authors: Alessia Aspide; Lorenzo Mascioli; Gabriele Beretta; Camilla Locatelli
articles_hidden.abstract: The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is the primary financial instrument of the EU’s ambitious pandemic response initiative, NextGenerationEU (NGEU). This report examines Italy’s capacity to implement its ambitious National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) effectively. It opens with a comparative analysis of the NRRPs of the four largest EU economies: Germany, France, Italy, and Spain. Focusing then on Italy, the largest recipient, the report explores how state capacity shapes the implementation of ambitious reforms and investments, emphasizing the challenges of translating NGEU’s transformative goals into tangible outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Issues and Challenges of Poverty and International Labor Migration in Nepal
articles_hidden.authors: Shyam Kumar Karki
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper aims to discuss the opportunity and challenges of the foreign labor market for Nepalese workers and Nepal’s government policy. The study was carried out in the form of a qualitative research method, where secondary data were used. The collected data were analyzed using the content analysis method after a close reading of the sources. This paper discussed the current situation of government policy, manpower agencies, problems of migrant workers, and the way of using the remittance. This research found that the government policy is less effective, and manpower agencies are not following the government rules and regulations. Since the last two decades, remittances have been a significant contributor to the Nepalese economy. Many scholars argued that remittance helps to reduce the country’s poverty rates. However, Nepalese workers face numerous problems in the home country and destination countries. Migrant workers are being charged high service charges and misguided by the local agent and manpower agencies in the home country Nepal. They face problems in destination countries such as low remuneration, sexual abuse, and risky job environment. Most of the remittances are using daily expenses such as purchasing foods. This paper explores these vulnerabilities of migrant workers and suggests stakeholder interventions to make safer migration and sustainably use a remittance.

articles_hidden.title: Women's Land Rights in India: A Learning Document
articles_hidden.authors: ISST; Jahnvi Andharia; Benu Verma; Saee Pawar; Ashmeet Kaur; Kritika Goel
articles_hidden.abstract: Womanity has decided to strategically accelerate gender equality and economic empowerment of women in India by developing and supporting sustainable models that look at women's land rights pathways that can be adapted and scaled across the country. The program focuses on increasing land literacy, women’s land ownership and long-term land access to secure livelihoods for 50,000 women at the community level. Womanity’s Theory of Change (ToC) Document outlines the rationale and the pathway to advance gender equality and economic empowerment of women through sustainable models and strategic interventions. Womanity has outlined three phases to reach 50,000 women – Build, Enhance and Scale. In the Build phase, it seeks to identify challenges, evolve prototype sustainable models, measure effectiveness and impact, support implements, invest in research, and develop a comprehensive evidence plan. This learning document prepared by ISST contributes to the efforts of the Build phase of Womanity. The objective of this document is to capture the learnings of the various partner organizations, key members of the Womanity team, and the other stakeholders (referred as the Womanity ecosystem in India) in the first 18 months of the project period, as well as their future learning needs. Through a thorough analysis of the data collected over six months, a learning framework was expected to map all possible needs for building knowledge and strengthening capacities within the Womanity ecosystem to effectively address various WLR issues

articles_hidden.title: Long-Term Sequences of State-Building and Violent Conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander De Juan
articles_hidden.abstract: A large body of research demonstrates that state capacity is an important correlate of intrastate conflict. However, similar levels of present-day state capacity can result from different historical trajectories of state-building. I argue that specific sequences of state-building can shape the risk of violent conflict in the long run: geographical obstacles can isolate territories from state-building processes for extended periods, strengthening non-state institutions. The risk of violence increases once the state has accumulated sufficient capabilities to close this state-building gap. The extension of authority into peripheral territories triggers resistance from among local elites that mobilize their constituencies against the central state. I exploit exogenous variation in early state-penetration in Nepal to investigate this argument. Areas located below the Himalayan foothills were heavily Malaria-infested preventing the state from establishing meaningful presence until the implementation of a malaria eradication program in the 1950/60s. I make use of this specificity in Regression Discontinuity (RD) estimations. The findings lend support to the primary arguments of the paper and underscore the role of long-term sequences of development.

articles_hidden.title: Rounding and the bill-size gradient in tipping
articles_hidden.authors: Toby Qin; Vrund Gurjar
articles_hidden.abstract: Restaurant tip percentages often decline as bills increase. Rounding is one proposed explanation because a fixed upward adjustment adds more to the tip percentage on a small bill. We examine how much of the observed decline can be explained by adjustments of up to one dollar. We analyzed 22,446 checks with positive recorded tips, no automatic gratuity and bills of $10–$200 from three North Carolina restaurant outlets. For checks with a whole-dollar tip or reconstructed final payment, we allowed the pre-rounding tip to fall anywhere from one dollar below the recorded amount to the recorded amount, with a minimum of zero. We calculated the smallest and largest bill-size coefficients across these possible amounts, controlling for outlet, month, guest count, opening hour and weekday. Bootstrap checks resampled dates, weeks and servers. Each scheme used 999 draws, with the rounding bounds recalculated for each resampled dataset. Tip percentages fell by 4.29 points per bill doubling. Even the adjustments that most reduce this decline leave a coefficient of −1.62 points, which remains negative across all three bootstrap checks. Five-dollar rounding or restricting bills to $30–$200 allows the fitted decline to disappear. Upward dollar rounding cannot fully explain the negative gradient in the primary sample. Larger rounding increments and the exclusion of small bills produce ranges containing zero.
